X_k is connected, so the only such decomposition is the trivial one and H^0(X_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^n)=\mathbb Z/\ell^n. Passing to the limits defining \ell-adic cohomology:
  H^0(X_k,\Lambda)=(\varprojlim_n \mathbb Z/\ell^n)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell=\mathbb Z_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\Lambda=\Lambda,
  H^0(X_k,\bar\Lambda)=\mathbb Z_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\bar\Lambda=\bar\Lambda,
and the natural map H^0(X_k,\Lambda)\otimes_\Lambda\bar\Lambda\to H^0(X_k,\bar\Lambda) is the isomorphism \lambda\otimes c\mapsto c\lambda.

STEP 4 (both endomorphism algebras are the coefficient field). Steps 2 and 3 give canonical algebra isomorphisms
  End_{Perv(X_k,\Lambda)}(\Lambda[d])\cong\Lambda, \qquad End_{Perv(X_k,\bar\Lambda)}(\bar\Lambda[d])\cong\bar\Lambda,
both inverse to \lambda\mapsto\lambda\cdot\mathrm{id}. In particular each is a 1-dimensional vector space over its coefficient field with basis \{\mathrm{id}\}; equivalently \Lambda[d] and \bar\Lambda[d] are absolutely simple objects of the respective perverse categories. This proves the second assertion of the lemma.

STEP 5 (the scalar-extension map is an isomorphism of \bar\Lambda-algebras). The t-exact additive functor -\otimes_\Lambda\bar\Lambda induces, for P\in Perv(X_k,\Lambda), a natural map
  \beta_P:\ End_{Perv(X_k,\Lambda)}(P)\otimes_\Lambda\bar\Lambda \longrightarrow End_{Perv(X_k,\bar\Lambda)}(P\otimes\bar\Lambda), \qquad u\otimes c\longmapsto c\cdot(u\otimes\mathrm{id}),
which is \bar\Lambda-linear by construction and multiplicative because (u\circ v)\otimes\mathrm{id}=(u\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(v\otimes\mathrm{id}) and \mathrm{id}\otimes\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}; i.e. \beta_P is a unital \bar\Lambda-algebra homomorphism. For P=\Lambda[d] we have P\otimes\bar\Lambda=\bar\Lambda[d], and by Step 4 the source is \Lambda\otimes_\Lambda\bar\Lambda\cong\bar\Lambda and the target is \bar\Lambda, both 1-dimensional over \bar\Lambda. Since \beta(1\otimes 1)=\mathrm{id}\neq 0, \beta is a nonzero \bar\Lambda-linear map between 1-dimensional \bar\Lambda-vector spaces, hence an isomorphism of vector spaces, and being a unital algebra homomorphism it is an isomorphism of \bar\Lambda-algebras. This proves the first assertion. (Concretely, by naturality of the adjunction isomorphisms and of the base-change morphism of Step 2, \beta is carried by \theta_\Lambda\otimes\mathrm{id} and \theta_{\bar\Lambda} to the base-change isomorphism H^0(X_k,\Lambda)\otimes_\Lambda\bar\Lambda\xrightarrow{\sim}H^0(X_k,\bar\Lambda) of Step 3.)

STEP 6 (the canonical arithmetic Frobenius structure induces the identity on End). Let F_X:X_k\to X_k be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius and \varphi:F_X^*\bar\Lambda[d]\xrightarrow{\sim}\bar\Lambda[d] the canonical arithmetic Frobenius structure on \bar\Lambda[d] (coming from the canonical identification F_X^*\bar\Lambda=\bar\Lambda of constant sheaves: the inverse image of a constant sheaf of rings is the constant sheaf of rings). As in lemma_39 — whose defining formula for the induced automorphism on Ext makes sense verbatim with \bar\Lambda in place of \mathbb Q_\ell — \varphi induces
  F_\varphi:\ End_{\bar D}(\bar\Lambda[d])\to End_{\bar D}(\bar\Lambda[d]), \qquad u\longmapsto \varphi\circ F_X^*(u)\circ\varphi^{-1}.
We claim F_\varphi is \bar\Lambda-linear. For a morphism of schemes f, f^*M=f^{-1}M\otimes_{f^{-1}\bar\Lambda}\bar\Lambda, and under the canonical identification f^{-1}\bar\Lambda=\bar\Lambda one has f^{-1}(\lambda_M)=\lambda_{f^{-1}M} for every \lambda\in\bar\Lambda; hence f^*(\lambda\cdot u)=\lambda\cdot f^*(u) on Hom groups, i.e. F_X^* is a \bar\Lambda-linear functor. Composition with the fixed isomorphisms \varphi,\varphi^{-1} is likewise \bar\Lambda-linear. So F_\varphi is a \bar\Lambda-linear automorphism. It fixes the identity morphism: F_\varphi(\mathrm{id})=\varphi\circ\mathrm{id}\circ\varphi^{-1}=\mathrm{id}, since any functor sends identity morphisms to identity morphisms. By Step 1, End_{\bar D}(\bar\Lambda[d])=End_{Perv(X_k,\bar\Lambda)}(\bar\Lambda[d]), which by Step 4 is the 1-dimensional space \bar\Lambda\cdot\mathrm{id}. A \bar\Lambda-linear automorphism of a 1-dimensional space that fixes a nonzero vector is the identity; therefore F_\varphi=\mathrm{id} on End_{Perv(X_k,\bar\Lambda)}(\bar\Lambda[d]). This proves the third assertion (and the identical argument with \Lambda in place of \bar\Lambda shows the induced automorphism on End_{Perv(X_k,\Lambda)}(\Lambda[d])\cong\Lambda is also the identity).

STEP 7 (consistency check). Under \theta_{\bar\Lambda}, the automorphism F_\varphi corresponds to the automorphism of H^0(X_k,\bar\Lambda)=\Gamma(X_k,\bar\Lambda) induced by the Frobenius structure R\mathcal Hom(\varphi^{-1},\varphi)\circ c on R\mathcal Hom(\bar\Lambda[d],\bar\Lambda[d])\cong\bar\Lambda, i.e. to the canonical structure on the constant sheaf. A global section of a constant sheaf on a connected space is a constant function, and the structure map is the identity on the value \bar\Lambda, so that automorphism is the identity — in agreement with Step 6.

All three assertions of the lemma are established: the scalar-extension map is an isomorphism of \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell-algebras, both endomorphism algebras are canonically isomorphic to their coefficient fields (\mathbb Q_\ell and \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell respectively, via \lambda\mapsto\lambda\,\mathrm{id}), and the canonical arithmetic Frobenius structure on \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d] induces the identity on End_{Perv(X_k,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)}(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d]).

lemma_55_2.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let X be a smooth projective variety over F_q, let k=overline{F}_q, and let ell != p. Let O be an orbit of the q-power arithmetic Frobenius on the geometric connected components of X_k, of length r. All components in O have the same dimension d. Let K_O be the direct summand of IC_X supported on O, namely K_O = direct sum_{C in O} Q_ell[d] extended by zero to X_k, with the induced arithmetic Frobenius structure. Choose C_0 in O and let L_0 be Q_ell_bar[d] extended by zero to X_k. After scalar extension to Q_ell_bar, K_O is isomorphic in Perv(X_k,Q_ell_bar) to direct sum_{j=0}^{r-1} F_X^{j*}L_0; the Q_ell_bar-vector space Hom_{Perv(X_k,Q_ell_bar)}(L_0,K_O) is one-dimensional; and the r-th power of arithmetic Frobenius acts on this Hom space as the identity.
lemma_55_2.proof:
We write $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $X_k=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$, and $F=F_X=(\mathrm{id}_X,\sigma):X_k\to X_k$ for the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius, where $\sigma(a)=a^q$. Let $\pi_0=\{C_1,\dots,C_m\}$ be the set of geometric connected components of $X_k$, let $O=\{C_0,C_1',\dots\}$ be the given orbit of length $r$ (we fix a choice $C_0\in O$), and let $i_C:C\hookrightarrow X_k$ denote the immersion of a component.

**Step 1. Basic properties of the components and of $F$.** Since $X$ is projective over $\mathbb F_q$, $X_k$ is of finite type over $k$, hence noetherian; therefore $\pi_0$ is finite and every component $C\in\pi_0$ is open *and* closed in $X_k$, and $X_k=\bigsqcup_{C\in\pi_0}C$ as a scheme (finite disjoint union). Each $C$ is smooth over $k$ (open subscheme of the smooth $X_k$) and projective over $k$ (closed subscheme of the projective $X_k$); write $d_C=\dim C$.

The map $F$ is an automorphism of the *scheme* $X_k$, with inverse $\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma^{-1}$. Hence $F$ permutes $\pi_0$ bijectively, and for each $C$ the restriction $F|_{F^{-1}(C)}:F^{-1}(C)\xrightarrow{\sim}C$ is an isomorphism of schemes; equivalently $F|_C:C\xrightarrow{\sim}F(C)$ is an isomorphism of schemes. Dimension is invariant under isomorphism of schemes, so $d_{F(C)}=d_C$. By induction along the orbit, **all components of $O$ have the same dimension**; we denote this common value by $d$.

Also, for every $j\ge 0$ the power $F^j$ is a scheme automorphism, so $F^{j*}$ is a $t$-exact auto-equivalence of $D^b_c(X_k,-)$ (pullback along an isomorphism equals $f_!=f_*$, which preserves the perverse $t$-structure), and for $A$ on $C$ one has the canonical identification $F^{j*}i_{C*}A=i_{F^{-j}(C)*}(F^j|_{F^{-j}(C)})^*A$.

**Step 2. The standard Frobenius structure on a constant sheaf is the identity.** Let $\mathrm{pr}_2:X_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ be the second projection and $\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}=\mathrm{pr}_2^{-1}\mathbb Q_\ell$ the constant sheaf. Since $\mathrm{pr}_2\circ F=\sigma\circ\mathrm{pr}_2$, there is a canonical isomorphism $F^*\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}\cong \mathrm{pr}_2^*\sigma^*\mathbb Q_{\ell,\operatorname{Spec}k}\cong \mathrm{pr}_2^*\mathbb Q_{\ell,\operatorname{Spec}k}=\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}$: the middle map is the canonical identification of the pullback of a *constant* sheaf along any morphism with the constant sheaf (it is the identity on sections, hence the identity on every geometric stalk). The "standard arithmetic Frobenius structure" $\psi:F^*\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}$ referred to in lemma_39 is precisely this identification. Because it is the identity on stalks, all its iterates $\psi^{(j)}:F^{j*}\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}\to\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}$ (composites of identity maps) are again the identity under the canonical identification $F^{j*}\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}=\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}$; the same holds verbatim with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ replaced by $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

**Step 3. The summand $K_O$ and its Frobenius structure.** By lemma_1, $\mathrm{IC}_X\cong\bigoplus_{C\in\pi_0}\mathbb Q_\ell[d_C]_C$ in $\mathrm{Perv}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, where $\mathbb Q_\ell[d_C]_C:=i_{C*}\mathbb Q_\ell[d_C]$, and the canonical arithmetic Frobenius structure $\varphi_{\mathrm{IC}}:F^*\mathrm{IC}_X\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{IC}_X$ permutes these summands according to the action of $F$ on $\pi_0$. Concretely, using Step 1 and Step 2,
$$F^*\Big(\bigoplus_{C\in\pi_0}\mathbb Q_\ell[d_C]_C\Big)=\bigoplus_{C\in\pi_0}\mathbb Q_\ell[d_{F(C)}]_{F^{-1}(C)},$$
and $\varphi_{\mathrm{IC}}$ is, under the displayed identification, the direct sum over $C$ of the identity maps $\mathbb Q_\ell[d_{F(C)}]_{F^{-1}(C)}\to\mathbb Q_\ell[d_{F(C)}]_{F^{-1}(C)}$ (this can be checked on geometric stalks: at $\bar x\in C'$ the map is the canonical Frobenius identification of the stalk $\mathbb Q_\ell$ with itself, which is the identity by Step 2).

Since $O\subset\pi_0$ is $F$-stable and $d_C=d$ for all $C\in O$, the partial sum
$$K_O:=\bigoplus_{C\in O}\mathbb Q_\ell[d]_C$$
is a direct summand of $\mathrm{IC}_X$ stable under $\varphi_{\mathrm{IC}}$; denote by $\varphi_O:F^*K_O\xrightarrow{\sim}K_O$ the induced structure. By the description above, $\varphi_O$ permutes the summands by $C\mapsto F^{-1}(C)$ with identity maps on the constant sheaves; consequently for every $j\ge0$, under the canonical identifications $F^{j*}\mathbb Q_\ell[d]_C=\mathbb Q_\ell[d]_{F^{-j}(C)}$,
$$\varphi_O^{(j)}:F^{j*}K_O=\bigoplus_{C\in O}\mathbb Q_\ell[d]_{F^{-j}(C)}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }K_O=\bigoplus_{C\in O}\mathbb Q_\ell[d]_C$$
is the direct sum of the identity maps. In particular, since $F^r$ fixes every element of $O$ (as $F^r(C_0)=C_0$ implies $F^r(C_j)=C_j$), we have
$$\varphi_O^{(r)}=\mathrm{id}_{K_O}\ \ \text{under the canonical identification }F^{r*}K_O\cong K_O. \tag{3.1}$$

**Step 4. Scalar extension and the decomposition into Frobenius translates.** Enumerate the orbit by $C_j:=F^{j}(C_0)$, $j\in\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z$. Put $L_C:=i_{C*}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d]$ for $C\in O$ and $L_0:=L_{C_0}=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d]$ extended by zero from $C_0$. Extending scalars, $K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z/r}L_{C_j}$. Since $F^{j*}L_{C_0}=L_{F^{-j}(C_0)}=L_{C_{-j}}$ and $j\mapsto -j$ is a bijection of $\mathbb Z/r$, the assignment $F^{j*}L_0\mapsto L_{C_{-j}}$ gives an isomorphism in $\mathrm{Perv}(X_k,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$
$$\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}F^{j*}L_0\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. \tag{4.1}$$
(Each $F^{j*}L_0$ is perverse because $F^j$ is a scheme automorphism, hence $t$-exact.) This proves the first claim.

**Step 5. $\mathrm{Hom}(L_0,K_O)$ is one-dimensional.** First, all objects involved are perverse: $C$ is smooth of pure dimension $d$ over the algebraically closed field $k$, so $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d]$ is perverse on $C$ by lemma_11; and because $X_k=\bigsqcup_{C\in\pi_0}C$ is a disjoint union of open-and-closed subschemes, the decomposition of the derived category $D^b_c(X_k,-)\simeq\bigoplus_{C\in\pi_0}D^b_c(C,-)$ identifies the perverse $t$-structure on $X_k$ with the product $t$-structure (perversity is the support/cosupport dimension condition, which is checked componentwise). Hence $i_{C*}$ is $t$-exact and fully faithful, $\mathrm{Perv}(X_k,-)\simeq\bigoplus_{C}\mathrm{Perv}(C,-)$, and for perverse objects $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Perv}}=\mathrm{Hom}_{D^b_c}$ (the heart is a full subcategory). Therefore
$$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Perv}(X_k,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)}(L_0,\,K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z/r}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Perv}(C_j,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)}\big(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d],\,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d]\big)\ \ \text{restricted to the }C_0\text{-factor},$$
more precisely $\mathrm{Hom}(L_0,L_{C_j})=0$ for $j\ne0$ (morphisms between objects living in different factors of a direct sum of categories vanish) and $\mathrm{Hom}(L_0,L_{C_0})\cong\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{Perv}(C_0,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)}(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d])$ by fully faithfulness.

It remains to compute this endomorphism algebra. By lemma_27 applied to $X$ and the orbit $O$ of length $r$, the component $C_0$ is the base change to $k$ of a smooth projective *geometrically connected* variety $Y_0$ over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$, and $F^r|_{C_0}$ is the $q^r$-power arithmetic Frobenius of $Y_0$. Applying lemma_56 to $Y_0/\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (whose dimension is $d$) gives canonical isomorphisms
$$\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{Perv}((Y_0)_k,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)}(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d])\cong\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.$$
Since $(Y_0)_k=C_0$, we obtain $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Perv}(X_k,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)}(L_0,K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\cong\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, a one-dimensional $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-vector space. A generator is the inclusion of the $C_0$-summand
$$\iota:L_0\hookrightarrow K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell,$$
which corresponds to $1\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=\mathrm{End}(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d]_{C_0})$. This proves the second claim.

**Step 6. The action of $F^r$ on the Hom space.** Both $L_0$ and $K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ carry arithmetic Frobenius structures: $\lambda_0:=\psi^{(r)}:F^{r*}L_0\xrightarrow{\sim}L_0$ (the $r$-fold iterate of the standard structure of the constant sheaf, extended by zero; the identity under the canonical identification, by Step 2) and $\varphi_O^{(r)}:F^{r*}(K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. By the formula of lemma_39 for the automorphism induced on $\mathrm{Ext}^0=\mathrm{Hom}$ (which is stable under the scalar extension $\mathbb Q_\ell\to\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, as scalar extension is functorial and commutes with pullback), $F^r$ acts on $\mathcal H:=\mathrm{Hom}(L_0,K_O\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$ by
$$T(u)=\varphi_O^{(r)}\circ F^{r*}(u)\circ\lambda_0^{-1},\qquad u\in\mathcal H.$$
We evaluate $T$ on the generator $\iota$. Since $F^r$ fixes each $C_j$ with $j\in\mathbb Z/r$, the canonical identifications give $F^{r*}L_{C_j}=L_{C_j}$, and $F^{r*}(\iota):F^{r*}L_0\to\bigoplus_{j}F^{r*}L_{C_j}$ is, under these identifications, again the inclusion of the $C_0$-summand, because $\iota$ is the identity map on the constant sheaf $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[d]$ over $C_0$ and zero on the other components, and pullback along $F^r$ together with the canonical identification of Step 2 leaves the identity map of a constant sheaf unchanged. Composing with $\varphi_O^{(r)}$, which is the identity on each summand by (3.1), and with $\lambda_0^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$, we obtain
$$T(\iota)=\varphi_O^{(r)}\circ F^{r*}(\iota)\circ\lambda_0^{-1}=\iota.$$
As $\mathcal H=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\cdot\iota$ is one-dimensional and $T$ is $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linear with $T(\iota)=\iota$, $T$ is the identity automorphism of $\mathcal H$.

**Step 7. Conclusion.** Steps 1–6 establish exactly the three assertions of the lemma: (i) all components in $O$ have the common dimension $d$; (ii) after scalar extension to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ there is an isomorphism $K_O\cong\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}F^{j*}L_0$ in $\mathrm{Perv}(X_k,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$ (equation (4.1)); (iii) $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Perv}(X_k,\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)}(L_0,K_O)$ is one-dimensional (Step 5); and (iv) the $r$-th power of arithmetic Frobenius acts on it as the identity (Step 6). $\blacksquare$

lemma_60.statement: Let \ell be a prime, let V be a nonzero finite-dimensional \mathbb{Q}_\ell-vector space, and let T\in\mathrm{GL}(V). Write the characteristic polynomial as \chi_T(t)=\prod_f f(t)^{e_f}, the product over the monic irreducible polynomials f\in\mathbb{Q}_\ell[t] dividing it, and for each such f put V[f]:=\ker f(T) and V[f^{\infty}]:=\bigcup_{N\ge1}\ker f(T)^N. Then the following are equivalent: (i) T is semisimple; (ii) the minimal polynomial \mu_T of T is squarefree in \mathbb{Q}_\ell[t]; (iii) V[f]\cap f(T)V=0 for every f\mid\chi_T; (iv) the inclusion V[f]\hookrightarrow V induces an isomorphism V[f]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }V/f(T)V for every f\mid\chi_T; (v) V=\bigoplus_{f\mid\chi_T}V[f]; (vi) V[f^{\infty}]=V[f] for every f\mid\chi_T. Moreover, regarding V as a module over R:=\mathbb{Q}_\ell[t^{\pm1}] via t\cdot v=T(v), the ring R is a principal ideal domain and for each irreducible f\in R there are canonical R-module isomorphisms \mathrm{Hom}_R(R/(f),V)\cong V[f] and \mathrm{Ext}^1_R(R/(f),V)\cong V/f(T)V under which the map in (iv) is the natural one; one always has \dim V[f]=\dim V/f(T)V, so (iii) and (iv) are equivalent to each other and to injectivity (equivalently surjectivity) of that single map, and no dimension count can prove semisimplicity. Finally, T is semisimple on V if and only if T is semisimple on each primary piece V[f^{\infty}]. The proof must be pure linear algebra over \mathbb{Q}_\ell and must not cite any external theorem.
lemma_60.proof:
Proof (pure linear algebra over $K:=\mathbb{Q}_\ell$; every ingredient is proved below, nothing external is cited). Let $n:=\dim_K V\ge 1$ and fix a $K$-basis, so $T$ is given by a matrix $A\in M_n(K)$.

=== 0. Conventions and first formalities ===
$V$ is a $K[t]$-module via $t\cdot v=T(v)$; $T$-stable $K$-subspaces are exactly the $K[t]$-submodules, and $T$-simple subspaces are exactly the simple submodules. The set $\operatorname{Ann}(V):=\{p\in K[t]:p(T)=0\}$ is a nonzero ideal: $\operatorname{id},T,\dots,T^{n^2}$ are $n^2+1$ elements of the $n^2$-dimensional space $\operatorname{End}_K(V)$, hence linearly dependent. Let $\mu_T$ be its monic generator; then $p(T)=0\iff \mu_T\mid p$ (divide $p$ by $\mu_T$ inside the ideal $\operatorname{Ann}(V)$, using that $\operatorname{Ann}(V)$ is an ideal).
Since $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $\chi_T(0)=\det(0I-A)=(-1)^n\det T\neq 0$; hence no monic irreducible factor $f$ of $\chi_T$ is divisible by $t$, i.e. $f(0)\neq 0$. The same will hold for $\mu_T$ once $\mu_T\mid\chi_T$ is established (\S 2).

=== 1. $K[t]$ is a Euclidean domain; a coprime-idempotent lemma ===
Division algorithm: given $p,g\in K[t]$, $g\ne0$, with $\deg p=m$, $\deg g=r$, induct on $m$. If $m<r$ take $q=0$. Otherwise, with leading terms $a t^m$ and $b t^r$, $p-(a/b)t^{m-r}g$ has degree $<m$, so equals $b'g+q'g$ with $\deg q'<r$ by induction; hence $p=(b'+(a/b)t^{m-r})g+q'$. Consequently every ideal $I\ne 0$ is principal: take $0\ne g\in I$ of least degree; for $p\in I$, $p=qg+r$ with $r\in I$, $\deg r<\deg g$, so $r=0$.
It follows that coprime $a,b\in K[t]$ satisfy Bezout's identity $\alpha a+\beta b=1$ (the ideal $(a,b)$ is principal, generated by a greatest common divisor, which is a unit up to scalar).

Lemma 1. Let $h_1,\dots,h_r\in K[t]$ be pairwise coprime, $h=\prod_i h_i$, and suppose $h(T)=0$ on $V$. Then $V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r\ker h_i(T)$.
Proof. For each $i$ choose, by repeated Bezout, $\varepsilon_i\in K[t]$ with $\varepsilon_i\equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ h_i)$ and $\varepsilon_i\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ h_j)$ for $j\ne i$ (take $\varepsilon_i=\beta_i\prod_{j\ne i}h_j$ with $\alpha_i h_i+\beta_i\prod_{j\ne i}h_j=1$). Then $\sum_i\varepsilon_i-1$ is divisible by each $h_i$, hence by $h$, so $\sum_i\varepsilon_i(T)=\mathrm{id}_V$; and $\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j$ is divisible by $h$ for $i\ne j$, so $E_i:=\varepsilon_i(T)$ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with sum $\mathrm{id}$. Hence $V=\bigoplus_i \mathrm{im}\,E_i$. Now $h_i\varepsilon_i$ is divisible by $h$, so $h_i(T)E_i=0$, i.e. $\mathrm{im}\,E_i\subseteq\ker h_i(T)$; conversely if $h_i(T)v=0$ then $(\varepsilon_i-1)(T)v=0$ because $\varepsilon_i-1$ is a multiple of $h_i$, so $v=E_iv\in\mathrm{im}\,E_i$. Thus $\mathrm{im}\,E_i=\ker h_i(T)$. $\square$

=== 2. Cayley--Hamilton ===
Let $M=tI_n-A\in M_n(K[t])$ and let $\operatorname{adj}(M)$ be the adjugate, $\operatorname{adj}(M)_{jk}=(-1)^{j+k}\det M(\text{row }k,\text{col }j)$. Then $(M\operatorname{adj}M)_{ik}=\sum_j M_{ij}(-1)^{j+k}\det M(j|k)$ equals $\det M$ for $i=k$ (Laplace expansion along row $i$) and $0$ for $i\ne k$ (Laplace expansion along row $k$ of the matrix whose row $k$ is replaced by row $i$, which has two equal rows). So $M\operatorname{adj}M=\chi_T(t)I_n$ with $\chi_T(t)=\det(tI_n-A)=t^n+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jt^j$. Write $\operatorname{adj}(M)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}t^kB_k$, $B_k\in M_n(K)$, and set $B_{-1}=B_n=0$. From $(tI-A)\sum_k t^kB_k=\sum_k t^{k+1}B_k-\sum_k t^kAB_k$ and comparison of the coefficient of $t^j$:
$j=n$: $B_{n-1}=I_n$; \quad $0\le j\le n-1$: $B_{j-1}-AB_j=c_jI_n$.
Left-multiplying the second identity by $A^j$ gives $A^jB_{j-1}-A^{j+1}B_j=c_jA^j$; summing $j=0,\dots,n-1$ telescopes the left side to $-A^nB_{n-1}=-A^n$. Hence $A^n+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jA^j=0$, i.e. $\chi_T(T)=0$. In particular $\mu_T\mid\chi_T$, so every irreducible factor of $\mu_T$ occurs among $\{f:f\mid\chi_T\}$ and $\mu_T(0)\ne0$.

=== 3. Primary decomposition ===
Write $\mu_T=\prod_{g\mid\mu_T}g^{m_g}$ (product over the finitely many monic irreducibles $g$ dividing $\mu_T$). Applying Lemma 1 with $h_g=g^{m_g}$ and $h=\mu_T$ gives
\qquad (3.1) $V=\bigoplus_{g\mid\mu_T}W_g$, where $W_g:=\ker g(T)^{m_g}$.
Each $W_g$ is $T$-stable (the operators $g(T)$ commute with $T$), and $W_g\ne0$: if $W_g=0$ then $\mu_T/g^{m_g}$ annihilates every $W_{g'}$ (it contains $g'^{m_{g'}}$ for $g'\ne g$, and kills $W_g=0$), hence annihilates $V$, contradicting the minimality of $\mu_T$.

(3.2) $V[g^{\infty}]=W_g$. Indeed, write $v=\sum_{g'}v_{g'}$ with $v_{g'}\in W_{g'}$. If $g(T)^Nv=0$ then $\sum_{g'}g(T)^Nv_{g'}=0$ with each term in the $T$-stable $W_{g'}$, so each term vanishes by directness. For $g'\ne g$, $\gcd(g^N,g'^{m_{g'}})=1$, so Bezout gives $\alpha g^N+\beta g'^{m_{g'}}=1$, and $\alpha(T)g(T)^N=\mathrm{id}$ on $W_{g'}$; thus $v_{g'}=0$. Hence $v=v_g\in W_g\cap\ker g(T)^N=\ker g(T)^{\min(N,m_g)}$, proving $V[g^N]=\ker g(T)^{\min(N,m_g)}$ and therefore $V[g^\infty]=W_g$.

(3.3) If $f\mid\chi_T$ but $f\nmid\mu_T$, then $\gcd(f,\mu_T)=1$, so Bezout gives $\alpha f+\beta\mu_T=1$, hence $\alpha(T)f(T)=\mathrm{id}$: $f(T)\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, and consequently $V[f]=0$, $V[f^\infty]=0$, $f(T)V=V$.

=== 4. Semisimple: two equivalent meanings, and the link with diagonalizability ===
Lemma A. For $T\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$ the following are equivalent: (a) every $T$-stable subspace has a $T$-stable complement; (b) $V$ is a direct sum of $T$-simple subspaces.
Proof. (a)$\Rightarrow$(b): let $S$ be the sum of all $T$-simple subspaces ($T$-stable), and $U$ a $T$-stable complement. If $U\ne0$, among the nonzero $T$-stable subspaces of $U$ choose one of minimal dimension (possible since $\dim V<\infty$); it is $T$-simple, so lies in $S\cap U=0$, contradiction. Thus $V=S$, and since the sum is finite-dimensional a finite subsum already equals $V$; deleting redundant summands gives $V=\bigoplus_i S_i$.
(b)$\Rightarrow$(a): let $V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^mS_i$ with $S_i$ simple, $W\subseteq V$ stable. Choose $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,m\}$ maximal with $W+\sum_{j\in J}S_j$ direct. For $i\notin J$ maximality gives $0\ne x\in W\cap(S_i+\sum_JS_j)$; write $x=s_i+u$: then $s_i\ne0$ (else $x\in\sum_JS_j$), and $s_i\in W+\sum_JS_j$, which is stable, so $S_i=K[t]s_i\subseteq W+\sum_JS_j$. Hence $V=\sum_iS_i\subseteq W+\sum_JS_j$, i.e. $V=W\oplus\sum_JS_j$. $\square$
We take (a) (equivalently (b)) as the meaning of (i) "T is semisimple".

Lemma B. $T$ is semisimple iff $\bar T:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ on $V\otimes_K\bar K$ is diagonalizable.
Proof. If (i) holds, by (v) below (which we prove without using Lemma B) $V=\bigoplus_fV[f]$; $\bar K$ is flat over $K$, so $\ker f(\bar T)=V[f]\otimes\bar K$. In characteristic $0$ the irreducible $f$ is separable ($f'\ne0$ and $\deg f'<\deg f$ force $\gcd(f,f')=1$), so $f=c\prod_\lambda(t-\lambda)$ over $\bar K$ with distinct roots; Lemma 1 over $\bar K$ gives $V[f]\otimes\bar K=\bigoplus_\lambda\ker(\bar T-\lambda)$, hence $V\otimes\bar K$ is a direct sum of eigenspaces. Conversely, if $\bar T$ is diagonalizable its minimal polynomial $\mu_{\bar T}\in\bar K[t]$ is squarefree; but $\mu_{\bar T}=\mu_T$ since for $p\in K[t]$, $p(T)=0\iff p(\bar T)=0$ (as $V$ spans $V\otimes\bar K$ over $\bar K$). If $\mu_T$ had $g^2\mid\mu_T$ with $g$ nonconstant, then over $\bar K$ some root $\lambda$ of $g$ would give $(t-\lambda)^2\mid\mu_T$, contradiction. So $\mu_T$ is squarefree, i.e. (ii), which implies (i) by \S 5. $\square$

=== 5. Equivalence of (i)--(vi) ===
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii). By Lemma A, $V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^mS_i$ with $S_i$ simple. For $0\ne s\in S_i$, $S_i=K[t]s\cong K[t]/\operatorname{Ann}(s)$, and $\operatorname{Ann}(s)$ is a maximal ideal (a submodule of $S_i$ corresponds to an ideal containing $\operatorname{Ann}(s)$), hence $\operatorname{Ann}(s)=(p_i)$ with $p_i$ monic irreducible (in a PID a maximal ideal is generated by an irreducible: if $p_i=ab$ then $(a)=(p_i)$ or $(a)=K[t]$). Also $p_i(0)\ne0$, else $p_i=t$ and $T|_{S_i}=0$, impossible for invertible $T$ on a nonzero space. Moreover $\operatorname{Ann}(S_i)=\operatorname{Ann}(s)=(p_i)$. Since $\mu_T$ annihilates $V$, $p_i\mid\mu_T$ for all $i$; and $\prod_{\text{distinct}}p_i$ annihilates every $S_i$, hence $V$, so $\mu_T\mid\prod p_i$. Thus $\mu_T=\prod_{\text{distinct}}p_i$ is squarefree.
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(v). $\mu_T=\prod_{f\mid\mu_T}f$; Lemma 1 with $h_f=f$ gives $V=\bigoplus_{f\mid\mu_T}V[f]$, and by (3.3) $V[f]=0$ for $f\mid\chi_T$, $f\nmid\mu_T$; so $V=\bigoplus_{f\mid\chi_T}V[f]$.
(v)$\Rightarrow$(i). On $V[f]$ the ring $L_f:=K[t]/(f)$ (a field, $f$ irreducible) acts, since $f(T)=0$ there. Choose an $L_f$-basis $\{e\}$ of $V[f]$; then $V[f]=\bigoplus_eL_fe$ as $K[t]$-modules, and each $L_fe\cong K[t]/(f)$ is simple because $(f)$ is maximal. So $V$ is a direct sum of simple submodules; Lemma A gives (i).
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(vi). Under (ii) all $m_f=1$, so $V[f^\infty]=W_f=\ker f(T)=V[f]$ by (3.2).
(vi)$\Rightarrow$(v). $V[f]=V[f^\infty]=W_f$ by (3.2), so (3.1) gives $V=\bigoplus_{f\mid\mu_T}V[f]=\bigoplus_{f\mid\chi_T}V[f]$ using (3.3).
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii). Fix $f\mid\chi_T$. If $f\nmid\mu_T$ then $V[f]=0$ by (3.3) and there is nothing to show. Otherwise, by (ii)$\Rightarrow$(v), $V=\bigoplus_{g\mid\mu_T}V[g]$, and $f(T)V=\bigoplus_{g\ne f}V[g]$: indeed $f(T)=0$ on $V[f]$, while for $g\ne f$, $\gcd(f,g)=1$ gives Bezout $\alpha f+\beta g=1$, so $\alpha(T)f(T)=\mathrm{id}$ on $V[g]$. Since the sum is direct, $V[f]\cap f(T)V=0$.
(iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii). Fix $f\mid\mu_T$ and put $m=m_f$, $W=W_f=V[f^\infty]$ (3.2). Then $W[f]=W\cap V[f]=V[f]$ (as $V[f]\subseteq V[f^\infty}=W$) and $f(T)W\subseteq f(T)V$, so $W[f]\cap f(T)W\subseteq V[f]\cap f(T)V=0$. If $m\ge2$: $f(T)^{m-1}|_W\ne0$, for otherwise $\mu_T/f$ would annihilate $W$ and also each $W_g$ ($g\ne f$), contradicting minimality of $\mu_T$. Choose $v\in W$ with $0\ne w:=f(T)^{m-1}v$. Then $f(T)w=f(T)^mv=0$, so $w\in W[f]$; and $w=f(T)(f(T)^{m-2}v)\in f(T)W$. Thus $0\ne w\in W[f]\cap f(T)W=0$, contradiction. Hence $m_f=1$ for every $f\mid\mu_T$, i.e. $\mu_T$ is squarefree.
(iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv) is proved in \S 6.
This closes the chain (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv)$\Leftrightarrow$(v)$\Leftrightarrow$(vi).

=== 6. Dimensions; (iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv) ===
Let $\varphi_f:V[f]\to V/f(T)V$, $v\mapsto v+f(T)V$, the map induced by the inclusion $V[f]\hookrightarrow V$ (this is exactly the map of (iv)). Its kernel is $V[f]\cap f(T)V$, so (iii) says precisely that every $\varphi_f$ is injective. By rank--nullity applied to the $K$-linear map $f(T):V\to V$ (note $f(T)V=\mathrm{im}\,f(T)$):
\qquad $\dim_KV/f(T)V=\dim_KV-\dim_K\mathrm{im}\,f(T)=\dim_K\ker f(T)=\dim_KV[f]$.
Thus $\varphi_f$ is a map between spaces of equal finite dimension, so it is injective $\iff$ surjective $\iff$ bijective. Hence (iii) $\iff$ (iv) $\iff$ "all $\varphi_f$ injective" $\iff$ "all $\varphi_f$ surjective".

=== 7. The ring $R=K[t^{\pm1}]$ ===
Because $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $t^{-1}$ may be made to act as $T^{-1}$, and $V$ is an $R$-module; $R$-submodules $=$ $K[t]$-submodules $=$ $T$-stable subspaces.
$R=S^{-1}K[t]$ with $S=\{t^n:n\ge0\}$. Every element of $R$ has the form $t^{-m}p$ with $p\in K[t]$; writing $p=ct^{m'}g$ with $c\in K^\times$, $g\in K[t]$ monic and $g(0)\ne0$, gives $r=ct^{m'-m}g$, unique since $K[t]\to R$ is injective and $t$ is prime in $K[t]$. Hence $R^\times=\{ct^n\}$, and the irreducibles of $R$ are, up to associates, exactly the monic irreducibles $g\in K[t]$ with $g(0)\ne0$: if such $g$ factored as $g=r_1r_2$ in $R$, write $r_i=c_it^{n_i}g_i$ with $g_i\in K[t]$ monic, $g_i(0)\ne0$; then $g=c_1c_2t^{n_1+n_2}g_1g_2$ in $K[t]$, so $n_1+n_2=0$ and $g=g_1g_2$ (as $c_1c_2=1$ after normalising), forcing $g_1$ or $g_2$ to be $1$ by irreducibility in $K[t]$.
$R$ is a PID: $K[t]$ is a PID (\S 1), and if $J\triangleleft R$ then with $I=J\cap K[t]$, for $x/s\in J$ we have $x=s(x/s)\in J\cap K[t]=I$, so $x/s\in S^{-1}I$; the reverse inclusion is clear. Thus $J=S^{-1}I=S^{-1}(g)=(g)$ is principal.

Fix an irreducible $f\in R$, represented by its monic polynomial in $K[t]$ (this choice only affects the identifications below by the automorphism attached to a unit of $R$, cf. the remark at the end). Since $R$ is a domain and $f\ne0$, multiplication by $f$ is injective, so
\qquad (7.1) $0\to R\xrightarrow{\ \cdot f\ }R\xrightarrow{\ q\ }R/(f)\to0$
is a free resolution of $R/(f)$ of length $1$.

(a) $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R/(f),V)\cong V[f]$, canonically: $\Phi\mapsto\Phi(\bar 1)$, with inverse $v\mapsto(\overline{h}\mapsto h(T)v)$. The inverse is well defined: if $h\equiv h'\ (\mathrm{mod}\ f)$ then $h-h'=fq$, so $(h-h')(T)v=q(T)f(T)v=0$ for $v\in V[f]$. These maps are mutual inverses and $R$-linear (over the field $R/(f)$); naturality in $V$ is immediate.

(b) $\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(R/(f),V)\cong V/f(T)V$, canonically: apply $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,V)$ to (7.1). Using $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R,V)\cong V$, $\psi\mapsto\psi(1)$, the induced map $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R,V)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(R,V)$ is $\psi\mapsto\psi\circ(\cdot f)$, $1\mapsto\psi(f)=f\cdot\psi(1)$, i.e. $v\mapsto f(T)v$; and $\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(R,V)=0$ because $R$ is free over itself. The resulting exact sequence $V\xrightarrow{f(T)}V\xrightarrow{\partial}\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(R/(f),V)\to0$ identifies $\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(R/(f),V)$ with $\operatorname{coker}(f(T))=V/f(T)V$, and under this identification the connecting homomorphism $\partial$ is the quotient map $V\twoheadrightarrow V/f(T)V$.

(c) The map of (iv) is the natural composite. Consider
\qquad $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R/(f),V)\xrightarrow{\ q^*\ }\operatorname{Hom}_R(R,V)\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(R/(f),V)$,
where $q^*(\Phi)=\Phi\circ q$ is restriction along the quotient of (7.1) and $\partial$ is the connecting homomorphism: this is the canonical map attached to (7.1) and to the inclusion of the kernel into $V$. Under the identifications (a) and (b) it is $\varphi_f$: if $\Phi(\bar1)=v\in V[f]$, then $q^*(\Phi)(1)=\Phi(q(1))=\Phi(\bar1)=v$, and $\partial(q^*(\Phi))=v+f(T)V$. That is exactly the map induced by $V[f]\hookrightarrow V$. (Remark on choices: replacing $f$ by an associate $ct^kf$ multiplies both identifications by the automorphism $cT^k$ of $V$ and of $V/f(T)V$, which is well defined since $f(T)V$ is $T$- and $T^{-1}$-stable; the statement of (iv) and the injectivity/surjectivity assertions are unaffected.)

=== 8. No dimension count can prove semisimplicity ===
By \S 6, $\dim_KV[f]=\dim_KV/f(T)V$ holds for every $T$ and every $f$, semisimple or not; it is an instance of rank--nullity and carries no information about $T$. What matters is whether the specific map $\varphi_f$ is injective. Example showing the equality of dimensions is compatible with non-semisimplicity: take $V=K^2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\chi_T=(t-1)^2$ and $f=t-1$. Then $f(T)=T-I=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has $\ker f(T)=Ke_1$ and $\mathrm{im}\,f(T)=Ke_1$, so $\dim V[f]=1=\dim V/f(T)V$, yet $\varphi_f:Ke_1\to K^2/Ke_1$ is the zero map (as $Ke_1=f(T)V$), so (iii) and (iv) fail. Consistently, $\mu_T=(t-1)^2$ is not squarefree, $V[f^\infty]=\ker(T-I)^2=K^2\ne V[f]$, and $Ke_1$ is $T$-stable with no $T$-stable complement (a complement would be $K(ae_1+be_2)$ with $b\ne0$, but $T(ae_1+be_2)=(a+b)e_1+be_2$ is a multiple of $ae_1+be_2$ only if $b=0$). Hence any "proof" of semisimplicity that only compares $\dim V[f]$ with $\dim V/f(T)V$ proves nothing.

=== 9. Primary pieces ===
$T$ is semisimple on $V$ $\iff$ $T|_{V[f^\infty]}$ is semisimple for every $f\mid\chi_T$.
($\Rightarrow$) By (vi), $V[f^\infty]=V[f]$, which is a vector space over the field $L_f=K[t]/(f)$; every $L_f$-subspace has an $L_f$-complement (basis extension), and $L_f$-subspaces are exactly the $T$-stable subspaces of $V[f]$. Hence $T|_{V[f^\infty]}$ satisfies condition (a) of Lemma A, i.e. is semisimple.
($\Leftarrow$) By (3.1) and (3.2), $V=\bigoplus_{f\mid\chi_T}V[f^\infty]$ (the pieces with $f\nmid\mu_T$ being $0$ by (3.3)). If each piece is semisimple, Lemma A writes each as a direct sum of $T$-simple subspaces; a $T$-simple subspace of a piece is $T$-simple in $V$ (its $T$-stable subspaces are the same), so $V$ is a direct sum of $T$-simple subspaces, and Lemma A gives (i).

All assertions of the lemma are thus established. $\blacksquare$

lemma_59.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power and let l != p be a prime. Assume the following hypothesis (GC): for every integer m >= 1 and every smooth projective GEOMETRICALLY CONNECTED variety Y over F_{q^m}, arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^m} acts semisimply on H^n_et(Y_{Fbar_q},Q_l) for every n >= 0. Then the conjecture holds in full: for every smooth projective variety X over F_q (not assumed connected or equidimensional) and every i >= 0, geometric Frobenius acts semisimply on H^i_et(X_{Fbar_q},Q_l), and its induced action on H^i_et(X_{Fbar_q},Q_l) tensor_{Q_l} Q_l_bar is diagonalizable. (The proof should run as follows: apply lemma_27/lemma_31 to pass from X to a representative C_s of each Frobenius orbit on the geometric connected components of X_bar, with F_q^{m_s} acting; identify F_q^{m_s} with arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^{m_s}} on the F_{q^{m_s}}-model of C_s via lemma_27 and lemma_44; apply (GC) to that smooth projective geometrically connected model; then lemma_25/lemma_9 to reassemble the orbits, lemma_4 and lemma_6a to invert arithmetic into geometric Frobenius, and lemma_5 to upgrade to Q_l_bar-diagonalizability.)
lemma_59.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_59. Assume (GC). We prove that for every smooth projective X over F_q (no connectedness or equidimensionality hypothesis) and every i ≥ 0, geometric Frobenius is semisimple on H^i_et(X̄, Q_ℓ), and diagonalizable after extending scalars to Q̄_ℓ.

═══════════════════════════════════════════
0. NOTATION.
═══════════════════════════════════════════
Write F := F_q, k := F̄_q, and σ: k → k, a ↦ a^q. For an F-scheme Z write Z̄ := Z ×_{Spec F} Spec k, and let F_q := id_Z × σ, the q-power arithmetic Frobenius: a σ-semilinear automorphism of the k-scheme Z̄, equivalently an isomorphism of the underlying schemes Z̄ → Z̄ over Spec F. For m ≥ 1 put Z₍m₎ := Z ×_{Spec F} Spec F_{q^m}. Since F ⊂ F_{q^m} ⊂ k there is a canonical isomorphism of k-schemes
   Z₍m₎ ×_{Spec F_{q^m}} Spec k  ≅  Z ×_{Spec F} Spec k = Z̄ ,      (0.1)
because both sides represent Z ×_F Spec k. Under (0.1) the arithmetic Frobenius of the F_{q^m}-scheme Z₍m₎ base changed to k, which is by definition id × σ^m (σ^m is the q^m-power map on k and fixes F_{q^m}), is literally the automorphism id_Z × σ^m = F_q^m of Z̄. We use the convention that for an open-and-closed subscheme U ⊂ Y cut out by the idempotent e_U ∈ Γ(Y, O_Y) (the characteristic function of U), a morphism f: Y′ → Y satisfies f^{−1}(U) = Spec-fibre cut out by f^*(e_U); this is immediate since f^* is a ring homomorphism sending 1_U to 1_{f^{−1}U}.

═══════════════════════════════════════════
1. FINITE-DIMENSIONALITY AND THE TWO FROBENIUSES.
═══════════════════════════════════════════
Let X be smooth projective over F_q and n ≥ 0; set V := H^n_et(X̄, Q_ℓ). X is proper over F_q, so lemma_45_finite_frob applied to K = Q_{ℓ,X̄} ∈ D^b_c(X̄, Q_ℓ) shows V is finite-dimensional over Q_ℓ. By lemma_6a, F_ar := (id_X × σ)^* and F_geo := (id_X × σ^{−1})^* are then invertible Q_ℓ-linear operators on V with F_geo = F_ar^{−1}. If X = ∅ then V = 0 and every assertion below is trivial (the zero operator is semisimple), so assume X ≠ ∅. Functoriality of pullback gives (F_ar)^m = (F_q^m)^* for all m ≥ 1.

═══════════════════════════════════════════
2. THE GEOMETRIC COMPONENTS ARE OPEN AND CLOSED.
═══════════════════════════════════════════
X is smooth over F, hence X̄ is smooth over the field k; so X̄ is noetherian and every local ring O_{X̄,x} is a regular local ring, hence a domain. The irreducible components of X̄ containing a point x correspond bijectively to the minimal primes of O_{X̄,x}, which is a domain, so x lies on exactly one irreducible component. Thus the irreducible components Z_1,…,Z_N of X̄ (finitely many, X̄ being of finite type over k) are pairwise disjoint; each Z_i = X̄ \ ⋃_{j≠i} Z_j is therefore open as well as closed. Each Z_i is irreducible, hence connected, so {Z_1,…,Z_N} is exactly π_0(X̄). Since X̄ is smooth over k it is reduced, so each component C_j := Z_i, with its open-and-closed subscheme structure, is reduced and is a connected component. Write e_j ∈ Γ(X̄, O) for the corresponding idempotent. As F_q is a homeomorphism of X̄, it permutes π_0(X̄) = {C_1,…,C_N}. This is precisely the finite set and decomposition used in lemma_27.

═══════════════════════════════════════════
3. SUBLEMMA (DESCENT OF AN INVARIANT COMPONENT TO A MODEL).
═══════════════════════════════════════════
Statement. Let Z be a separated scheme of finite type over F, let C ⊂ Z̄ be an open-and-closed subscheme, and let m ≥ 1 satisfy (F_q^m)^{−1}(C) = C. Then:
(a) there is a unique open-and-closed subscheme D ⊂ Z₍m₎ with D ×_{F_{q^m}} k = C (as open-and-closed subschemes of Z̄, via (0.1));
(b) if Z is smooth (resp. projective) over F then D is smooth (resp. projective) over F_{q^m};
(c) if C is connected then D is geometrically connected over F_{q^m};
(d) the arithmetic Frobenius of D over F_{q^m} acts on H^n(C, Q_ℓ) = H^n(D ×_{F_{q^m}} k, Q_ℓ) as (F_q^m)^*|_{H^n(C)}.

Proof of (a), uniqueness. Spec k → Spec F_{q^m} is faithfully flat (k is a free F_{q^m}-module), so Z₍m₎ ×_{F_{q^m}} k → Z₍m₎ is faithfully flat; fpqc descent for quasi-coherent sheaves gives that Γ(Z₍m₎, O) → Γ(Z̄, O) is injective (the unit O → π_*π^*O is injective for a faithfully flat morphism). An open-and-closed subscheme is determined by its idempotent in Γ(−, O), so D is unique.

Proof of (a), existence. Let e ∈ Γ(Z̄, O) be the idempotent of C.
Claim 1: Γ(Z̄, O) = colim_{N} Γ(Z₍N₎, O), N running over the positive integers ordered by divisibility. Indeed k = ∪_N F_{q^N} is a filtered union, so Z̄ = colim_N Z₍N₎ with affine transition morphisms (base changes of the finite, hence affine, morphisms Spec Z₍N′₎ → Spec Z₍N₎). Take a finite affine open cover Z = U_1 ∪ … ∪ U_s (Z is noetherian). For each multi-index I the intersection U_I := ⋂_{i∈I} U_i is affine (Z is separated over the field F), and (U_I)₍N₎ = U_I ×_F F_{q^N} is affine with Γ((U_I)₍N₎, O) = A_I ⊗_F F_{q^N} where U_I = Spec A_I; hence colim_N Γ((U_I)₍N₎, O) = A_I ⊗_F k = Γ((U_I)̄, O), since tensor products commute with filtered colimits. The sheaf equalizer 0 → Γ(W, O) → ∏_i Γ(W_i, O) ⇒ ∏_{i,j} Γ(W_i ∩ W_j, O) applied to the covers {(U_i)₍N₎} of Z₍N₎ and {(U_i)̄} of Z̄, together with exactness of filtered colimits of abelian groups and the fact that (U_i ∩ U_j)₍N₎ = (U_i)₍N₎ ∩ (U_j)₍N₎, gives Claim 1.
Claim 2: if N′ is a multiple of m, then Γ(Z₍m₎, O) = Γ(Z₍N′₎, O)^{⟨σ^m⟩}, the invariants for the action induced by id_Z × σ^m. Indeed F_{q^N′}/F_{q^m} is finite Galois with cyclic group generated by σ^m|_{F_{q^N′}}, whose order is N′/gcd(m,N′) = N′/m = [F_{q^N′} : F_{q^m}], so it generates. The morphism Z₍N′₎ → Z₍m₎ is finite locally free, hence fpqc, so Γ(Z₍m₎, O) is the equalizer of Γ(Z₍N′₎, O) ⇒ Γ(Z₍N′₎ ×_{F_{q^m}} Z₍N′₎, O). Since F_{q^N′}/F_{q^m} is Galois, F_{q^N′} ⊗_{F_{q^m}} F_{q^N′} = ∏_{g} F_{q^N′} (a ⊗ b ↦ (g(a)b)_g), so Z₍N′₎ ×_{F_{q^m}} Z₍N′₎ = ⨿_g Z₍N′₎ and the two projections are id and g; the equalizer is exactly the invariant subgroup.
Now by Claim 1, e is the image of some e_0 ∈ Γ(Z₍N₀₎, O) for some N₀. Let N′ := lcm(N₀, m) and let e′ ∈ Γ(Z₍N′₎, O) be the image of e_0. Since (F_q^m)^{−1}(C) = C, pulling back idempotents gives (F_q^m)^*(e) = e in Γ(Z̄, O). Because m | N′, the automorphism σ^m preserves F_{q^N′}, so (F_q^m)^* restricts to an automorphism of Z₍N′₎ over F and to the σ^m-action of Claim 2 on Γ(Z₍N′₎, O); both (F_q^m)^*(e) and e are images of elements of Γ(Z₍N′₎, O), and Γ(Z₍N′₎, O) → Γ(Z̄, O) is injective (faithfully flat base change along F_{q^N′} → k), so (σ^m)^*(e′) = e′. Hence e′ is fixed by the group ⟨σ^m⟩ = Gal(F_{q^N′}/F_{q^m}), and by Claim 2 it is the image of a unique idempotent e′′ ∈ Γ(Z₍m₎, O). Let D ⊂ Z₍m₎ be the open-and-closed subscheme cut out by e′′. The image of e′′ in Γ(Z̄, O) is e, hence D ×_{F_{q^m}} k = C as open-and-closed subschemes of Z̄. This proves (a).

Proof of (b). The inclusion D → Z₍m₎ of an open-and-closed subscheme is simultaneously an open immersion (hence étale, hence smooth) and a closed immersion. Z₍m₎ → Spec F_{q^m} is smooth (resp. projective) because Z → Spec F is and smoothness/projectivity are stable under base change. Smoothness is preserved under composition, so D is smooth over F_{q^m}; a closed subscheme of a projective F_{q^m}-scheme is projective over F_{q^m}, so D is projective.

Proof of (c). D is of finite type over F_{q^m}, and k = F̄_q is algebraic over F_{q^m} and algebraically closed, hence is an algebraic closure of F_{q^m}. By (a), D ×_{F_{q^m}} k = C is connected. By the standard criterion for geometric connectedness of a finite-type scheme over a field (connectedness after base change to one/any algebraic closure), D is geometrically connected over F_{q^m}.

Proof of (d). By definition the arithmetic Frobenius of D/F_{q^m} is the σ^m-semilinear automorphism id_D × σ^m of D ×_{F_{q^m}} k. Under the identification (0.1) the subscheme D ×_{F_{q^m}} k is C ⊂ Z̄ and id_D × σ^m is the restriction to C of id_Z × σ^m = F_q^m. Étale cohomology is functorial for morphisms of schemes (not only of k-schemes), so the induced operator on H^n(C, Q_ℓ) = H^n(D ×_{F_{q^m}} k, Q_ℓ) is exactly (F_q^m)^*|_{H^n(C)}. ∎(sublemma)

═══════════════════════════════════════════
4. GEOMETRICALLY CONNECTED MODELS FOR THE ORBIT REPRESENTATIVES, AND APPLICATION OF (GC).
═══════════════════════════════════════════
Apply lemma_27 to X: it gives the orbits O_1,…,O_r of F_q on {C_1,…,C_N}, representatives C_{s_t} ∈ O_t, lengths m_t = |O_t|, and the canonical decomposition H^n(X̄, Q_ℓ) = ⊕_{j=1}^N H^n(C_j, Q_ℓ) with F_q permuting the summands along its action on the components.
Fix t. Since the F_q-orbit of C_{s_t} has length m_t, F_q^{m_t} maps C_{s_t} onto itself as a subset; as F_q^{m_t} is a homeomorphism, (F_q^{m_t})^{−1}(C_{s_t}) = C_{s_t} as open-and-closed subschemes. The sublemma of Step 3, applied with Z = X, C = C_{s_t}, m = m_t, yields an open-and-closed subscheme D_t ⊂ X₍m_t₎ such that:
  • D_t is smooth and projective over F_{q^{m_t}} (X is smooth and projective over F_q);
  • D_t is geometrically connected over F_{q^{m_t}} (C_{s_t} is a connected component, and it is nonempty since X̄ ≠ ∅);
  • D_t ×_{F_{q^{m_t}}} k = C_{s_t} as k-schemes;
  • the arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^{m_t}} acts on H^n(C_{s_t}, Q_ℓ) as (F_q^{m_t})^* = (F_ar)^{m_t}|_{H^n(C_{s_t})}.
This last identification is also the one supplied by lemma_44: applied to X with m = m_t, lemma_44 asserts that the canonical Q_ℓ-linear identification H^n(X̄, Q_ℓ) = H^n((X₍m_t₎)̄, Q_ℓ) coming from (0.1) intertwines arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^{m_t}} with F_q^{m_t}; since D_t is an open-and-closed subscheme of X₍m_t₎ whose base change to k is C_{s_t}, this intertwining restricts to the summand H^n(C_{s_t}, Q_ℓ), giving the same conclusion as (d).
Now (GC) applies with the integer m := m_t ≥ 1 and Y := D_t, a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_{q^{m_t}} (whose base change to F̄_q is exactly D_t ×_{F_{q^{m_t}}} k = C_{s_t}). Since t and n were arbitrary, we obtain:
   (★)  for every t = 1,…,r and every n ≥ 0, the operator (F_q^{m_t})^*|_{H^n(C_{s_t}, Q_ℓ)} = (F_ar)^{m_t}|_{H^n(C_{s_t}, Q_ℓ)} is semisimple.

═══════════════════════════════════════════
5. REASSEMBLY OF THE ORBITS (lemma_25 AND lemma_9).
═══════════════════════════════════════════
Fix n ≥ 0 and write V = ⊕_{j=1}^N V_j with V_j := H^n(C_j, Q_ℓ). Concretely, V_j = e_j·V where e_j is the idempotent of C_j; since F_ar = (F_q)^* and (F_q)^*(e_j) = e_{C′} where C′ = F_q^{−1}(C_j), we have F_ar(V_j) = V_{j′} with C_{j′} = F_q^{−1}(C_j); equality (not merely inclusion) holds because F_ar is an isomorphism whose inverse is (F_q^{−1})^*. Each V_j is a direct summand of the finite-dimensional space V, hence finite-dimensional.
For each orbit O_t, enumerate it as C_{t,0} := C_{s_t} and C_{t,j} := F_q^{−j}(C_{s_t}) for j = 0,…,m_t−1 (indices mod m_t); then F_q^{−1}(C_{t,j}) = C_{t,j+1}. Put V_{t,j} := H^n(C_{t,j}, Q_ℓ), so that F_ar(V_{t,j}) = V_{t,j+1} for all j modulo m_t, and put W_t := ⊕_{j=0}^{m_t−1} V_{t,j}. The W_t are the partial sums of the decomposition of lemma_27 over the orbits, so V = ⊕_{t=1}^r W_t and F_ar(W_t) = W_t; thus F_ar = ⊕_{t=1}^r F_ar|_{W_t}.
For each t, apply lemma_25 to the finite-dimensional spaces V_{t,0},…,V_{t,m_t−1}, their direct sum W_t, and the automorphism T := F_ar|_{W_t}, which satisfies T(V_{t,j}) = V_{t,j+1} (indices mod m_t). lemma_25 gives: T is semisimple on W_t if and only if T^{m_t}|_{V_{t,0}} is semisimple on V_{t,0}. But T^{m_t} = (F_ar)^{m_t} restricted to H^n(C_{t,0}, Q_ℓ) = H^n(C_{s_t}, Q_ℓ), which is semisimple by (★). Hence F_ar|_{W_t} is semisimple for every t. Finally, lemma_9 applied to V = ⊕_{t=1}^r W_t and the operators F_ar|_{W_t} shows that F_ar is semisimple on V = H^n(X̄, Q_ℓ). (This is exactly the equivalence asserted in lemma_27; we have derived it from lemma_25 and lemma_9 and verified that every hypothesis needed is satisfied.) Since n was arbitrary, arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^i_et(X̄, Q_ℓ) for every i ≥ 0.

═══════════════════════════════════════════
6. PASSAGE TO GEOMETRIC FROBENIUS AND TO Q̄_ℓ.
═══════════════════════════════════════════
By Step 1 (lemma_6a), on the finite-dimensional space H^i(X̄, Q_ℓ) the geometric Frobenius is the inverse of the arithmetic Frobenius: F_geo = F_ar^{−1}. By lemma_4, a linear automorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space is semisimple if and only if its inverse is; hence F_geo is semisimple on H^i_et(X̄, Q_ℓ) for every i ≥ 0. This is the first assertion of the conjecture.
For the equivalent formulation, apply lemma_5 to the finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector space H^i(X̄, Q_ℓ) and the operator T = F_geo: T is semisimple if and only if the induced operator on H^i(X̄, Q_ℓ) ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Q̄_ℓ is semisimple, i.e. diagonalizable. Hence geometric Frobenius acts diagonizably on H^i_et(X_{F̄_q}, Q_ℓ) ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Q̄_ℓ for every i ≥ 0.

═══════════════════════════════════════════
7. CONCLUSION.
═══════════════════════════════════════════
The variety X was an arbitrary smooth projective F_q-variety, not assumed connected or equidimensional (note that neither Step 2 nor Step 3 nor Step 5 uses any equidimensionality: no intersection complexes, no Poincaré duality, and no purity input are involved), and i ≥ 0 was arbitrary. We have shown that (GC) implies that geometric Frobenius acts semisimply on H^i_et(X_{F̄_q}, Q_ℓ), equivalently diagonizably on H^i_et(X_{F̄_q}, Q_ℓ) ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Q̄_ℓ, for all i. That is precisely the conjecture in full. ∎

REMARK on the point raised in the previous rejection. The descent input needed here is supplied entirely by Step 3, which never computes the action of Frobenius on the factors of E ⊗_F F̄ through σ-semilinear evaluation maps. Instead it works with the idempotent e_C ∈ Γ(X̄, O) and uses only two elementary and fully verified facts: (i) Γ(−, O) commutes with the filtered limit X̄ = colim_N X₍N₎ (proved from the affine case plus the sheaf equalizer for a finite affine cover, using separatedness of X over F and exactness of filtered colimits), and (ii) fpqc descent along the finite Galois cover X₍N′₎ → X₍m₎ identifies Γ(X₍m₎, O) with the Gal(F_{q^N′}/F_{q^m})-invariants, that Galois group being cyclic generated by σ^m because m | N′. No appeal to flat base change for H^0 of a proper morphism, and no appeal to Stein factorization, is made; properness is used only for projectivity of the model D and for finite-dimensionality of cohomology (lemma_45_finite_frob). The variance of the permutation of summands is handled explicitly in Steps 3(d) and 5 by using inverse images: F_ar maps the summand of C to the summand of F_q^{−1}(C), and the orbit sets and their lengths m_t are unchanged, so lemma_25 applies verbatim.

lemma_64.statement: (Semisimplicity is insensitive to a characteristic-zero ground-field extension.) Let k be a field of characteristic 0, K/k a field extension, V a finite-dimensional k-vector space and T a T-linear automorphism of V. (i) The minimal polynomial of T tensor id_K on V tensor_k K equals the minimal polynomial m_T of T (viewed in K[x]): k[T] is isomorphic to k[x]/(m_T) and embeds in End_k(V); tensor with the flat k-module K and identify K tensor_k End_k(V) with End_K(V tensor_k K) (V finite dimensional) to see that the kernel of K[x] -> End_K(V tensor K) is generated by m_T. (ii) For 0 != g in k[x] with char k = 0, g is squarefree if and only if gcd(g,g') = 1, and this gcd is unchanged after extending scalars to K because Bezout coefficients are produced by the Euclidean algorithm inside k[x]. State explicitly that this equivalence FAILS in positive characteristic (x^p - t over F_p(t) has zero derivative), so the characteristic-0 hypothesis is used. (iii) Conclude: T is semisimple on V if and only if T tensor id_K is semisimple on V tensor_k K, using that an operator on a finite-dimensional space over any field is semisimple exactly when its minimal polynomial is squarefree. (iv) Specialise to k = Q_ell and K a finite extension of Q_ell, and add the companion facts, valid over every field, that semisimplicity passes to duals V^*, to Tate-twist-like scalar multiples cT with c != 0, and to T^{-1}. Prove all of this from linear algebra only; do not cite lemma_5 or lemma_8 (stated only over Q_ell), and do not treat K = overline{Q}_ell as a filtered colimit of finite extensions.
lemma_64.proof:
## Reading of the statement, and scope

The phrase in the statement "\(T\) a \(T\)-linear automorphism of \(V\)" is a typo for "\(T\) a \(k\)-linear automorphism of \(V\)"; we prove the lemma for \(T\in \mathrm{GL}_k(V)\). In fact Parts (i)–(iii) use only \(T\in \mathrm{End}_k(V)\); invertibility is used only in Part (iv)(B)(3). Everything below is pure linear algebra and commutative algebra over an arbitrary field (with the characteristic stated in each part). No result from the provided lists is cited; in particular **lemma_5 and lemma_8 are not cited** (their content over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) is re-established here from scratch, in Part (iv)(C)), and \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is never treated as a filtered colimit of finite extensions.

The trivial case \(V=0\) is harmless throughout (all operators are semisimple, all minimal polynomials are \(1\), which is squarefree), so we tacitly assume spaces nonzero where it matters.

## 0. Definitions and elementary facts

Let \(F\) be any field, \(W\) a finite-dimensional \(F\)-vector space, \(S\in\mathrm{End}_F(W)\).

**(0.1) Minimal polynomial.** The set \(I_S:=\{f\in F[x]: f(S)=0\}\) is an ideal of the PID \(F[x]\); it is nonzero because \(\dim_F\mathrm{End}_F(W)=(\dim_F W)^2<\infty\) forces a linear relation among \(1,S,\dots,S^{(\dim W)^2}\). Its monic generator is the minimal polynomial \(m_S\). By the division algorithm, \(f(S)=0\iff m_S\mid f\). Moreover \(F[S]:=F[x]/I_S\cong k[x]/(m_S)\hookrightarrow \mathrm{End}_F(W)\) is an \(F\)-algebra isomorphism onto the subalgebra generated by \(S\).

**(0.2) Semisimple operator.** We call \(S\) *semisimple* if every \(S\)-stable subspace \(U\subseteq W\) (\(S(U)\subseteq U\)) admits an \(S\)-stable complement. This is equivalent to \(W\) being a direct sum of \(S\)-*simple* stable subspaces (nonzero stable subspaces with no proper nonzero stable subspace):

*($\Leftarrow$)* Write \(W=\bigoplus_{j\in J}L_j\) with \(J\) finite and each \(L_j\) simple, and let \(U\subseteq W\) be stable. Choose \(I\subseteq J\) maximal with \(U\cap\sum_{i\in I}L_i=0\) (possible: \(J\) finite). For \(j\notin I\), maximality gives \(0\neq u=\sigma+\ell\in U\) with \(\sigma\in\sum_{i\in I}L_i\), \(\ell\in L_j\); \(\ell\neq0\) since \(U\cap\sum_I L_i=0\). Then \(L_j=F[x]\ell\subseteq F[x](u-\sigma)\subseteq U+\sum_{i\in I}L_i\), since \(U\) and \(\sum_I L_i\) are stable. Hence \(W=U+\sum_I L_i\), and \(U\cap\sum_I L_i=0\) by construction, so \(\sum_I L_i\) is a stable complement of \(U\).

*($\Rightarrow$)* Take a decomposition into a maximal finite number of nonzero stable summands (exists by finite dimensionality: splitting strictly increases the number of summands). Each summand is simple, otherwise splitting it contradicts maximality.

A stable subspace of a semisimple operator is again semisimple: if \(N\subseteq W\) is stable and \(L\subseteq N\) is stable, a stable complement \(P\) of \(L\) in \(W\) gives \(N=L\oplus(P\cap N)\).

**(0.3) Simple modules.** If \(L\) is \(S\)-simple, then \(L\cong F[x]/(p)\) as \(F[x]\)-modules (\(x\) acting as \(S\)) for a unique monic irreducible \(p\in F[x]\): the annihilator of a nonzero \(v\in L\) is a nonzero ideal \((q)\), \(F[x]v=L\) by simplicity, and \(q\) is irreducible else \(q=q_1q_2\) would give the proper nonzero stable subspace \(q_1(S)L\).

## Part (i). The minimal polynomial is unchanged by scalar extension

Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic \(0\), \(K/k\) a field extension, \(V\) finite dimensional over \(k\), \(T\in\mathrm{End}_k(V)\), \(m_T\in k[x]\) its minimal polynomial, and \(T_K:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}_K\in\mathrm{End}_K(V_K)\) with \(V_K:=V\otimes_k K\).

**Step 1 (flatness).** \(K\) is a vector space over \(k\), hence has a \(k\)-basis, hence is a free, therefore flat, \(k\)-module.

**Step 2 (the two identifications).** Since \(k[x]=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}k\cdot x^i\) is free over \(k\), \(K\otimes_k k[x]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }K[x]\), \(\sum\lambda_i\otimes x^i\mapsto\sum\lambda_i x^i\). Since \(V\) is finite dimensional, choosing a \(k\)-basis identifies \(\mathrm{End}_k(V)\cong M_n(k)\) and \(\mathrm{End}_K(V_K)\cong M_n(K)\), and the canonical map
\[\Phi:\;K\otimes_k\mathrm{End}_k(V)\longrightarrow \mathrm{End}_K(V_K),\qquad \Phi(\lambda\otimes\varphi)(v\otimes\mu)=\lambda\mu\otimes\varphi(v)\]\nis an isomorphism of \(K\)-algebras (entrywise inclusion \(M_n(k)\hookrightarrow M_n(K)\) after choosing the basis; a change of basis conjugates both sides by the same matrix, so \(\Phi\) is basis-independent). Note \(\Phi(1\otimes T)=T_K\) and \(\Phi\) is a homomorphism, so \(\Phi(1\otimes f(T))=f(T_K)\) for every \(f\in k[x]\).

**Step 3 (the kernel).** Consider the commutative diagram of \(K\)-algebra maps
\[K[x]\ \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{ev}_{T_K}\ }\ \mathrm{End}_K(V_K),\qquad K[x]\cong K\otimes_k k[x]\ \twoheadrightarrow K\otimes_k k[T]\ \hookrightarrow K\otimes_k\mathrm{End}_k(V)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \mathrm{End}_K(V_K).\]
The middle injection is injective because \(k[T]\hookrightarrow\mathrm{End}_k(V)\) is and \(K\) is flat over \(k\); the surjection has kernel the image of \(K\otimes_k(m_T)\to K\otimes_k k[x]\). Multiplication by \(m_T\) identifies \(k[x]\) with the ideal \((m_T)\) as \(k\)-module, so the image of \(K\otimes_k(m_T)\) in \(K[x]\) is exactly the extended ideal \(m_T\cdot K[x]\). The composite equals \(\mathrm{ev}_{T_K}\) by Step 2, and it factors through the injection \(K\otimes_k k[T]\hookrightarrow\mathrm{End}_K(V_K)\). Hence
\[\ker(\mathrm{ev}_{T_K})=m_T\cdot K[x].\]
Since \(m_T\) is monic, it is the monic generator of this ideal, i.e. **\(m_{T_K}=m_T\) viewed in \(K[x]\)**. (Equivalently, \(K[x]/(m_T)\cong K\otimes_k k[T]\hookrightarrow\mathrm{End}_K(V_K)\).)

## Part (ii). Squarefreeness, the gcd criterion, and the characteristic-0 hypothesis

**(A) The criterion in characteristic 0.** Let \(0\neq g\in k[x]\), \(\mathrm{char}\,k=0\). Then \(g\) is squarefree (all exponents \(1\) in its factorisation into monic irreducibles) if and only if \(\gcd(g,g')=1\).

Write \(g=c\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i^{e_i}\) with \(c\in k^\times\), the \(p_i\) distinct monic irreducibles, \(e_i\ge1\). If \(r=0\) (\(g\) constant), then \(g'=0\) and \(\gcd(g,0)=1\) since \(g\) is a unit; the statement holds with the empty product squarefree. Assume \(r\ge1\). Differentiating,
\[g'=c\sum_{j=1}^{r} e_j\,p_j^{\,e_j-1}p_j'\prod_{i\ne j}p_i^{\,e_i}.\]
Fix \(j\). Every summand with index \(j'\ne j\) contains \(p_j^{e_j}\), hence is divisible by \(p_j\). The \(j\)-th summand has \(p_j\)-adic valuation \((e_j-1)+v_{p_j}(e_jp_j')\). Because \(\mathrm{char}\,k=0\) and \(e_j\ge1\), \(e_j\ne0\) in \(k\); and since \(\deg p_j\ge1\), \(p_j'\ne0\) with \(\deg p_j'<\deg p_j\), so \(p_j\nmid p_j'\). Thus \(v_{p_j}(e_jp_j')=0\) and \(v_{p_j}(g')=e_j-1\). Therefore \(v_{p_j}(\gcd(g,g'))=\min(e_j,e_j-1)=e_j-1\), so
\[\gcd(g,g')=\text{(unit)}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^r p_j^{\,e_j-1}.\]
This is \(1\) iff every \(e_j=1\), i.e. iff \(g\) is squarefree.

**(B) The gcd is unchanged by extending scalars.** Let \(g\in k[x]\setminus\{0\}\) and \(K/k\) any extension. Run the Euclidean algorithm on the pair \((g,g')\): \(r_{-1}=g\), \(r_0=g'\), \(r_{i-1}=q_ir_i+r_{i+1}\) with \(r_{i+1}=0\) or \(\deg r_{i+1}<\deg r_i\). At each step the pair \((q_i,r_{i+1})\) is *uniquely* determined by these conditions, and long division computes them from the coefficients of \(r_{i-1},r_i\) using only field operations in \(k\). Hence the same sequence of remainders is obtained whether the algorithm is run in \(k[x]\) or in \(K[x]\), and the monic gcd — the last nonzero remainder divided by its leading coefficient — is the same polynomial in both rings. In particular, when the gcd is \(1\), the Bézout identity \(1=ag+bg'\) is produced inside \(k[x]\) by back-substitution and remains valid in \(K[x]\); the Euclidean-algorithm argument gives the converse implication as well. So
\[\gcd_{k[x]}(g,g')=1\iff\gcd_{K[x]}(g,g')=1.\]

**(C) Squarefreeness is preserved and reflected.** Apply (A) over \(k\) and over \(K\) (note \(\mathrm{char}\,K=0\) since \(K/k\) is an extension of a characteristic-\(0\) field), and glue with (B):
\[g\ \text{squarefree in }k[x]\iff\gcd_{k[x]}(g,g')=1\iff\gcd_{K[x]}(g,g')=1\iff g\ \text{squarefree in }K[x].\]
(Concretely: a factor \(p_i\) may split over \(K\) as \(\prod_a q_{ia}\), and then \(g=c\prod_{i,a}q_{ia}^{e_i}\); the exponents are unchanged, which is exactly what (B) computes.)

**(D) The statement is false in characteristic \(p>0\); the hypothesis is used.** Let \(k=\mathbb F_p(t)\) and \(g(x)=x^p-t\in k[x]\). Then \(g'(x)=px^{p-1}=0\), so \(\gcd(g,g')=\gcd(g,0)=g\), which has degree \(p\ge2\) and is therefore not a unit: the criterion of (A) fails. Nevertheless \(g\) *is* squarefree in \(k[x]\): \(g\) is irreducible by Eisenstein's criterion applied in the PID \(\mathbb F_p[t][x]\) at the prime element \(t\) (the polynomial is monic, \(t\mid t\), \(t^2\nmid t\), \(t\nmid1\)), and Gauss's lemma transfers irreducibility to \(\mathrm{Frac}(\mathbb F_p[t])[x]=\mathbb F_p(t)[x]\); an irreducible polynomial with exponent \(1\) is squarefree. Moreover squarefreeness is not even preserved by extension of scalars in characteristic \(p\): with \(s=t^{1/p}\) and \(K=\mathbb F_p(s)\), \(g=x^p-s^p=(x-s)^p\) in \(K[x]\) by the freshman's dream, which is highly non-squarefree. Thus both (A) and (C), and hence the argument of Part (iii), genuinely require \(\mathrm{char}\,k=0\).

## Part (iii). The squarefree criterion over an arbitrary field, and the descent/ascension statement

**Theorem.** Let \(F\) be any field, \(W\) finite dimensional over \(F\), \(S\in\mathrm{End}_F(W)\). Then \(S\) is semisimple if and only if \(m_S\) is squarefree in \(F[x]\).

*($\Leftarrow$)* Suppose \(m_S=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i\) with the \(p_i\) distinct monic irreducibles. Since the \(p_i\) are pairwise coprime, Bézout gives \(e_i\in F[x]\) with \(e_i\equiv\delta_{ij}\pmod{p_j}\) for all \(j\). Put \(\pi_i:=e_i(S)\). Then \(\sum_i e_i\equiv1\pmod{m_S}\), so \(\sum_i\pi_i=\mathrm{id}\); \(e_ie_j\equiv0\pmod{m_S}\) for \(i\ne j\), so \(\pi_i\pi_j=0\); hence the \(\pi_i\) are commuting projections and \(W=\bigoplus_i W_i\) with \(W_i:=\mathrm{im}\,\pi_i\), each stable under \(S\) (polynomials in \(S\) commute with \(S\)). For each \(i\), \(p_ie_i\equiv0\pmod{p_j}\) for every \(j\) (for \(j\ne i\) because \(p_i\equiv0\pmod{p_j}\), for \(j=i\) because \(p_ie_i\equiv0\pmod{p_i}\)), hence \(p_ie_i\equiv0\pmod{m_S}\) and \(p_i(S)\pi_i=0\): \(p_i(S)\) vanishes on \(W_i\). Therefore \(W_i\) is a module over the field \(E_i:=F[x]/(p_i)\), via \((f\bmod p_i)\cdot v:=f(S)v\), well defined because \(p_i(S)|_{W_i}=0\). Taking an \(E_i\)-basis of \(W_i\), \(W_i\) is a direct sum of \(1\)-dimensional \(E_i\)-subspaces; each is \(S\)-stable and has no proper nonzero \(S\)-stable \(F\)-subspace (an \(S\)-stable \(F\)-subspace is an \(F[x]\)-submodule, i.e. an \(E_i\)-subspace, since \(F[x]\to E_i\) is surjective). So each \(W_i\) is a sum of simple stable subspaces, hence so is \(W\), and \(S\) is semisimple by (0.2).

*($\Rightarrow$)* We argue by contrapositive. Suppose \(m_S\) is not squarefree: write \(m_S=p^{e}h\) with \(p\in F[x]\) monic irreducible, \(e\ge2\), and \(p\nmid h\).

**Step 1.** Set \(W':=\ker p(S)^{e}\) and \(W'':=\ker h(S)\); both are \(S\)-stable. Choose \(a,b\in F[x]\) with \(ap^{e}+bh=1\). For \(v\in W\), \(v=a(S)p(S)^{e}v+b(S)h(S)v\), where \(b(S)h(S)v\in W'\) because \(p(S)^{e}b(S)h(S)v=b(S)m_S(S)v=0\), and \(a(S)p(S)^{e}v\in W''\) similarly. If \(w\in W'\cap W''\) then \(w=a(S)p(S)^{e}w+b(S)h(S)w=0\). Hence \(W=W'\oplus W''\), with projections \(\mathrm{pr}_{W'}=b(S)h(S)\) and \(\mathrm{pr}_{W''}=a(S)p(S)^{e}\), both commuting with \(S\).

**Step 2: \(m_{S|_{W'}}=p^{e}\).** Let \(f:=m_{S|_{W'}}\). Since \(p(S)^{e}\) kills \(W'\) by definition, \(f\mid p^{e}\), so \(f=p^{e'}\) with \(e'\le e\). Conversely, \(p^{e'}=f\) kills \(W'\) and \(h\) kills \(W''\) by definition, so the polynomial \(p^{e'}h\) kills \(W'+W''=W\) (polynomials in \(S\) commute: \(p(S)^{e'}h(S)(w'+w'')=h(S)p(S)^{e'}w'+p(S)^{e'}\cdot0=0\)). Hence \(m_S=p^{e}h\mid p^{e'}h\) in \(F[x]\), i.e. \(p^{e}\mid p^{e'}\), so \(e\le e'\). Thus \(e'=e\) and \(f=p^{e}\). (This includes the case \(h=1\), where \(W''=0\), \(W=W'\): then \(p^{e'}\) kills \(W\), so \(p^{e}\mid p^{e'}\) and again \(e'=e\).)

**Step 3: \(U:=\ker\big(p(S)|_{W'}\big)\) is nonzero and proper in \(W'\), and is \(S\)-stable.** Stability: \(p(S)S=Sp(S)\). Nonzero: since \(m_{S|_{W'}}=p^{e}\) and \(e-1<e\), \(p(S)^{e-1}\ne0\) on \(W'\); pick \(w\in W'\) with \(p(S)^{e-1}w\ne0\); then \(p(S)\big(p(S)^{e-1}w\big)=p(S)^{e}w=0\), so \(0\ne p(S)^{e-1}w\in U\). Proper: \(p(S)\ne0\) on \(W'\) because \(e\ge1\) and \(m_{S|_{W'}}=p^{e}\), so \(W'\not\subseteq U\).

**Step 4: \(U\) has no \(S\)-stable complement in \(W'\).** Suppose \(W'=U\oplus C\) with \(C\) stable. Then \(p(S)|_{C}\colon C\to C\) is injective (\(\ker p(S)|_C=C\cap U=0\)), hence bijective (\(C\) finite dimensional). But \(p(S)^{e}|_{C}=0\) since \(p(S)^{e}=m_{S|_{W'}}(S)\) kills \(W'\supseteq C\) and \(e\ge1\). A power of a bijection is a bijection, so \(C=0\), forcing \(W'=U\), contradicting Step 3. Hence \(S|_{W'}\) is not semisimple.

**Step 5: transfer to \(W\).** Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(S\) is semisimple on \(W\). Then the stable subspace \(U\oplus W''\subseteq W\) has a stable complement \(C\): \(W=(U\oplus W'')\oplus C\). Put \(C':=\mathrm{pr}_{W'}(C)\subseteq W'\); \(C'\) is stable since \(\mathrm{pr}_{W'}=b(S)h(S)\) commutes with \(S\). We claim \(W'=U\oplus C'\). *Intersection:* if \(c\in C\) and \(w':=\mathrm{pr}_{W'}(c)\in U\), write \(c=w'+w''\) with \(w''\in W''\); then \(c=w'+w''\in (U\oplus W'')\cap C=0\), so \(c=0\) and \(w'=0\). *Sum:* for \(w\in W'\) write \(w=u+w''+c\) with \(u\in U\), \(w''\in W''\), \(c\in C\); applying \(\mathrm{pr}_{W'}\) (which is the identity on \(W'\) and on \(U\subseteq W'\), and zero on \(W''\)) gives \(w=u+\mathrm{pr}_{W'}(c)\in U+C'\). Thus \(U\) has a stable complement in \(W'\), contradicting Step 4. Hence \(S\) is not semisimple, proving the contrapositive. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary (the lemma's Part (iii)).** Let \(k, K, V, T\) be as in the statement, \(\mathrm{char}\,k=0\). By the theorem over \(k\), over \(K\), by (i) and by (ii)(C):
\[T\ \text{semisimple on }V\;\overset{\text{thm}}{\iff}\; m_T\ \text{squarefree in }k[x]\;\overset{(\mathrm{iiC})}{\iff}\; m_T\ \text{squarefree in }K[x]\;\overset{(\mathrm{i})}{\iff}\; m_{T_K}\ \text{squarefree in }K[x]\;\overset{\text{thm}}{\iff}\; T_K\ \text{semisimple on }V_K.\]
So semisimplicity is insensitive to the characteristic-\(0\) extension \(K/k\). $\blacksquare$

## Part (iv). The \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) case and companion facts

**(A) Specialisation.** Take \(k=\mathbb Q_\ell\) (characteristic \(0\)) and \(K/\mathbb Q_\ell\) a finite extension; \(K\) is again of characteristic \(0\). For \(V\) finite dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) and \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\), Part (iii) gives: \(T\) semisimple on \(V\) if and only if \(T\otimes\mathrm{id}_K\) is semisimple on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\). (Finiteness of \(K/\mathbb Q_\ell\) is not used; it holds for every extension.)

**(B) Companion facts, valid over every field \(F\).** Let \(W\) be finite dimensional over \(F\) and \(S\in\mathrm{End}_F(W)\).

*(1) Duals.* Let \(S^{\vee}:W^{*}\to W^{*}\), \(\varphi\mapsto\varphi\circ S\). For endomorphisms \(A,B\) one has \((A\circ B)^{\vee}=B^{\vee}\circ A^{\vee}\), since \(((A\circ B)^{\vee}\varphi)(v)=\varphi(ABv)=(B^{\vee}(A^{\vee}\varphi))(v)\); by induction \((S^{n})^{\vee}=(S^{\vee})^{n}\). Hence for \(f(x)=\sum a_ix^i\),
\[f(S^{\vee})=\textstyle\sum_i a_i(S^{\vee})^{i}=\sum_i a_i(S^{i})^{\vee}=\big(\textstyle\sum_i a_iS^{i}\big)^{\vee}=f(S)^{\vee}.\]
An endomorphism is zero iff its transpose is zero (if \(A\ne0\) pick \(v\) with \(Av\ne0\), extend to a basis and take a dual functional detecting \(Av\)). Thus \(f(S^{\vee})=0\iff f(S)=0\), so \(\ker\mathrm{ev}_{S^{\vee}}=\ker\mathrm{ev}_{S}\) and \(m_{S^{\vee}}=m_S\); the theorem of Part (iii) gives \(S^{\vee}\) semisimple \(\iff S\) semisimple. *Remark (why no structural proof is attempted):* for a general endomorphism one does **not** have \((\ker p(S))^{*}=\ker p(S^{\vee})\); the correct relation is that \(\ker p(S^{\vee})\) is the annihilator of the sum of the *other* primary pieces, and that identification already presupposes the semisimple direct-sum decomposition being proved. The minimal-polynomial argument above is complete on its own.

*(2) Scalar multiples.* Let \(c\in F^{\times}\). *Primary argument:* a subspace \(U\subseteq W\) satisfies \(S(U)\subseteq U\) if and only if \((cS)(U)\subseteq U\) (multiply by \(c\) or by \(c^{-1}\)); so \(S\) and \(cS\) have exactly the same lattice of stable subspaces, and the property "every stable subspace has a stable complement" is identical for the two operators. Hence \(cS\) is semisimple \(\iff S\) is semisimple. *Minimal-polynomial check:* put \(n:=\deg m_S\) and \(M(x):=c^{\,n}m_S(x/c)\). If \(m_S(Y)=Y^{n}+b_{n-1}Y^{n-1}+\dots+b_0\) then \(M(x)=x^{n}+cb_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+c^{n}b_0\in F[x]\): its leading term is \(c^{n}(x/c)^{n}=x^{n}\), so \(M\) is **monic** (note that the naive expression \(c^{-n}m_S(x/c)\) would have leading coefficient \(c^{-2n}\) and is not the minimal polynomial). Also \(M(cS)=c^{n}m_S(cS/c)=c^{n}m_S(S)=0\). Conversely, if \(f(cS)=0\) then \(m_S(Y)\mid f(cY)\) in \(F[Y]\), say \(f(cY)=m_S(Y)h(Y)\) with \(d:=\deg h\); substituting \(Y=x/c\) gives \(f(x)=m_S(x/c)\,h(x/c)=\big[c^{n}m_S(x/c)\big]\cdot\big[c^{-n-d}c^{d}h(x/c)\big]=M(x)\cdot\big[c^{-n-d}c^{d}h(x/c)\big]\) with the second factor in \(F[x]\), so \(M\mid f\). Thus \(M\) is the monic generator of \(\ker\mathrm{ev}_{cS}\), i.e. \(m_{cS}(x)=c^{\,n}m_S(x/c)\). Since \(\sigma:F[x]\xrightarrow{\sim}F[x]\), \(x\mapsto x/c\) (inverse \(x\mapsto cx\)) is an \(F\)-algebra automorphism, it preserves multiplicities in factorisations into irreducibles, so \(m_{cS}\) is squarefree \(\iff m_S\) is — agreeing with the stable-subspace argument. (This is the formal counterpart of the invariance of Frobenius semisimplicity under Tate twists, where Frobenius is multiplied by \(\ell^{-n}\).)

*(3) Inverses.* Assume \(S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\). *Stable-subspace argument:* suppose \(S(U)\subseteq U\). Then \(S|_{U}\colon U\to U\) is injective (as \(S\) is), so \(\dim S(U)=\dim U\); with \(S(U)\subseteq U\) and \(U\) finite dimensional this forces \(S(U)=U\). Now \(S^{-1}(U)=S^{-1}(S(U))=U\): the inclusion \(U\subseteq S^{-1}(U)\) is immediate from \(S(U)=U\); for the reverse, if \(w\in S^{-1}(S(U))\) then \(S(w)=S(u)\) for some \(u\in U\), and injectivity of \(S\) gives \(w=u\in U\). Hence \(U\) is \(S^{-1}\)-stable. Applying the same reasoning to the invertible operator \(S^{-1}\) shows that every \(S^{-1}\)-stable subspace is \(S\)-stable. So \(S\) and \(S^{-1}\) have the same stable subspaces, the same stable complements, and are semisimple simultaneously.

*Minimal-polynomial check:* write \(m_S(x)=x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+a_1x+a_0\). First, \(a_0\ne0\): otherwise \(m_S=x\,q\) with \(q\) monic of degree \(n-1\ge1\) (as \(S\ne0\)), and \(0=S^{-1}\big(m_S(S)\big)=S^{-1}Sq(S)=q(S)\), contradicting the minimality of \(n\). Define the monic reciprocal
\[m'(x):=a_0^{-1}x^{n}m_S(1/x).\]
Since \(x^{n}m_S(1/x)=1+a_{n-1}x+a_{n-2}x^{2}+\dots+a_1x^{n-1}+a_0x^{n}\), we have explicitly
\[m'(x)=x^{n}+\frac{a_1}{a_0}x^{n-1}+\frac{a_2}{a_0}x^{n-2}+\dots+\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_0}x+\frac1{a_0},\]\nwhich is monic of degree \(n\) (the previous version of this expansion, with the coefficients in the order \(a_{n-1},\dots,a_1\), was wrong). Evaluating at \(S^{-1}\) (a homomorphism \(F[x]\to F[S^{-1}]\)) gives \(m'(S^{-1})=a_0^{-1}(S^{-1})^{n}m_S(S)=0\). Let \(n':=\deg m_{S^{-1}}\). Since \(m'\) annihilates \(S^{-1}\), \(m_{S^{-1}}\mid m'\), so \(n'\le n\). Applying the same construction to \(S^{-1}\) (whose minimal polynomial has nonzero constant term, because \((S^{-1})^{-1}=S\) exists) produces a monic polynomial of degree \(n'\) annihilating \(S\), so \(n\le n'\). Hence \(n'=n\) and, both being monic with \(m_{S^{-1}}\mid m'\) of equal degree, \(m_{S^{-1}}=m'\). Finally, the reciprocal map \(p\mapsto p^{*}(x):=x^{\deg p}p(1/x)\) is multiplicative (over the domain \(F[x]\), \(\deg(pq)=\deg p+\deg q\)), is an involution (\((p^{*})^{*}=p\)), preserves degrees, and sends irreducibles to irreducibles (if \(p^{*}=ab\) then \(p=a^{*}b^{*}\) and \(\deg a^{*}=\deg a\), \(\deg b^{*}=\deg b\), so one factor is constant). Hence \(m_S=\prod p_i^{e_i}\) gives \(m'=a_0^{-1}\prod p_i^{*\,e_i}\) with the same exponents, so \(m_{S^{-1}}=m'\) is squarefree \(\iff m_S\) is — again agreeing with the stable-subspace argument.

*(4) Combination.* If \(S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\), then \((S^{-1})^{\vee}=(S^{\vee})^{-1}\), which is semisimple by (1) and (3) applied in either order.

**(C) The passage to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), without filtered colimits.** Let \(V\) be finite dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) and \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\). We prove directly that \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\) if and only if \(T\otimes\mathrm{id}\) is **diagonalisable** on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), using exactly two applications of Part (iii) to single field extensions.

*Step 1.* Let \(K:=\mathbb Q_\ell(\text{roots of }m_T\ \text{in }\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\). This is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) (a simple algebraic extension generated by finitely many algebraic elements). By (iii) applied to \(k=\mathbb Q_\ell\), \(K/k\): \(T\) semisimple on \(V\iff T_K\) semisimple on \(V\otimes K\). Over \(K\), \(m_{T_K}=m_T\) splits as \(\prod_i(x-\lambda_i)\); by the theorem of (iii) (or by the proof of ($\Leftarrow$) there, where each \(E_i=K[x]/(x-\lambda_i)\cong K\) is \(1\)-dimensional, so the primary pieces \(\ker(T_K-\lambda_i)\) are genuine eigenlines) semisimplicity of \(T_K\) is equivalent to the \(\lambda_i\) being pairwise distinct, i.e. to \(T_K\) being diagonalisable over \(K\).

*Step 2.* Apply (iii) again, now with base field \(k'=K\) (still characteristic \(0\)) and extension \(K\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\): \(T_K\) semisimple on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\iff T\otimes\mathrm{id}\) semisimple on \((V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K)\otimes_K\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\); and over the algebraically closed field \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), semisimple \(\iff\) diagonalisable by the same observation.

Chaining Step 1 and Step 2 yields: \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\) over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) if and only if \(T\otimes\mathrm{id}\) is diagonalisable on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), and by (B)(3) the same holds with \(T\) replaced by \(T^{-1}\) (so geometric Frobenius may be substituted for arithmetic Frobenius), and by (B)(1) on the dual space. No filtered-colimit argument is used: each step is Part (iii) for one explicit extension.

This completes the proof of (i), (ii) (including the explicit positive-characteristic counterexample showing the necessity of \(\mathrm{char}=0\)), (iii) and (iv). $\blacksquare$

lemma_65.statement: Let l be a prime, let V be a nonzero finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space, and let A be a finite-dimensional commutative unital Q_l-subalgebra of End_Q_l(V). Suppose A is equipped with a Q_l-linear anti-involution dagger, so that (ab)^dagger = b^dagger a^dagger and (a^dagger)^dagger = a for all a,b in A. Assume the trace form Tr_V(a a^dagger) is anisotropic on A: Tr_V(a a^dagger) is nonzero for every nonzero a in A. Then A has no nonzero nilpotent element. Consequently, for every T in A, the minimal polynomial of T over Q_l is squarefree and T is semisimple on V. The argument is pure linear algebra: if a is nilpotent, then a a^dagger is nilpotent and has trace zero; a finite-dimensional commutative Q_l-algebra with no nonzero nilpotents is reduced, so Q_l[T] is reduced and the minimal polynomial mu_T is squarefree; since Q_l has characteristic zero, mu_T remains squarefree over Q_lbar and splits into distinct linear factors, giving diagonalizability over Q_lbar and hence semisimplicity over Q_l.
lemma_65.proof:
Proof of lemma_65.

Notation and conventions. Write k = Q_l and Omega = kbar = Q_l_bar. All vector spaces, algebras and traces are over k unless otherwise stated. Since A is a unital subalgebra of End_k(V), its unit is 1_A = id_V; because V is nonzero, id_V != 0, so A != 0. Recall that a linear operator S on a finite-dimensional space W over a field F is called semisimple if W is a semisimple F[t]-module via t.w = S(w); equivalently every S-stable F-subspace of W has an S-stable complement. Lemma_5 (applied with F = k = Q_l) identifies this notion, over Q_l, with diagonalizability of S tensor id on W tensor_k Q_l_bar; we use only that direction, in Step 7(d).

Step 1. Formal properties of the anti-involution.
(a) 0^dagger = 0 by k-linearity, and (.)^dagger: A -> A is a bijection since it is its own inverse ((a^dagger)^dagger = a).
(b) A is commutative, so (ab)^dagger = b^dagger a^dagger = a^dagger b^dagger; combined with additivity, (.)^dagger is multiplicative.
(c) 1^dagger = 1. Set e := 1^dagger. Then e^2 = (1*1)^dagger = 1^dagger = e, so e is an idempotent. For any a in A, a^dagger = (1*a)^dagger = a^dagger * 1^dagger = a^dagger e. Since (.)^dagger is surjective, every b in A equals a^dagger for some a, hence b = b e for all b in A. Taking b = 1 gives 1 = 1*e = e.
(d) From (b),(c), (.)^dagger is a k-algebra automorphism of A of order dividing 2, hence it preserves and reflects nilpotence: a^N = 0 if and only if (a^dagger)^N = (a^N)^dagger = 0.

Step 2. A nilpotent endomorphism of V has trace zero.
Let u in End_k(V) satisfy u^N = 0, and put W_j := u^j V for j = 0,...,N, so V = W_0 >= W_1 >= ... >= W_N = 0. Each W_j is u-stable because u(W_j) = u^{j+1}V = W_{j+1} <= W_j. Choose a k-basis of V adapted to this filtration (lift to W_j a basis of W_j/W_{j+1}, successively for j = 0,...,N-1). In that basis the matrix of u is block upper triangular whose j-th diagonal block is the endomorphism induced by u on W_j/W_{j+1}; but u(W_j) = W_{j+1}, so that induced map is zero. Hence every diagonal entry is 0 and Tr_V(u) = 0.

Step 3. A has no nonzero nilpotent element (A is reduced).
Let a in A with a^N = 0 for some N >= 1. By Step 1(d), (a^dagger)^N = 0. Since A is commutative, (a a^dagger)^N = a^N (a^dagger)^N = 0. Thus a a^dagger is a nilpotent element of A, i.e. a nilpotent endomorphism of V, and Step 2 yields Tr_V(a a^dagger) = 0. The anisotropy hypothesis says Tr_V(a a^dagger) != 0 for every nonzero a in A; therefore a = 0.

Step 4. The subalgebra k[T] and the minimal polynomial.
Fix T in A and let mu_T in k[t] be the minimal polynomial of the k-linear operator T on V. Since V != 0, mu_T != 1 (mu_T = 1 would assert id_V = 0). Consider the evaluation homomorphism phi: k[t] -> End_k(V), f |-> f(T). Its image is k[T], which lies in A because A is a k-subalgebra containing 1_A = id_V and T; its kernel is the ideal of polynomials killing T, namely (mu_T). Hence k[T] is k-algebra-isomorphic to k[t]/(mu_T).

Step 5. k[t]/(mu_T) is reduced, hence mu_T is squarefree.
As a subalgebra of the reduced algebra A (Step 3), k[T] has no nonzero nilpotents, so k[t]/(mu_T) is reduced. Write mu_T = c * prod_{i=1}^r f_i^{e_i} with c in k^x, the f_i distinct monic irreducibles and e_i >= 1.
