Each nonzero $R/(f_\alpha)$ has $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$-dimension $\deg f_\alpha\ge1$ (Step a3), so the hypothesis $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}_\ell}V_i<\infty$ forces the index set $\{\alpha:n_\alpha=-i\}$ to be finite; write $V_i\cong\bigoplus_{k=1}^{m}R/(g_k)$. The action of $R$ on $V_i$ then factors through $R/(\prod_{\text{distinct }k} g_k)$, so $\mu_{T_i}$ divides the squarefree polynomial $\prod_{\text{distinct}} g_k$; by lemma_60 (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i), $T_i$ is semisimple on $V_i$. (Concretely: $V_i\otimes\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell\cong\bigoplus_k \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell[t]/(g_k)$, and since $\operatorname{char}\mathbb{Q}_\ell=0$ each $g_k=\prod_{\lambda}(t-\lambda)$ has distinct roots, so $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell[t]/(g_k)\cong\prod_\lambda\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ with $t$ acting by the scalars $\lambda$; the operator is diagonalisable, which by lemma_5 is equivalent to semisimplicity over $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$.) $\blacksquare$

Steps c1–c4 give (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii).

Step c5 (the parenthetical reformulations). For a fixed $i$ and $f$ the sequence $0\to V_i[f]\to V_i\xrightarrow{f} fV_i\to0$ is exact by definition of kernel and image, and $\dim V_i[f]=\dim V_i-\dim fV_i=\dim V_i/fV_i$, so the canonical map $V_i[f]\to V_i/fV_i$ is an isomorphism if and only if it is injective, i.e. $V_i[f]\cap fV_i=0$, if and only if $V_i=V_i[f]\oplus fV_i$; this is lemma_60 (iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv). "No Jordan block of size $>1$ occurs for any $f$" means: over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ the operator $T_i\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalisable. By lemma_5 this is equivalent to (i), hence to (iii); in the dictionary of Step c0 it says exactly that all $e_{i,k}=1$, and the two directions of that equivalence are the computations in Steps c2 and c4 (a summand $R/(g^e)$, $e\ge2$, becomes over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ a direct sum of Jordan blocks of size $e$, one for each root of $g$, using $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell[t]/(g^e)\cong\prod_{\lambda\mid g}\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell[t]/((t-\lambda)^e)$ by Chinese remainders, valid because $g$ is separable in characteristic $0$). $\blacksquare$ (c)

=====================================================================
PART (d): THE WARNING, MADE EXPLICIT.

Nothing in (a)–(c) refers to varieties, Frobenius, or weights: the proofs used only (i) the Euclidean algorithm on $\mathbb{Q}_\ell[t]$, (ii) localisation, (iii) the transfinite basis argument a4, (iv) the formal properties of truncation triangles plus $\operatorname{Ext}^2_R=0$, and (v) elementary module theory over the PID $R$. So (a)–(c) are purely structural statements about the derived category of the Frobenius group ring: they say that the *shape* of an object of $D^b(R)$ is read off from its graded cohomology, and that semisimplicity of $T$ on each $H^i$ is equivalent to the absence of higher elementary divisors. They place no restriction at all on which operators $T$ occur.

Concretely, purity does not force (i)–(iii). Let $\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}_\ell^\times$ be a scalar of Weil absolute value $q^{n/2}$ for some integer $n$ (for instance $\lambda=q^{n/2}$ with $n$ even; the case $n=0,\lambda=1$ already suffices), let $V=\mathbb{Q}_\ell^{2}$ with basis $e_1,e_2$, and set $T=\lambda(I+N)$ where $Ne_1=0$, $Ne_2=e_1$, i.e. $T=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&\lambda\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}$. Then:
* $T$ is invertible, its only eigenvalue (over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$) is $\lambda$, of Weil absolute value $q^{n/2}$, so $V$ with the automorphism $T$ is pure of weight $n$ in the sense used by lemma_12/lemma_20a/lemma_20c (purity constrains only the eigenvalues, not the Jordan form).
* $T$ is **not** semisimple: $T-\lambda I=\lambda N\ne0$ but $(T-\lambda I)^2=0$, so $\mu_T=(t-\lambda)^2$ is not squarefree (lemma_60 (ii) fails), and $T$ has a single Jordan block of size $2$.
* Condition (iii) fails for the irreducible $f=t-\lambda$: $V[f]=\ker(\lambda N)=\langle e_1\rangle$ and $fV=\operatorname{im}(\lambda N)=\langle e_1\rangle$, so $V[f]\subseteq fV$ and the canonical map $V[f]\to V/fV$ is the zero map on a $1$-dimensional space, not an isomorphism; equivalently $V[f]\cap fV=\langle e_1\rangle\ne0$.
* Condition (ii) fails: $V\cong R/(t-\lambda)^2$, which is not a direct sum of modules $R/(f)$ with $f$ irreducible (its submodule $(t-\lambda)V=\langle e_1\rangle$ has no complement, since the only submodules of $R/(t-\lambda)^2$ are $0\subset\langle t-\lambda\rangle/(t-\lambda)^2\subset R/(t-\lambda)^2$).
Hence a complex with a single cohomology group $V$ in degree $0$ and $T$ as above satisfies every purity hypothesis that lemma_12/lemma_20a/lemma_20c can supply, while violating (i), (ii) and (iii). Combining (a)–(c) with those purity results therefore cannot yield semisimplicity; any proof of the conjecture must supply input that actually controls the Jordan form (e.g. a trace/Hankel non-degeneracy criterion as in lemma_68, or a positive-definiteness/anisotropy argument as in lemma_65), and not merely the shape of objects of $D^b(\mathbb{Q}_\ell[t^{\pm1}])$. $\blacksquare$

This completes the proof of (a), (b) and (c), together with the required warning.

lemma_72.statement: (Fixed-factor obstruction to anisotropy of a *-trace form.) Let k = Q_l, let V be a nonzero finite-dimensional k-vector space, and let A be a finite-dimensional commutative unital k-subalgebra of End_k(V). Suppose dagger is a k-linear anti-involution of A and define B(a,b) = Tr_V(a b^dagger). Let N be the nilradical of A, and let A_red = A/N be a product of finite separable field extensions K_i of k. The anti-involution descends to a k-algebra automorphism sigma of A_red of order at most 2, hence permutes the simple factors K_i. If some simple factor is moved by sigma, equivalently if for the primitive idempotent e_i of A_red one has sigma(e_i) != e_i, then B is isotropic: there exists a nonzero a in A with B(a,a) = 0. One proof lifts e_i to an idempotent e in A, observes that e e^dagger maps to e_i sigma(e_i) = 0 in A_red, hence is nilpotent, and therefore has trace zero.
lemma_72.proof:
Throughout, k = \mathbb{Q}_\ell (a field of characteristic 0), V is a nonzero finite-dimensional k-vector space, A \subset \mathrm{End}_k(V) is a finite-dimensional commutative unital k-subalgebra (so 1_A = \mathrm{id}_V), \dagger : A \to A is a k-linear anti-involution, i.e. (ab)^\dagger = b^\dagger a^\dagger and (a^\dagger)^\dagger = a, and B(a,b) := \mathrm{Tr}_V(a\,b^\dagger). We write N for the nilradical of A, \pi : A \twoheadrightarrow A_{\mathrm{red}} := A/N for the quotient map, and we use the given description A_{\mathrm{red}} \cong \prod_{i\in I} K_i as a finite product of finite separable field extensions K_i/k, with e_i \in A_{\mathrm{red}} the idempotent having 1 in the i-th factor and 0 elsewhere. Note I \neq \emptyset since A_{\mathrm{red}} \neq 0 (A is unital and V \neq 0, so 1_A \neq 0).

STEP 1. N is nilpotent and consists exactly of the nilpotent elements of A.
By definition N is the set of nilpotent elements; since A is commutative this is an ideal. A is finite-dimensional over k, hence noetherian, so N = (n_1,\dots,n_s) with each n_j nilpotent, say n_j^{m_j} = 0. Every element of N^M is a k-linear combination of monomials n_1^{a_1}\cdots n_s^{a_s} with a_1+\dots+a_s = M (commutativity is used to reorder factors). If M \ge m_1+\dots+m_s then some a_j \ge m_j, so every such monomial vanishes; hence N^M = 0.

STEP 2. \dagger preserves N, and descends to an automorphism \sigma of A_{\mathrm{red}} with \sigma^2 = \mathrm{id}.
For a \in A and m \ge 1 one has (a^\dagger)^m = (a^m)^\dagger (induction on m using anti-multiplicativity; powers of a single element commute, so no ambiguity). Thus a^m = 0 iff (a^\dagger)^m = 0, i.e. \dagger(N) = N. Define \sigma : A_{\mathrm{red}} \to A_{\mathrm{red}} by \sigma(\pi(a)) := \pi(a^\dagger). Well-definedness: if \pi(a) = \pi(a') then a - a' \in N, so a^\dagger - (a')^\dagger \in N by the preceding sentence. It is k-linear because \dagger is, and multiplicative: \sigma(\pi(a)\pi(b)) = \pi((ab)^\dagger) = \pi(b^\dagger a^\dagger) = \pi(a^\dagger)\pi(b^\dagger) = \sigma(\pi(a))\sigma(\pi(b)) (commutativity of A is used in the middle step). Finally \sigma^2(\pi(a)) = \pi((a^\dagger)^\dagger) = \pi(a), so \sigma^2 = \mathrm{id}; in particular \sigma is a k-algebra automorphism of order dividing 2.

STEP 3. The idempotents of A_{\mathrm{red}}, and the equivalence "K_i is moved by \sigma" \Leftrightarrow "\sigma(e_i) \neq e_i".
An element of \prod_{i\in I} K_i is a tuple (\lambda_i)_i; it is idempotent iff \lambda_i^2 = \lambda_i for all i, and each K_i is a field, hence has only the idempotents 0 and 1. So the idempotents of A_{\mathrm{red}} are exactly the sums \sum_{i\in S} e_i (S \subset I); they satisfy e_i e_j = \delta_{ij} e_i and \sum_{i\in I} e_i = 1. The primitive idempotents (nonzero idempotents that are not a sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents) are exactly the e_i. Now \sigma(e_i) is idempotent, hence \sigma(e_i) = \sum_{j\in S} e_j for some S; if |S| \ge 2 this writes e_i = \sigma(\sigma(e_i)) = \sum_{j\in S}\sigma(e_j) as a sum of \ge 2 pairwise orthogonal nonzero idempotents (each \sigma(e_j) is idempotent, nonzero since \sigma is a unital automorphism, and mutually orthogonal), contradicting primitivity of e_i. Thus \sigma(e_i) = e_{\iota(i)} for a unique \iota(i) \in I, and \iota is an involution of I because \sigma^2 = \mathrm{id}. Under the identification A_{\mathrm{red}} \cong \prod_i K_i, the simple factor K_i is precisely e_i A_{\mathrm{red}}, and \sigma maps e_i A_{\mathrm{red}} isomorphically onto \sigma(e_i) A_{\mathrm{red}} = e_{\iota(i)} A_{\mathrm{red}} = K_{\iota(i)}. Hence the factor K_i is moved by \sigma (i.e. \iota(i) \neq i) iff \sigma(e_i) \neq e_i; this is the announced equivalence. Note also that this forces |I| \ge 2, since \sigma(1) = 1 and 1 = \sum_i e_i.

STEP 4. Idempotent lifting modulo an ideal contained in N.
Claim: if I' \subset N is an ideal and \varepsilon \in A/I' is an idempotent, then there is an idempotent e \in A with \pi(e) = \varepsilon. Proof: choose x \in A with \pi(x) = \varepsilon and put n := x^2 - x; then n \in I' \subset N, so n is nilpotent. Let B := k[x] \subset A and let g \in k[T] be the monic minimal polynomial of x (g exists and is nonzero because x lies in the finite-dimensional k-algebra A, so 1,x,x^2,\dots are linearly dependent). Then B \cong k[T]/(g), and the class of T^2 - T in k[T]/(g) is nilpotent, say (T^2-T)^r \in (g). For any root \alpha of g in \bar k, g(\alpha)=0 gives (\alpha^2-\alpha)^r = 0, hence \alpha^2 = \alpha, so \alpha \in \{0,1\}. As k has characteristic 0, 0 and 1 are distinct, so g = T^a (T-1)^b with a,b \ge 0 and a+b = \deg g \ge 1.
 - If a = 0: x - 1 is nilpotent, so x-1 \in N \subset I' and \varepsilon = \pi(x) = 1 = \pi(1); take e = 1.
 - If b = 0: x is nilpotent, x \in I', \varepsilon = 0 = \pi(0); take e = 0.
 - If a \ge 1 and b \ge 1: T^a and (T-1)^b are coprime in k[T], so the Chinese remainder theorem gives a k-algebra isomorphism \varphi: B \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } k[T]/(T^a) \times k[T]/((T-1)^b), with T \mapsto (T \bmod T^a,\; T \bmod (T-1)^b). Let e \in B be the element with \varphi(e) = (0,1). Then e^2 = e. Moreover \varphi(e - T) = (-T \bmod T^a,\; 1-T \bmod (T-1)^b); the first component lies in the ideal (T) of k[T]/(T^a), which is nilpotent, and the second lies in the ideal (T-1) of k[T]/((T-1)^b), also nilpotent. An element of a product ring is nilpotent iff each component is, so e - x is nilpotent in B, hence in A, hence e - x \in N \subset I'. Therefore \pi(e) = \pi(x) = \varepsilon. This proves the claim. \quad(\ast)

STEP 5. Trace of a nilpotent endomorphism is 0.
Let z \in \mathrm{End}_k(V) with z^m = 0. The descending chain V \supset zV \supset z^2V \supset \dots \supset z^mV = 0 can be refined to a full flag V = W_0 \supset W_1 \supset \dots \supset W_{D-1} \supset W_D = 0 with \dim_k W_j/W_{j+1} = 1 and zW_j \subset W_{j+1}. Choosing a basis adapted to the flag, the matrix of z is strictly upper triangular, so \mathrm{Tr}_V(z) = 0. (Equivalently: the characteristic polynomial of a nilpotent endomorphism is T^{\dim V}.)

STEP 6. Construction of the isotropic vector (the argument indicated in the statement).
Assume some simple factor is moved; by Step 3 this means there is i \in I with \sigma(e_i) = e_j \neq e_i. By the lifting claim (\ast) applied to I' = N and \varepsilon = e_i, choose an idempotent e \in A with \pi(e) = e_i. Then:
(a) \pi(e^\dagger) = \sigma(\pi(e)) = \sigma(e_i) = e_j, by the definition of \sigma in Step 2;
(b) \pi(e\,e^\dagger) = \pi(e)\,\pi(e^\dagger) = e_i e_j = 0 by the orthogonality of Step 3, since i \ne j;
(c) hence e\,e^\dagger \in N, so e\,e^\dagger is nilpotent in A; as A \subset \mathrm{End}_k(V) is a subalgebra with the same unit, (e\,e^\dagger)^m = 0 in A means exactly that e\,e^\dagger is a nilpotent endomorphism of V;
(d) by Step 5, \mathrm{Tr}_V(e\,e^\dagger) = 0, i.e. B(e,e) = 0;
(e) e \neq 0, because \pi(e) = e_i \neq 0.
Thus 0 \neq e \in A satisfies B(e,e) = 0, so B is isotropic. In fact e may be taken to be a nonzero idempotent.

STEP 7. Variant (no idempotent lifting needed).
The same conclusion follows more directly: for ANY lift x \in A of e_i one has \pi(x\,x^\dagger) = e_i\sigma(e_i) = 0, so x\,x^\dagger \in N is nilpotent, hence B(x,x) = \mathrm{Tr}_V(x\,x^\dagger) = 0, and x \neq 0 because \pi(x) = e_i \neq 0. Step 4 shows one can additionally arrange the isotropic vector to be an idempotent, which is the version stated in the hint. (Note that Step 6 also works verbatim with any lift, so the two arguments agree after replacing x by its idempotent approximation.)

STEP 8. Remarks on hypotheses and on what is used.
- Commutativity of A is used twice: in Step 1 (N is an ideal generated by nilpotents, and N^M = 0 by reordering) and in Steps 2 (\sigma is multiplicative, so an automorphism rather than merely an anti-automorphism) and 6(b) (\pi(e)\pi(e^\dagger) = \pi(e\,e^\dagger) is automatic, but the identification of \pi(e\,e^\dagger) with e_i\sigma(e_i) as a product of commuting idempotents is what gives orthogonality).
- The hypothesis that the K_i are fields is used in Step 3 to conclude that the only idempotents of \prod_i K_i are the \{0,1\}-valued tuples, hence that the primitive idempotents are exactly the e_i. In characteristic 0 this is automatic for any finite-dimensional commutative k-algebra: A_{\mathrm{red}} is an artinian reduced k-algebra, hence a finite product of finite field extensions of k, and these are separable because k has characteristic 0.
- The argument is characteristic-free apart from the last point: nilpotent endomorphisms have trace 0 in every characteristic (Step 5), and idempotents lift modulo nil ideals in every characteristic (Step 4).
- No symmetry of B is needed: isotropy only asks for one nonzero a with B(a,a) = 0. (Indeed B need not be symmetric here, since \mathrm{Tr}_V(y) = \mathrm{Tr}_V(y^\dagger) was not assumed.)

STEP 9. Contrapositive form (the point of the lemma in applications).
Combining Steps 3 and 6: if B is anisotropic on A (i.e. B(a,a) \neq 0 for every 0 \neq a \in A, the hypothesis used in the trace-form criterion for semisimplicity), then the involution \sigma of Step 2 must fix every primitive idempotent e_i of A_{\mathrm{red}}, hence must preserve each simple factor K_i. Equivalently, the existence of a Frobenius-stable decomposition of A_{\mathrm{red}} in which the induced involution interchanges two factors is an obstruction to anisotropy of the *-trace form, and therefore also an obstruction to the semisimplicity conclusion that anisotropy is meant to deliver.

This completes the proof of the lemma. \hfill\blacksquare

lemma_73.statement: (Weight-separated Frobenius modules split: the Sylvester-map criterion.) Let l be a prime, V a finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space, T in GL(V), and 0 -> V' -> V -> V'' -> 0 an exact sequence with V' T-stable and V'' := V/V'. Write T' := T|_{V'} and T'' for the induced operator on V''. (i) The Sylvester map Phi: Hom_Q_l(V'',V') -> Hom_Q_l(V'',V'), Phi(X) = T' X - X T'', is invertible if and only if chi_{T'} and chi_{T''} are coprime in Q_l[t]. Proof route: identify Hom(V'',V') with V' tensor (V'')^* and note Phi = T' tensor id - id tensor (T'')^vee, where (T'')^vee is the transpose on the dual; over Q_l_bar, if alpha_1,...,alpha_r and beta_1,...,beta_s are the eigenvalues of T' and T'' with multiplicity, the eigenvalues of Phi are exactly the differences alpha_i - beta_j (upper-triangularise both operators; the eigenvalues of (T'')^vee are those of T''). Hence Phi is invertible iff no alpha_i equals some beta_j, i.e. iff chi_{T'} and chi_{T''} have no common root in Q_l_bar, i.e. iff their gcd is 1 (equivalently the resultant Res(chi_{T'},chi_{T''}) is nonzero). Also record the multiplicative variant Psi(X) = T' X (T'')^{-1} - X, whose eigenvalues are alpha_i/beta_j, invertible under the same condition. (ii) CONSEQUENCE (splitting and reassembly): if chi_{T'} and chi_{T''} are coprime then the sequence splits T-equivariantly - choose any linear section s: V'' -> V, check that u := T s - s T'' takes values in V', and replace s by s' = s + X with X := -Phi^{-1}(u), which is a T-equivariant section; moreover, if in addition T is semisimple on V' and on V'', then T is semisimple on V (use V = V' (+) s'(V'') and the minimal-polynomial/lcm criterion, or lemma_60(v)). (iii) WEIGHT FORM: fix an embedding iota: Q_l_bar -> C and integers a != b. If every eigenvalue alpha of T' satisfies iota(|alpha|) = q^{a/2} and every eigenvalue beta of T'' satisfies |iota(beta)| = q^{b/2}, then chi_{T'} and chi_{T''} are coprime (a common root would give q^{a/2} = q^{b/2}), so the conclusions of (ii) hold. In particular Ext^1 between pure Frobenius modules of different weights is semisimple, and semisimplicity is stable under such extensions. (iv) FILTERED VERSION: if V carries a finite T-stable filtration 0 = V_0 subset ... subset V_m = V such that T is semisimple on each graded piece gr_j and the characteristic polynomials of T on the gr_j are pairwise coprime, then T is semisimple on V (induction on m using (ii)). (v) Sharpness, to be stated explicitly: coprimeness cannot be dropped. Over Q_l take V = Q_l^2, T given by the matrix [[1,1],[0,1]], V' = Q_l e_1; then chi_{T'} = chi_{T''} = t - 1, Phi = 0 is not invertible, the extension does not split T-equivariantly, and T is not semisimple (mu_T = (t-1)^2, lemma_60(ii)). Pure linear algebra; do not cite lemma_5, lemma_8, lemma_60 beyond the quoted equivalence, and do not use any geometry.
lemma_73.proof:
Everything is pure linear algebra over $k:=\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}$; no geometry and no other provided lemma is used. We first fix conventions and prove two preliminary facts (P1, P2) that are quoted throughout, then prove (i)-(v).

=== CONVENTIONS ===
(1) For $W$ a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space and $S\in\operatorname{End}_k(W)$, $\chi_S(t):=\det(t\,\mathrm{id}_W-S)\in k[t]$, monic of degree $\dim W$. If $W=0$ this is the empty determinant, i.e. $\chi_S=1$. The minimal polynomial $\mu_S$ is the monic generator of $\{P\in k[t]:P(S)=0\}$; for $W=0$ this ideal is all of $k[t]$, so $\mu_S:=1$.
(2) Resultant convention. For monic $f=\prod_{a=1}^{r}(t-\alpha_a)$ and $g=\prod_{c=1}^{s}(t-\beta_c)$ in $\overline{k}[t]$ (roots listed with multiplicity) we set $\operatorname{Res}(f,g):=\prod_{a=1}^{r} g(\alpha_a)=\prod_{a=1}^{r}\prod_{c=1}^{s}(\alpha_a-\beta_c)$. With this convention $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=0$ iff $f$ and $g$ have a common root, and $\operatorname{Res}(g,f)=(-1)^{rs}\operatorname{Res}(f,g)$; the opposite sign appears only if one uses the other convention. Empty products are $1$.
(3) "Semisimple" for an endomorphism is defined by (and the proof of) P1 below; the three conditions there are equivalent, so the definition is unambiguous and matches both the primary-decomposition and the $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}$-diagonalisability meanings.

=== P1 (square-free minimal polynomial criterion; valid for every endomorphism of every finite-dimensional $k$-space, including $W=0$) ===
Let $W$ be finite dimensional over $k=\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ and $S\in\operatorname{End}_k(W)$. The following are equivalent:
(a) $W=\bigoplus_{f} W[f]$, where $f$ runs over the monic irreducibles of $k[t]$ and $W[f]:=\ker f(S)$ (only finitely many are non-zero);
(b) $\mu_S$ is square-free in $k[t]$;
(c) $S\otimes_k \overline{k}$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$.
Proof. (a)$\Rightarrow$(b): if $W=\bigoplus_{i\in I}W[f_i]$ with the $f_i$ distinct irreducibles, then $P:=\prod_{i\in I}f_i$ satisfies $P(S)=0$: for $w=\sum_i w_i$ one has $P(S)w=\sum_i P(S)w_i$, and the factor $f_i(S)$ kills $w_i$ while all factors commute. Hence $\mu_S\mid P$, and a divisor of a square-free polynomial is square-free.
(b)$\Rightarrow$(a): write $\mu_S=\prod_{i=1}^{n}f_i$ with distinct monic irreducibles (for $W=0$ there is nothing to do). The Chinese remainder theorem gives a $k$-algebra isomorphism $k[t]/(\mu_S)\xrightarrow{\sim}\prod_i k[t]/(f_i)$; let $\bar e_i$ be the idempotent mapping to $(0,\dots,1,\dots,0)$ and set $e_i\in k[t]$ for any lift. Then $\sum_i \bar e_i=\overline{1}$ in $k[t]/(\mu_S)$, so $\mathrm{id}_W=\sum_i e_i(S)$, and $e_i(S)e_j(S)=0$ for $i\neq j$ because $\bar e_i\bar e_j=0$. Thus $W=\bigoplus_i W_i$ with $W_i:=\operatorname{im} e_i(S)$, each $W_i$ $S$-stable. Since $f_i\bar e_i=0$ in $k[t]/(\mu_S)$ we get $f_i(S)|_{W_i}=0$, i.e. $W_i\subseteq W[f_i]$. For $j\neq i$, $\gcd(f_i,f_j)=1$ gives $a,b\in k[t]$ with $af_i+bf_j=1$, hence $a(S)f_i(S)=\mathrm{id}$ on $W_j$ (as $f_j(S)|_{W_j}=0$); so $f_i(S)$ is invertible on $W_j$ and $W[f_i]\cap W_j=0$. Consequently $W[f_i]=W_i$ and $W=\bigoplus_i W[f_i]$, which is (a).
(b)$\Leftrightarrow$(c): $\overline{k}$ is flat over $k$, so the ideal of polynomials in $\overline{k}[t]$ killing $\overline{S}:=S\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is $\overline{k}\cdot(\mu_S)$ (compute $\operatorname{End}_k(W)\to\operatorname{End}_{\overline{k}}(\overline{W})$ entrywise in a basis: $P(\overline S)=0$ iff all entries of $P(S)$ vanish, iff $P(S)=0$). Hence $\mu_{\overline S}$ is the image of $\mu_S$ in $\overline{k}[t]$. Over the algebraically closed field $\overline{k}$, $\overline S$ is diagonalisable with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m$ iff $\prod_i(\overline S-\lambda_i\mathrm{id})=0$ and no proper subproduct vanishes, i.e. iff $\mu_{\overline S}=\prod_i(t-\lambda_i)$ has distinct roots: if $\overline W=\bigoplus_i\ker(\overline S-\lambda_i)$ then $\prod_i(\overline S-\lambda_i)=0$, so $\mu_{\overline S}$ is square-free; conversely if $\mu_{\overline S}=\prod_i(t-\lambda_i)$ with the $\lambda_i$ distinct, the argument of (b)$\Rightarrow$(a) applied with the linear factors $f_i=t-\lambda_i$ gives $\overline W=\bigoplus_i\ker(\overline S-\lambda_i)$, i.e. diagonalisability. Finally $\mu_S$ is square-free in $k[t]$ iff $\mu_{\overline S}$ is square-free in $\overline{k}[t]$: square-freeness means $\gcd(\mu,\mu')=1$, and $\mu'\in k[t]$ is non-zero whenever $\mu$ is non-constant because $\operatorname{char}k=0$; the gcd is computed by the Euclidean algorithm inside $k[t]$, and a Bézout identity $1=a\mu+b\mu'$ in $k[t]$ is also one in $\overline{k}[t]$, while a non-constant common divisor in $k[t]$ remains one in $\overline{k}[t]$. (For $W=0$, $\mu_S=1$ and (a),(b),(c) are all trivially true.) This proves P1. We use it for arbitrary endomorphisms (not only invertible ones, not only on non-zero spaces); it specialises to the equivalence (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii) of lemma_60 in that case, but we do not rely on lemma_60.

=== P2 (triangularisation over an algebraically closed field) ===
Let $K$ be algebraically closed, $U$ a finite-dimensional $K$-space, $L\in\operatorname{End}_K(U)$. Then $L$ admits a complete invariant flag $0=U_0\subset U_1\subset\cdots\subset U_{\dim U}=U$ with $\dim U_j=j$: induct on $\dim U$; $\chi_L$ has a root $\lambda\in K$, so $\ker(L-\lambda)\neq0$; take $U_1$ inside it and pass to the quotient. Choosing $g_j\in U_j\setminus U_{j-1}$, the matrix of $L$ is upper triangular (with the convention $Lg_j=\sum_i M_{ij}g_i$, upper triangular means $M_{ij}=0$ for $i>j$, which is exactly $L(U_j)\subseteq U_j$) with diagonal entries $\gamma_j:=$ the scalar by which $L$ acts on $U_j/U_{j-1}$. Hence $\chi_L(t)=\prod_j(t-\gamma_j)$: the multiset $\{\gamma_j\}$ is the multiset of eigenvalues of $L$ counted with algebraic multiplicity, and it depends only on $L$, not on the flag.

=== PART (i) ===
Let $r:=\dim_k V'$, $s:=\dim_k V''$.
Step 0 (zero-dimensional cases). If $r=0$ or $s=0$ then $\operatorname{Hom}_k(V'',V')=0$, and $\Phi$ is the identity map of the zero space, hence invertible. On the other hand the corresponding characteristic polynomial is $1$ by Convention (1), which is coprime to every polynomial. So both sides of the equivalence are true; from now on assume $r,s\ge1$ (all products below are then non-empty; with the empty-product convention the formulas also hold as written).
Step 1 ($T'$ and $T''$ are invertible). $T\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$ and $V'$ is $T$-stable, so $T':=T|_{V'}$ is injective on the finite-dimensional space $V'$, hence bijective: $T'\in\operatorname{GL}(V')$ and $T^{-1}(V')=V'$. For $\pi:V\twoheadrightarrow V''$, define $T''^{-1}(\pi v):=\pi(T^{-1}v)$: this is well defined because $v-\pi$-equivalent vectors differ by an element of $V'$, and $T^{-1}(V')=V'$; it is an inverse of $T''$ since $TT^{-1}=T^{-1}T=\mathrm{id}_V$. So $T''\in\operatorname{GL}(V'')$; in particular no eigenvalue of $T'$ or $T''$ is $0$.
Step 2 (the Sylvester map as a Kronecker difference). The map $V'\otimes_k (V'')^{*}\to\operatorname{Hom}_k(V'',V')$, $\xi\otimes\varphi\mapsto X_{\xi,\varphi}$ with $X_{\xi,\varphi}(v'')=\varphi(v'')\xi$, is an isomorphism: if $f_1,\dots,f_s$ is a basis of $V''$ with dual basis $f^{*}_1,\dots,f^{*}_s$, the inverse is $X\mapsto\sum_{c=1}^{s}X(f_c)\otimes f^{*}_c$, and the two composites are the identity (check on pure tensors and on maps). Write $A:=T'\in\operatorname{End}(V')$ and $B:=(T'')^{\vee}\in\operatorname{End}((V'')^{*})$, $B\varphi=\varphi\circ T''$. Then for a pure tensor, $T'\circ X_{\xi,\varphi}=X_{A\xi,\varphi}$ (because $X_{\xi,\varphi}$ lands in $V'$, on which $T$ acts as $T'$), and $X_{\xi,\varphi}\circ T''=X_{\xi,B\varphi}$. By linearity and since pure tensors span, transport of structure along the above isomorphism gives
$\Phi\;\longleftrightarrow\; A\otimes\mathrm{id}_{(V'')^{*}}-\mathrm{id}_{V'}\otimes B.$
Step 3 (the transpose does not change the characteristic polynomial). In the dual basis to a basis of $V''$, the matrix of $B=(T'')^{\vee}$ is the transpose of the matrix of $T''$; since $\det N^{t}=\det N$, $\chi_B(t)=\det(tI-B^{t})=\det((tI-\text{matrix of }T'')^{t})=\chi_{T''}(t)$. Thus the eigenvalue multiset $\{\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_s\}$ of $B$ equals the eigenvalue multiset $\{\beta_1,\dots,\beta_s\}$ of $T''$.
Step 4 (simultaneous triangularisation and the determinant). Extend scalars to $\overline{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$; write the extended spaces and maps with a bar. Scalar extension is exact and faithful, and $\det_{\overline{k}}(\overline{\Phi})=\det_k(\Phi)$, so $\Phi$ is invertible iff $\overline{\Phi}$ is. By P2 choose a complete $A$-invariant flag $F_1\subset\cdots\subset F_r$ of $\overline{V'}$ with basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$, so $Ae_a=\alpha_a e_a+\sum_{b<a}c_{ba}e_b$ where $\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$ is the eigenvalue multiset of $T'$; and a complete $B$-invariant flag $G_1\subset\cdots\subset G_s$ of $\overline{(V'')^{*}}$ with basis $g_1,\dots,g_s$, so $Bg_c=\gamma_c g_c+\sum_{d<c}d_{dc}g_d$. Order the pairs $(a,c)\in\{1,\dots,r\}\times\{1,\dots,s\}$ lexicographically: $(b,d)\le(a,c)$ iff $b<a$, or $b=a$ and $d\le c$. In the ordered basis $w_{(a,c)}:=e_a\otimes g_c$ of $\overline{V'}\otimes\overline{(V'')^{*}}$ we have
$(A\otimes\mathrm{id})w_{(a,c)}=\alpha_a w_{(a,c)}+\sum_{b<a}c_{ba}w_{(b,c)}$ with $(b,c)<(a,c)$,
$(\mathrm{id}\otimes B)w_{(a,c)}=\gamma_c w_{(a,c)}+\sum_{d<c}d_{dc}w_{(a,d)}$ with $(a,d)<(a,c)$.
Both sums involve only basis vectors preceding $w_{(a,c)}$, so both operators are upper triangular in this single ordering, hence so is their difference $\overline{\Phi}$. (No flag $W_n$ and no dimension count is needed; the lexicographic order is a total order extending the product order, which is exactly what makes both matrices triangular.) Its diagonal entries are $\alpha_a-\gamma_c$ for $1\le a\le r$, $1\le c\le s$. By P2 applied to $\overline{\Phi}$,
$\chi_{\Phi}(t)=\prod_{a=1}^{r}\prod_{c=1}^{s}\bigl(t-(\alpha_a-\beta_c)\bigr)$,
so the eigenvalues of $\Phi$ on $\operatorname{Hom}_{\overline{k}}(\overline{V''},\overline{V'})$, counted with multiplicity, are exactly the differences $\alpha_a-\beta_c$, and (taking $t=0$)
$\det(\Phi)=\prod_{a,c}(\alpha_a-\beta_c)=\operatorname{Res}(\chi_{T'},\chi_{T''})$,
with NO factor $(-1)^{rs}$ under Convention (2); the factor $(-1)^{rs}$ appears only if one writes the resultant in the opposite order, $\operatorname{Res}(\chi_{T''},\chi_{T'})$. Both $\chi_{\Phi}$ and $\operatorname{Res}(\chi_{T'},\chi_{T''})$ lie in $k[t]$ resp. $k$, as they must, since the expressions are symmetric in each family of roots.
Step 5 (the equivalences). $\Phi$ is invertible $\iff\det\Phi\ne0\iff$ no $\alpha_a$ equals some $\beta_c\iff\chi_{T'}$ and $\chi_{T''}$ have no common root in $\overline{k}\iff\gcd(\chi_{T'},\chi_{T''})=1$ in $k[t]$. The last equivalence: a common divisor of positive degree has an irreducible factor $h$, and $h$ has a root in the algebraically closed field $\overline{k}$, which is a common root of both characteristic polynomials; conversely a common root $\gamma$ has a minimal polynomial over $k$ dividing both. Equivalently, by the displayed formula, $\Phi$ is invertible iff $\operatorname{Res}(\chi_{T'},\chi_{T''})\ne0$.
Step 6 (multiplicative variant). Let $M:\operatorname{Hom}(V'',V')\to\operatorname{Hom}(V'',V')$, $M(X)=T'X(T'')^{-1}$, and $\Psi(X)=M(X)-X=T'X(T'')^{-1}-X$. Transport of structure: $X_{\xi,\varphi}\mapsto X_{A\xi,\,B^{-1}\varphi}$, because $\varphi\circ(T'')^{-1}=((T'')^{\vee})^{-1}\varphi=B^{-1}\varphi$; hence $M\leftrightarrow A\otimes B^{-1}$ and $\Psi\leftrightarrow A\otimes B^{-1}-\mathrm{id}$. Each $G_c$ is $B^{-1}$-stable: $B(G_c)\subseteq G_c$ and $B$ is injective on the finite-dimensional $G_c$, so $B|_{G_c}\in\operatorname{Aut}(G_c)$ and $B^{-1}G_c=G_c$; the induced map on $G_c/G_{c-1}$ is $\gamma_c^{-1}$. Thus in the same ordered basis, $A\otimes B^{-1}$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $\alpha_a\gamma_c^{-1}=\alpha_a/\beta_c$: the eigenvalues of the multiplicative Sylvester operator $M$ are exactly the quotients $\alpha_a/\beta_c$, and those of $\Psi=M-\mathrm{id}$ are $\alpha_a/\beta_c-1$. Consequently
$\det(\Psi)=\prod_{a,c}(\alpha_a\beta_c^{-1}-1)=\Bigl(\prod_c\beta_c^{-1}\Bigr)^{r}\prod_{a,c}(\alpha_a-\beta_c)=(\det T'')^{-r}\operatorname{Res}(\chi_{T'},\chi_{T'')})$,
where $\det T''=\prod_c\beta_c\ne0$ by Step 1. Hence $\Psi$ is invertible iff no $\alpha_a/\beta_c$ equals $1$, i.e. under exactly the same coprimeness condition as $\Phi$. This completes (i).

=== PART (ii): splitting and reassembly ===
Assume $\chi_{T'}$ and $\chi_{T''}$ are coprime, so $\Phi$ is invertible by (i). If $V'=0$ or $V''=0$ the sequence splits trivially, so suppose $r,s\ge1$. Let $s:V''\to V$ be any $k$-linear section of $\pi$. Define $u:=T\circ s-s\circ T''\in\operatorname{Hom}_k(V'',V)$. Then $u$ lands in $V'$: $\pi u(v'')=\pi T s(v'')-sT''(v'')=T''\pi s(v'')-sT''(v'')=T''(v'')-T''(v'')=0$, using $\pi\circ T=T''\circ\pi$. Moreover, for $X\in\operatorname{Hom}(V'',V')$ we have $TX=\Phi$-precomposition... explicitly $\Phi(X)=T'X-XT''=T\circ X-X\circ T''$ as maps $V''\to V$, since $X$ lands in $V'$ where $T=T'$. Put $X:=-\Phi^{-1}(u)$ and $s':=s+X$. Then
$T\circ s'-s'\circ T''=u+\Phi(X)=u-u=0$, so $T\,s'(v'')=s'(T''v'')$ for all $v''$, i.e. $s'$ is $T$-equivariant; and $\pi s'=\pi s+\pi X=\mathrm{id}_{V''}+0$, since $\operatorname{im}X\subseteq V'=\ker\pi$, so $s'$ is a section. Hence $V=V'+s'(V'')$, and $V'\cap s'(V'')=0$ (if $v'=s'(w'')$ then applying $\pi$ gives $w''=0$, hence $v'=0$). Thus $V=V'\oplus s'(V'')$ as $T$-modules, with $T|_{s'(V'')}=s'T''s'^{-1}$.
Now suppose in addition that $T$ is semisimple on $V'$ and on $V''$. Under the decomposition, $P(T)=P(T')\oplus P(T''s'^{-1})$ for every $P\in k[t]$, so $P(T)=0$ iff $P$ kills both $T'$ and $T''$, iff $\mu_{T'}\mid P$ and $\mu_{T''}\mid P$. Therefore $\mu_T=\operatorname{lcm}(\mu_{T'},\mu_{T''})$. By P1, $\mu_{T'}$ and $\mu_{T''}$ are square-free, i.e. products of distinct monic irreducibles; their lcm takes the maximum of the two exponents at each irreducible, hence is again a product of distinct irreducibles, i.e. square-free. By P1 again, $T$ is semisimple on $V$. (Equivalently, in the notation of P1(a), $V[f]=V'[f]\oplus s'(V''[f])$ and the sum over $f$ is all of $V$.) This proves (ii).

=== PART (iii): weight form ===
Fix an embedding $\iota:\overline{k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$, a real number $q>1$ (in applications a prime power $p^{f}$; we deliberately do NOT write $q=p^{a}$ because $a$ is already used for a weight), and integers $a\ne b$. Assume $|\iota(\alpha)|=q^{a/2}$ for every eigenvalue $\alpha\in\overline{k}$ of $T'$ and $|\iota(\beta)|=q^{b/2}$ for every eigenvalue $\beta\in\overline{k}$ of $T''$ (complex modulus; these numbers are non-zero because $T',T''$ are invertible, Step 1 of (i)). If $\chi_{T'}$ and $\chi_{T''}$ had a common root $\gamma\in\overline{k}$, then $q^{a/2}=|\iota(\gamma)|=q^{b/2}$. The map $x\mapsto q^{x/2}$ is strictly increasing (hence injective) on $\mathbb{R}$ because $q>1$, so $a=b$, contradiction. Thus $\chi_{T'}$ and $\chi_{T''}$ are coprime, and by (i) $\Phi$ is invertible and by (ii) the sequence splits $T$-equivariantly; furthermore, if $T$ is semisimple on $V'$ and on $V''$, then $T$ is semisimple on $V$.
Reformulation in the category of Frobenius modules: let $\mathcal{C}$ be the abelian category of finite-dimensional $k$-spaces equipped with an automorphism (equivalently finitely generated torsion $k[t^{\pm1}]$-modules, $t$ acting as $T$). Extensions $0\to V'\to V\to V''\to0$ in $\mathcal{C}$ are classified by $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{C}}(V'',V')$, the zero class being the split extension. Saying "$V'$ is pure of weight $a$ and $V''$ pure of weight $b$" means exactly the modulus hypothesis above (with $q$ the size of the ground field). Hence (iii) says: $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{C}}(V'',V')=0$ for $a\ne b$, i.e. there are no non-trivial extensions between pure objects of different weights, and semisimplicity is stable under extensions of different weights. (This is the linear-algebra content of the weight-separation part of the decomposition theorem; note that the argument uses only the moduli of the eigenvalues, not their arithmeticity.)

=== PART (iv): filtered version ===
P3 (multiplicativity of $\chi$ in exact sequences). If $0\to U\to W\to Q\to0$ is exact with $U$ stable under $S\in\operatorname{End}(W)$, then $\chi_S=\chi_{S|_U}\,\chi_{S|_Q}$: take a basis $u_1,\dots,u_p$ of $U$, extend by lifts of a basis of $Q$; the matrix of $S$ is block upper triangular $\begin{pmatrix}S_U&*\\0&S_Q\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det(tI-S)$ is the product of the two diagonal block determinants.
Now let $0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_m=V$ be a $T$-stable filtration with $\operatorname{gr}_j:=V_j/V_{j-1}$, assume $T$ semisimple on each $\operatorname{gr}_j$ and that the $\chi_{T|\operatorname{gr}_j}$ are pairwise coprime. Induct on $m$. For $m=0$ ($V=0$) and $m=1$ ($V=\operatorname{gr}_1$) there is nothing to prove. For $m\ge2$ set $V':=V_{m-1}$ and $V'':=V/V_{m-1}\cong\operatorname{gr}_m$ (a $T$-equivariant isomorphism, since $V_{m-1}$ is $T$-stable). By P3 applied repeatedly to $0\to V_{j-1}\to V_j\to\operatorname{gr}_j\to0$, $\chi_{T|_{V'}}=\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}\chi_{T|\operatorname{gr}_j}$. If an irreducible $h\in k[t]$ divided both $\chi_{T|_{V'}}$ and $\chi_{T|\operatorname{gr}_m}$, then by Euclid's lemma (irreducible $=$ prime in the PID $k[t]$) $h$ would divide $\chi_{T|\operatorname{gr}_j}$ for some $j\le m-1$, contradicting pairwise coprimeness. Hence $\chi_{T|_{V'}}$ and $\chi_{T|_{V''}}$ are coprime, so by (ii) the sequence $0\to V'\to V\to V''\to0$ splits $T$-equivariantly. By the induction hypothesis $T$ is semisimple on $V'$ (its filtration $0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_{m-1}$ satisfies the same hypotheses), and $T$ is semisimple on $V''\cong\operatorname{gr}_m$ by assumption; the second part of (ii) gives that $T$ is semisimple on $V$. This proves (iv).

=== PART (v): sharpness ===
Take $V=k^{2}$ with basis $e_1,e_2$ and $T$ given by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, i.e. $T(e_1)=e_1$, $T(e_2)=e_1+e_2$. Then $T\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$ ($\det T=1$), and $V':=ke_1$ is $T$-stable, with quotient $V'':=V/V'$ one-dimensional, basis $\bar e:=e_2+V'$. We have $T'=\mathrm{id}_{V'}$ and $T''\bar e=T(e_2)+V'=e_2+V'=\bar e$, so $T''=\mathrm{id}_{V''}$; hence $\chi_{T'}=\chi_{T''}=t-1$, which are not coprime. Here $\operatorname{Hom}_k(V'',V')\cong k$ and $\Phi(X)=T'X-XT''=X-X=0$ for every $X$, so $\Phi$ is the zero endomorphism of a $1$-dimensional space: not invertible, in agreement with $\det\Phi=\prod_{a,c}(\alpha_a-\beta_c)=1-1=0=\operatorname{Res}(t-1,t-1)$ from (i). The extension does not split in the $T$-equivariant sense: a $T$-equivariant section $\sigma:V''\to V$ would have $\sigma(\bar e)=v=ae_1+be_2$ with $b=1$ (so that $\pi v=\bar e$) and $Tv=v$; but $Tv=(a+1)e_1+be_2$, so $a+1=a$, impossible. Finally $T$ is not semisimple: $(T-\mathrm{id})(e_2)=e_1$ and $(T-\mathrm{id})(e_1)=0$, so $(T-\mathrm{id})^{2}=0$ while $T\ne\mathrm{id}$, whence $\mu_T=(t-1)^{2}$, which is not square-free; by P1, $T$ is not semisimple. Concretely, the eigenvector equation $T(x,y)=\lambda(x,y)$, i.e. $(x+y,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda y)$, forces $y=0$ and $\lambda=1$, so the $1$-eigenspace is $ke_1$; after scalar extension to $\overline{k}$ the eigenspace is $\overline{k}e_1$, of dimension $1<2$, so $T\otimes\overline{k}$ is a non-trivial Jordan block and is not diagonalisable. Note also that $T'$ and $T''$ are both pure of weight $0$ here, so the hypothesis $a\ne b$ of (iii) is genuinely used. This shows that neither the coprimeness hypothesis in (i)-(ii) nor the distinct-weight hypothesis in (iii)-(iv) can be dropped.

All parts (i)-(v) are proved, and the proof uses only linear algebra over $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ (P1-P3 are proved inline; lemma_5, lemma_8 and lemma_60 are not cited).

lemma_74.statement: (The exact missing arithmetic input: (ND) is equivalent to (GC), and (ND) settles the conjecture.) Let q=p^a be a prime power and let l != p be a prime. Consider the hypothesis (ND): for every integer m >= 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected variety Y over F_{q^m} of pure dimension d, and every n >= 0, writing V := H^n_et(Y_{Fbar_q},Q_l) (nonzero finite dimensional over Q_l) and F for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of V, the bilinear form beta(a,b) := Tr_V(ab) on the finite-dimensional commutative unital Q_l-algebra A := Q_l[F] subset End_{Q_l}(V) is NONDEGENERATE, i.e. a in A with Tr_V(ab) = 0 for all b in A forces a = 0. Prove both directions of the equivalence (ND) <=> (GC), where (GC) is the hypothesis of lemma_59, and deduce the conjecture from (ND). Route: (1) for T := F, lemma_68(i)-(ii) identifies A with Q_l[t]/(mu_T) in the basis 1,T,...,T^{r-1} (r := deg mu_T) and shows det(s_{i+j}) != 0 <=> beta nondegenerate on A <=> T semisimple on V; do not reprove lemma_68. (2) Add the structural refinement, proved from lemma_66/lemma_68 inline: beta nondegenerate on A <=> A has no nonzero nilpotents <=> A is reduced <=> mu_F is squarefree <=> F is semisimple on V; and the radical of beta is exactly the nilradical of A. (3) Hence (ND) holds for (Y,m,n) if and only if arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n(Y_bar,Q_l), so (ND) <=> (GC) as statements; then lemma_59 gives the conjecture from (ND). (4) Record the two cautions that make this a diagnosis rather than a proof: (a) by lemma_68(iv) nondegeneracy of beta passes to Frobenius-stable direct summands, so it suffices to check (ND) on the primary pieces V[f^{infty}] of lemma_60 and on the isotypic pieces supplied by lemma_27/lemma_31; (b) replacing beta by h(a,b) := Tr_V(a sigma(b)) for an anti-involution sigma of A does not help by itself: if sigma is a Q_l-linear automorphism of A (as happens when A is stable under the adjoint of a perfect pairing, lemma_69(1)) then h is nondegenerate if and only if beta is, since sigma is bijective with sigma^2 = id, so nondegeneracy of h is again EQUIVALENT to (GC), while anisotropy of h is strictly stronger and is not equivalent to it. Do not assert (ND), do not cite any external semisimplicity or standard-conjecture theorem, and do not attempt a counterexample route.
lemma_74.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_74.

=====================================================================
§0. STANDING NOTATION AND THE TWO HYPOTHESES
=====================================================================
Fix q = p^a and a prime l != p, and write K := Q_l and kbar := Fbar_q. For each integer m >= 1 put q_m := q^m = p^{am} and K_m := F_{q_m} subset kbar; then kbar is also an algebraic closure of K_m, and a K_m-scheme Y has base change Y_{kbar}.

(GC) = the hypothesis of lemma_59: for every m >= 1 and every smooth projective GEOMETRICALLY CONNECTED variety Y over K_m, arithmetic Frobenius over K_m acts semisimply on H^n(Y_{kbar},K) for every n >= 0.

(ND) = the hypothesis of the present lemma: for every m >= 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected Y/K_m of pure dimension d, and every n >= 0, writing V := H^n_et(Y_{kbar},K) (nonzero finite-dimensional over K) and F for the q_m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of V, the K-bilinear form beta(a,b) := Tr_V(ab) on A := K[F] subset End_K(V) is NONDEGENERATE: beta(a,b) = 0 for all b in A forces a = 0.

(F1) A is a finite-dimensional commutative unital K-algebra: A is the image of the evaluation homomorphism ev_F: K[t] -> End_K(V), P |-> P(F), whose kernel is the ideal (mu_F) generated by the minimal polynomial, so A = K[t]/(mu_F) and dim_K A = deg mu_F <= dim_K V. Explicitly, by lemma_68(i), if r := deg mu_F then 1, F, ..., F^{r-1} is a K-basis of A, and in that basis beta has Gram matrix H = (s_{i+j})_{0<=i,j<=r-1} with s_k := Tr_V(F^k).

(F2) The operator F is LITERALLY THE SAME MAP in (ND) and in (GC); no comparison of Frobenius under ground-field extension is needed. Indeed, apply lemma_6a with the prime power q_m = p^{am} in the role of its q (the statement of lemma_6a holds for every prime power, since its q = p^a is arbitrary and am is a positive integer): for the K_m-scheme Y and the q_m-power automorphism sigma_m: kbar -> kbar, x |-> x^{q_m}, the pullback (id_Y x sigma_m)^* is a K-linear automorphism of H^n_et(Y_{kbar},K) whose inverse is (id_Y x sigma_m^{-1})^*, the geometric Frobenius. That automorphism (id_Y x sigma_m)^* is exactly what (ND) calls "the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius" and exactly what (GC) calls "arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^m}". Both hypotheses quantify over varieties Y ALREADY DEFINED over F_{q^m}, so nothing is being descended; in particular lemma_44 is deliberately NOT used, since it applies only to models obtained by base change from F_q, and a general smooth projective geometrically connected Y over F_{q^m} need not descend to F_q. (For such descended models one may of course add, as a remark only, that lemma_44 identifies F with the m-th power of the F_q-arithmetic Frobenius.)
Finite-dimensionality of V: Y is proper over K_m, so by lemma_45_finite_frob (applied with the prime power q_m in the role of its q, with Y in the role of its Y, and with the constant sheaf K) each H^n(Y_{kbar},K) is finite-dimensional over K. The case V = 0 is handled separately in §2.

(F3) The integer d in (ND) plays no role in the condition: beta is built from V and F alone. Conversely the "pure dimension" clause is vacuous on the class of varieties (GC) quantifies over: a smooth scheme of finite type over a field has locally constant dimension function y |-> dim_y (the structural morphism is open and flat with geometrically regular fibres), and a geometrically connected Y is connected; hence such Y is equidimensional, of some pure dimension d. Thus (ND) and (GC) range over exactly the same triples (m, Y, n).

=====================================================================
§1. THE LINEAR-ALGEBRAIC CORE
=====================================================================
Proposition. Let V != 0 be a finite-dimensional K = Q_l-vector space, let T in GL(V), let A := K[T] with beta(a,b) := Tr_V(ab), and write the minimal polynomial as mu_T = prod_h h^{e_h}, a finite product over the distinct monic irreducible polynomials h in K[t] dividing mu_T, with e_h >= 1. Then:
(P1) rad(beta) := {a in A : beta(a,b) = 0 for all b in A} = Nil(A), the nilradical of A (so rad(beta) is an ideal, it contains every nilpotent, and it contains nothing else);
(P2) the following are equivalent: (a) beta is nondegenerate on A; (b) A has no nonzero nilpotent element; (c) A is reduced; (d) mu_T is squarefree in K[t]; (e) T is semisimple on V.
Assertion (a) <=> (e) is also the content of lemma_68(i)-(ii) (det(s_{i+j}) != 0 <=> beta nondegenerate <=> T semisimple); we do NOT reprove lemma_68 and instead give the structural refinement (P1) and the intermediate equivalences, so that the equivalence is seen to be a statement about nilpotents of K[T] and not about any dimension count.

Proof of the Proposition.

Step 1 (primary decomposition of V and of A, by CRT only).
Work in the PID K[t]. Since the polynomials h^{e_h} for distinct h are pairwise coprime, the Chinese remainder theorem gives a K-algebra isomorphism
    K[t]/(mu_T)  --~-->  prod_h K[t]/(h^{e_h}),      (1.1)
the map being reduction modulo each h^{e_h}. Via A = K[t]/(mu_T) (F1) we transport (1.1) to an isomorphism A = prod_h A_h with A_h := K[t]/(h^{e_h}). Let eps_f in A denote the idempotent whose image under (1.1) has 1 in the f-slot and 0 in every other slot, and set W_f := eps_f(T) V subset V.

(a') V = (+)_f W_f. Indeed sum_f eps_f = 1 in A and eps_f eps_h = 0 for f != h, so the endomorphisms eps_f(T) are mutually orthogonal projectors with sum id_V; their images therefore give a direct-sum decomposition of V. Each W_f is T-stable because eps_f(T) commutes with T.

(b') h(T)^{e_f} annihilates W_f. In A the product f^{e_f} eps_f maps under (1.1) to the tuple whose f-component is f^{e_f} mod f^{e_f} = 0 and whose h-component (h != f) is 0 * (image of eps_f) = 0; hence f^{e_f} eps_f = 0 in A, i.e. f(T)^{e_f} eps_f(T) = 0 in End_K(V), which says exactly that f(T)^{e_f}|_{W_f} = 0.

(c') W_f = ker f(T)^{e_f} = V[f^infty] (the latter being lemma_60's definition V[f^infty] := union_{N>=1} ker f(T)^N). Inclusion "subset": by (b'). Inclusion "superset" for the kernel: if f(T)^{e_f} v = 0 and h != f, then under (1.1) the idempotent eps_h maps to a tuple that is 0 in the f-slot, i.e. eps_h lies in the ideal (f^{e_f})/(mu_T) of A; write eps_h = f^{e_f} g in A; then eps_h(T) v = f(T)^{e_f} g(T) v = 0. Hence v = sum_h eps_h(T) v = eps_f(T) v in W_f. Finally, for V[f^infty]: if v in ker f(T)^N with N >= e_f, then for h != f, eps_h(T)^N = f(T)^{e_f N} g(T)^N = g(T)^N f(T)^{e_f N} and f(T)^{e_f N} v = f(T)^{e_f N - N}(f(T)^N v) = 0 since e_f N >= N; as eps_h(T) is a projector, eps_h(T) v = eps_h(T)^N v = 0, so v = eps_f(T) v in W_f. Thus W_f = V[f^infty].

(d') W_f != 0 for every f. The element eps_f is nonzero in K[t]/(mu_T) because its image under the isomorphism (1.1) has f-component 1, which is nonzero in K[t]/(f^{e_f}) (this ring is nonzero since deg f >= 1, so f^{e_f} is not a unit). Since A = K[T] is by definition the IMAGE of K[t] in End_K(V), the identification A = K[t]/(mu_T) is an isomorphism onto its image, so eps_f(T) != 0 in End_K(V), and hence W_f = eps_f(T)V != 0. (Equivalently: if W_f = 0 then the element prod_{h != f} h(T)^{e_h}, which equals u(T) eps_f(T) for a unit u of A, would kill V, forcing mu_T | prod_{h != f} h^{e_h}, contradicting f | mu_T.)

(e') The minimal polynomial of T|_{W_f} is f^{e_f}. By (b') it divides f^{e_f}, so it equals f^{d_f} with 1 <= d_f <= e_f (d_f >= 1 by (d')). For a direct sum, the minimal polynomial is the lcm of the minimal polynomials of the blocks: P(T) = (+)_f P(T|_{W_f}), so P(T) = 0 iff f^{d_f} | P for all f. Hence mu_T = lcm_f f^{d_f} = prod_f f^{d_f}; comparing with mu_T = prod_f f^{e_f} (uniqueness of factorisation in the UFD K[t]) gives d_f = e_f for all f.

(f') The restriction map rho: A = K[T] -> prod_f K[T|_{W_f}], a |-> (a|_{W_f}), is a K-algebra isomorphism. By (e'), K[T|_{W_f}] = K[t]/(f^{e_f}) = A_f, and the composite K[t]/(mu_T) -> prod_f K[t]/(f^{e_f}) = prod_f K[T|_{W_f}] is exactly the CRT isomorphism (1.1). In particular rho is bijective, dim_K A = sum_f e_f deg f, and rho(eps_f) is the idempotent of the product with 1 in the f-slot (eps_f(T) is the identity on W_f and zero on W_h, h != f, by the orthogonality in (a')).

Step 2 (trace decomposition; rad(beta) = prod_f rad(beta_f)).
Every a in A equals P(T) for some P, hence preserves each W_f; write a_f := a|_{W_f} in A_f. Choosing K-bases of the W_f and their concatenation for V, the matrix of a is block diagonal with blocks a_f, so
    Tr_V(a) = sum_f Tr_{W_f}(a_f),  and  (ab)|_{W_f} = a_f b_f,  hence  beta(a,b) = sum_f beta_f(a_f, b_f),   (1.2)
where beta_f(x,y) := Tr_{W_f}(xy) on A_f. By (f') every tuple (x_f) with x_f in A_f is realised by a unique a in A. Now a in rad(beta) iff for every f and every x in A_f, choosing a~ in A with a~_f = x and a~_h = 0 for h != f, (1.2) gives 0 = beta(a, a~) = beta_f(a_f, x); that is, iff a_f in rad(beta_f) for all f. Hence
    rad(beta) = prod_f rad(beta_f) under the isomorphism rho.   (1.3)

Step 3 (the local computation rad(beta_f) = m_f = Nil(A_f)).
Fix f. The ring A_f = K[t]/(f^{e_f}) is LOCAL with maximal ideal m_f := (f)/(f^{e_f}): an element g mod f^{e_f} with g not in (f) satisfies gcd(g, f^{e_f}) = 1 in the PID K[t] and is therefore invertible, while every element of m_f is nilpotent because (f h)^{e_f} = 0 in A_f; consequently m_f = Nil(A_f) and every proper ideal of A_f is contained in m_f.
(i) m_f subset rad(beta_f): if x in m_f and y in A_f, then xy in m_f is nilpotent in A_f, hence nilpotent as an endomorphism of W_f (the ring structure of A_f is that of a subring of End_K(W_f)); a nilpotent endomorphism has all eigenvalues 0 over Kbar, hence trace 0, so beta_f(x,y) = Tr_{W_f}(xy) = 0.
(ii) rad(beta_f) is an ideal of A_f: it is a K-subspace, and for c in A_f, x in rad(beta_f), y in A_f we have beta_f(cx, y) = Tr_{W_f}(cxy) = Tr_{W_f}(x(cy)) = beta_f(x, cy) = 0.
(iii) rad(beta_f) is proper: beta_f(1,1) = Tr_{W_f}(id_{W_f}) = dim_K W_f, which is nonzero in K = Q_l because 0 < dim_K W_f < infinity and char K = 0 (this is exactly where characteristic zero is used). So 1 not in rad(beta_f).
By (ii)+(iii) and locality, rad(beta_f) subset m_f; with (i) this gives rad(beta_f) = m_f = Nil(A_f).

Step 4 (conclusion).
Combining (1.3) with Step 3, rad(beta) = prod_f Nil(A_f) = Nil(prod_f A_f) = Nil(A), proving (P1). Then:
(a) <=> rad(beta) = 0 <=> Nil(A) = 0 <=> (b) <=> (c) (a commutative ring is reduced iff it has no nonzero nilpotents, by definition);
(c) <=> (d): A = K[t]/(mu_T) and the nilradical of K[t]/(mu_T) is rad(mu_T)/(mu_T) = (prod_f f)/(mu_T), which is 0 iff (prod_f f) = (mu_T) iff e_f = 1 for all f iff mu_T is squarefree;
(d) <=> (e): this is lemma_60(ii) (T semisimple on V iff mu_T is squarefree in Q_l[t]).
This proves the Proposition. QED

Remark (why this is not a dimension count). lemma_60 (final paragraph) and lemma_68(iii) both warn that the criterion dim V[f] = dim V/f(T)V is automatically an equality and cannot detect Jordan blocks; the content of the Proposition is that beta detects nilpotents of K[T], which is strictly sharper (lemma_68(iii) computes det H by the Andreief/Gauss identity as (prod_j d_j) prod_{i<j}(alpha_i - alpha_j)^2, vanishing exactly when mu_T has a repeated root).

=====================================================================
§2. (ND) <=> (GC) AS STATEMENTS
=====================================================================
Fix a triple (m, Y, n) as in §0(F3), put V := H^n_et(Y_{kbar},K) and let F be the q_m-power arithmetic Frobenius of V.
If V = 0: the (GC)-assertion for the triple is vacuous (the zero operator on the zero space is semisimple), and (ND) imposes no condition on the triple, since (ND) is stated for nonzero V. So both sides agree for this triple.
If V != 0: F is a K-linear automorphism of V by §0(F2), so the Proposition applies with T := F. The (ND)-condition for the triple is precisely "beta nondegenerate on A = K[F]", i.e. condition (a); the (GC)-assertion for the triple is precisely "F semisimple on V", i.e. condition (e). By (a) <=> (e) they are equivalent. Moreover, by (P1) and (d), the common condition says that K[F] has no nonzero nilpotents, equivalently mu_F is squarefree.
Since (F2) shows both hypotheses refer to the same operator and (F3) shows they range over the same triples, (ND) and (GC) are equivalent statements. Also, by (P1), (ND) for (Y,m,n) is equivalent to: no nonzero element of K[F] is a nilpotent endomorphism of H^n(Y_{kbar},K).

=====================================================================
§3. CAUTION (a): WHAT REDUCTIONS ARE LEGITIMATE
=====================================================================
(i) Passing to summands is legitimate, in one direction only, by lemma_68(iv): if W subset V is a T-stable direct summand, then nondegeneracy of beta on A = K[T] implies nondegeneracy of the trace form of B := K[T|_W] on W. The converse fails for arbitrary summands: take V = K (+) K^2 with T = id_(+) [[1,1],[0,1]]; on the summand W = K the algebra is K.id with beta_W(lam id, mu id) = lam mu (nondegenerate), but on V one has mu_T = (t-1)^2, so T is not semisimple and beta is degenerate by the Proposition — explicitly, with N := T - id != 0, N^2 = 0, and A has K-basis 1, T with s_0 = Tr_V(id) = 3, s_1 = Tr_V(T) = 3, s_2 = Tr_V(T^2) = 1 + Tr(J^2) = 1 + 2 = 3, so H = [[3,3],[3,3]] and det H = 0; indeed N in Nil(A) = rad(beta).
(ii) For the PRIMARY pieces the reduction is an equivalence. By Step 1(a')/(c'), the W_f = V[f^infty] of lemma_60 are T-stable direct summands with V = (+)_f W_f, and by Step 1(f') K[T|_{W_f}] = A_f. Hence (1.2)-(1.3) and Step 3 give: beta nondegenerate on A <=> rad(beta_f) = 0 for every f <=> the trace form of K[T|_{W_f}] on W_f is nondegenerate for every f. So (ND)-for-(V,T) is EQUIVALENT to (ND)-for-each-primary-piece; the forward implication is lemma_68(iv), and the reverse uses mu_T = lcm_f mu_{T|W_f} = prod_f f^{d_f} (Step 1(e')) together with (1.2).
(iii) Geometrically, lemma_27 gives H^n(Xbar,K) = (+)_C H^n(C,K) over the geometric connected components, with F_q permuting the summands; hence for each Frobenius orbit O the subspace V_O := (+)_{C in O} H^n(C,K) is an F_q-stable direct summand, and lemma_68(iv) transfers nondegeneracy from (H^n(Xbar),F_q) to (V_O, F_q|_{V_O}) (these are the "isotypic pieces" alluded to in the route; lemma_31 is the corresponding semisimplicity statement).
(iv) What is NOT a statement about bilinear forms: the passage from an orbit piece V_O to a single component C_s with the operator F_q^{m_s}. Indeed K[F_q|_{V_O}] and K[F_q^{m_s}|_{H^n(C_s)}] are different algebras on different spaces, and lemma_68(iv) points the wrong way. That passage must be made through semisimplicity — lemma_25 (an operator cyclically permuting m summands is semisimple iff its m-th power is semisimple on one of them) — and then translated back into (ND) by §2. (One can check directly that the two nondegeneracy conditions are equivalent, but only because both are equivalent to the same semisimplicity, via the Proposition; there is no formal identity of the two Hankel determinants.)

=====================================================================
§4. CAUTION (b): TWISTING THE FORM BY AN ANTI-INVOLUTION BUYS NOTHING
=====================================================================
Let sigma: A -> A be a K-linear anti-involution (sigma(ab) = sigma(b)sigma(a), sigma^2 = id). Since A = K[T] is commutative, sigma is a K-algebra automorphism of A, in particular BIJECTIVE. Put h(a,b) := Tr_V(a sigma(b)). Then
    rad(h) = {a : Tr_V(a sigma(b)) = 0 for all b in A} = {a : Tr_V(a c) = 0 for all c in A} = rad(beta),
the middle equality using that c = sigma(b) runs over all of A. Hence h is nondegenerate <=> beta is nondegenerate <=> (by §2) arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple, i.e. <=> (GC) for the triple. So nondegeneracy of h is again EQUIVALENT to (GC): replacing beta by h is a reformulation, not a strengthening.
Where such a sigma comes from, hypothetically: by lemma_69(1), if V carries a perfect pairing <-,-> whose adjoint a |-> a^dagger satisfies T^dagger = c T^{-1} for some c in K^*, then dagger preserves A = K[T] = K[T,T^{-1}] and sigma := dagger|_A is a K-algebra anti-involution of A (sigma^2 = id_A). We explicitly do NOT claim that such a pairing exists on H^n(Y_{kbar},K): Poincare duality pairs H^n with H^{2d-n}(-d), not H^n with itself, and neither the self-pairing nor the adjoint relation T^dagger = cT^{-1} is supplied by any result cited here. The claim above is conditional: "whenever such a pairing is given, nondegeneracy of h is equivalent to nondegeneracy of beta, hence to (GC)".
Anisotropy is strictly stronger, and is not equivalent to (GC). Worked example over K (pure linear algebra, no geometry): V = K^2, T = diag(2,3). Then mu_T = (t-2)(t-3) is squarefree, so T is semisimple and beta is nondegenerate — check: A has K-basis 1, T, s_0 = 2, s_1 = 5, s_2 = 13, H = [[2,5],[5,13]], det H = 26 - 25 = 1 != 0, as lemma_68(ii) predicts. Equip V with the perfect pairing with Gram matrix G = [[0,1],[1,0]]. Then T^dagger = G^{-1} T^t G = G T G = [[0,1],[1,0]][[2,0],[0,3]][[0,1],[1,0]] = diag(3,2) = 6 T^{-1}, so c = 6 in K^* and lemma_69(1) applies: sigma = dagger|_A is the involution of A = K x K swapping the factors (with the idempotents e_1 = 3 - T = diag(1,0) and e_2 = T - 2 = diag(0,1), one checks e_1^dagger = 3I - diag(3,2) = diag(0,1) = e_2). For a = alpha e_1 + beta e_2 = diag(alpha,beta) one gets a sigma(a) = diag(alpha beta, alpha beta), hence h(a,a) = Tr_V(a sigma(a)) = 2 alpha beta; taking a = e_1 != 0 gives h(e_1,e_1) = 0. So h is ISOTROPIC although T is semisimple and beta is nondegenerate. This is exactly the mechanism of lemma_72: sigma moves the simple factor K e_1 of A_red = A, and the corresponding *-trace form is forced to be isotropic. Conclusion: anisotropy of h is strictly stronger than nondegeneracy of h, hence strictly stronger than (GC) and not equivalent to it; it cannot serve as the missing arithmetic input.

=====================================================================
§5. DEDUCTION OF THE CONJECTURE FROM (ND)
=====================================================================
Assume (ND). By §2, (ND) implies (GC). By lemma_59, (GC) implies the conjecture in full: for every smooth projective variety X over F_q (not assumed connected or equidimensional) and every i >= 0, geometric Frobenius acts semisimply on H^i_et(X_{Fbar_q},Q_l), and equivalently its action on H^i_et(X_{Fbar_q},Q_l) tensor_{Q_l} Qbar_l is diagonalisable (that Qbar_l-upgrade is part of the stated conclusion of lemma_59, so nothing further is needed here). Conversely, if the conjecture holds then arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on every H^n(Y_{kbar},K) for Y/F_{q^m} smooth projective geometrically connected (lemma_6a identifies geometric with the inverse of arithmetic Frobenius, and invertible operators are semisimple exactly when their inverses are), so (GC) holds, and §2 gives (ND). Thus (ND) <=> (GC) <=> (conjecture), and the proof of the lemma is complete.

=====================================================================
§6. DIAGNOSIS (why this is not a proof of the conjecture)
=====================================================================
(1) By §2, (ND) asserts for each triple (m,Y,n) exactly that K[F] contains no nonzero nilpotent endomorphism of H^n(Y_{kbar},K), i.e. exactly that mu_F is squarefree, i.e. exactly the semisimplicity demanded by (GC). The Hankel determinant det(Tr_V(F^{i+j}))_{0<=i,j<deg mu_F} of lemma_68 is nonzero if and only if it is nonzero, and it vanishes precisely when mu_F has a repeated root. So (ND) is (GC) written in the language of a bilinear form; it supplies no new arithmetic input, and nothing in §1-§4 proves (ND).
(2) The reductions available (§3) are all reversible reformulations of the same semisimplicity statement: primary pieces W_f = V[f^infty] (equivalence, §3(ii)), orbit summands V_O (one-way by lemma_68(iv), the converse through lemma_25/§2).
(3) The apparently richer variants (§4) are either equivalent (nondegeneracy of a sigma-twisted trace form) or strictly stronger and unjustified (anisotropy), and the natural geometric source of the needed anti-involution is not available: Poincare duality does not give a perfect self-pairing of H^n with T^dagger = cT^{-1} without extra structure. Hence the conjecture remains exactly as hard under (ND) as under (GC); the only conditional content proved here is (ND) <=> (GC) and (ND) => conjecture (via lemma_59).

lemma_66.statement: Let l be a prime, let V be a nonzero finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space, let A be a finite-dimensional commutative unital Q_l-subalgebra of End_Q_l(V), and let dagger be a Q_l-linear anti-involution of A. Define a bilinear form B on A by B(a,b) = Tr_V(a b^dagger). Let Rad(B) be the radical of B, namely the set of a in A such that B(a,b)=0 for every b in A, and let Nil(A) be the nilradical of A. Then Rad(B) = Nil(A). In particular, the following are equivalent: (i) B is nondegenerate; (ii) A is reduced; (iii) every element of A is semisimple on V. Anisotropy of B, meaning B(a,a) nonzero for every nonzero a, implies these conditions. However, nondegeneracy does not imply anisotropy: take A = Q_l x Q_l acting on V = A by left multiplication, with dagger(x,y) = (y,x). Then B((x,y),(u,v)) = xv + yu is nondegenerate, the element T = (1,-1) is semisimple and satisfies T^dagger = -T = -T^{-1}, but B((1,0),(1,0)) = 0. The inclusion Nil(A) subset Rad(B) follows because a nilpotent element times any element is nilpotent and hence has trace zero. For Rad(B) subset Nil(A), pass to A/Nil(A), which is a reduced finite-dimensional Q_l-algebra, hence a product of finite separable field extensions; the anti-involution permutes the factors, and the trace pairing on each faithful isotypic component is nondegenerate, so a nonzero element cannot be orthogonal to all of A.
lemma_66.proof:
Proof. Throughout, write k = ℚ_ℓ. The action A × V → V, (a,v) ↦ a(v), is **faithful**, because A is given as a subalgebra of End_k(V): Ann_A(V) = {a ∈ A : a(V) = 0} = 0. Write N = Nil(A) for the nilradical (a commutative ring, so N is the ideal of all nilpotent elements), and for a ∈ A write ā for its class in A/N. By hypothesis 1_A = Id_V.

**Step 0. Elementary properties of †.** Since A is commutative, †(ab) = †(b)†(a) = †(a)†(b), so † is an involutive k-linear ring automorphism of A (bijective, †² = id). It fixes the unit: for any b ∈ A write b = †(a); then †(1)·b = †(1)†(a) = †(a·1) = †(a) = b, so †(1) is a left identity of A, and taking b = 1 gives †(1) = †(1)·1 = 1. Also †(N) = N, since aⁿ = 0 ⟺ †(a)ⁿ = †(aⁿ) = 0.

**Step 1. Reformulation of the radical.** Because † : A → A is a bijection,
  a ∈ Rad(B) ⟺ Tr_V(a·†(b)) = 0 for all b ∈ A ⟺ Tr_V(a·c) = 0 for all c ∈ A.      (1)
Similarly the *right* radical is {b : Tr_V(c·†(b)) = 0 ∀c} = †⁻¹(Rad(B)) = †(Rad(B)). Hence once we prove Rad(B) = N, both radicals equal N (as †(N) = N). Since A is finite dimensional over k, vanishing of the left radical is equivalent to non-degeneracy of B (the map A → A*, a ↦ B(a,−), is then injective, hence an isomorphism, hence the right radical also vanishes); so "B non-degenerate" is unambiguous.

**Step 2. N ⊆ Rad(B).** Let a ∈ N and b ∈ A; if aⁿ = 0 then, by commutativity, (a·†(b))ⁿ = aⁿ·†(b)ⁿ = 0, so a†(b) is a nilpotent element of A ⊂ End_k(V). A nilpotent endomorphism of V has trace 0 (over k̄ it is upper-triangular with zero diagonal, and trace = sum of diagonal entries). Thus B(a,b) = Tr_V(a†(b)) = 0 for all b, i.e. a ∈ Rad(B).

**Step 3. Structure of A and of V.**

*3.1 N is nilpotent.* Let 𝒮 = {I ⊴ A : Iᵐ = 0 for some m ≥ 1}; 0 ∈ 𝒮. A is finite dimensional over k, hence noetherian, so 𝒮 has a maximal element J, say Jᵐ = 0. For x ∈ N with xⁿ = 0, every product of N₀ = m+n−1 factors from J + (x) expands into terms lying in Jᵃ(x)ᵇ with a+b = N₀, and each such term vanishes because a ≥ m or b ≥ n; so (J+(x))^{N₀} = 0. By maximality x ∈ J. Hence N ⊆ J, and J ⊆ N because every element of a nilpotent ideal is nilpotent. So J = N and Nˢ = 0 for some s.

*3.2 A/N is a product of separable fields.* A/N is a finite-dimensional reduced commutative k-algebra, hence artinian; in an artinian ring every prime is maximal, so the nilradical is the intersection of the maximal ideals, and A/N has only finitely many maximal ideals 𝔪̄₁,…,𝔪̄_r, with ∩ᵢ 𝔪̄ᵢ = 0. They are pairwise comaximal, so the Chinese remainder theorem gives a k-algebra isomorphism A/N → ∏ᵢ (A/N)/𝔪̄ᵢ =: ∏ᵢ Kᵢ. Each Kᵢ is a field and a finite extension of k; since char k = 0, k is perfect, so every Kᵢ/k is finite **separable**.

*3.3 Maximal ideals of A and the action of †.* Primes of A are exactly the inverse images of primes of A/N (they all contain N), so Max(A) = {m₁,…,m_r}, mᵢ = (A → A/N)⁻¹(𝔪̄ᵢ), with A/mᵢ = Kᵢ, and N = ∩ᵢ mᵢ = ∏ᵢ mᵢ (the mᵢ are pairwise comaximal, so intersection = product). Since † is an automorphism of A preserving N, it permutes {m₁,…,m_r}, hence permutes the factors of ∏ Kᵢ (equivalently, the primitive idempotents of A/N): †(mᵢ) = m_{τ(i)} and † restricts to a k-isomorphism Kᵢ ≅ K_{τ(i)}. (This permutation property is not needed below; only †(N) = N is.)

*3.4 Primary decomposition of V.* Fix t ≥ s with Nᵗ = 0. For i ≠ j, mᵢᵗ + mⱼᵗ = A: indeed A = (mᵢ+mⱼ)^{2t−1} ⊆ mᵢᵗ + mⱼᵗ, since every product of 2t−1 factors from mᵢ ∪ mⱼ has at least t factors in one of them. Hence the mᵢᵗ are pairwise comaximal, so ∩ᵢ mᵢᵗ = ∏ᵢ mᵢᵗ = (∏ᵢ mᵢ)ᵗ = Nᵗ = 0, and CRT gives a k-algebra isomorphism
  A ≅ ∏ᵢ Aᵢ,  Aᵢ := A/mᵢᵗ.
Each Aᵢ is local artinian: its maximal ideals are the mⱼ with mⱼ ⊇ mᵢᵗ, and mⱼ + mᵢᵗ = A for j ≠ i, so the unique maximal ideal is 𝔪ᵢ := mᵢ/mᵢᵗ, with residue field Aᵢ/𝔪ᵢ = A/mᵢ = Kᵢ; in particular every simple Aᵢ-module is Kᵢ. Let ε₁,…,ε_r ∈ A be the corresponding orthogonal idempotents (εᵢ ↦ 1 in Aᵢ, 0 in Aⱼ, j ≠ i), Σᵢ εᵢ = 1. Then εᵢA = ∩_{j≠i} mⱼᵗ, so mᵢᵗεᵢ ⊆ ∩ⱼ mⱼᵗ = 0. Setting
  Vᵢ := εᵢV = {v ∈ V : mᵢᵗ v = 0},
we get V = ⊕ᵢ Vᵢ (the sum is direct since the εᵢ are orthogonal and sum to 1; and if v ∈ Vᵢ ∩ Σ_{j≠i}Vⱼ then multiplying by εᵢ gives v = 0). Equality Vᵢ = {v : mᵢᵗv = 0}: "⊇" holds because εᵢ ≡ 1 (mod mᵢᵗ) (as εᵢ − 1 ∈ mᵢᵗA = ker(A → Aᵢ) = mᵢᵗ), so mᵢᵗv = 0 gives v = εᵢv + (1−εᵢ)v = εᵢv ∈ εᵢV; "⊆" holds since mᵢᵗεᵢ = 0. Thus each Vᵢ is A-stable and A acts on Vᵢ through the local artinian ring Aᵢ.

*3.5 Every Vᵢ is nonzero.* Put S := {i : Vᵢ ≠ 0}; S ≠ ∅ since V ≠ 0. For i ∈ S, mᵢᵗεᵢ = 0 gives mᵢᵗ ⊆ Ann_A(Vᵢ). Hence
  Ann_A(V) = ∩ᵢ Ann_A(Vᵢ) ⊇ ∩_{j∈S} mⱼᵗ ⊇ ∏_{j∈S} mⱼᵗ = (∏_{j∈S} mⱼ)ᵗ.
Via A → A/N = ∏ᵢ Kᵢ the ideal ∏_{j∈S} mⱼ maps to ∏_{i∉S} Kᵢ (at position i the factor is 0 as soon as i ∈ S, and K_i otherwise), so if S ⊊ {1,…,r} this image is nonzero, and then (∏_{j∈S}mⱼ)ᵗ has image (∏_{i∉S}Kᵢ)ᵗ = ∏_{i∉S}Kᵢ ≠ 0, hence is a nonzero ideal of A. Faithfulness (Ann_A(V) = 0) therefore forces S = {1,…,r}: **all Vᵢ are nonzero.**

*3.6 The trace formula.* Let nᵢ := length_{A}(Vᵢ) = length_{Aᵢ}(Vᵢ) ≥ 1. We claim that for all a ∈ A,
  Tr_V(a) = Σᵢ nᵢ · Tr_{Kᵢ/k}(āᵢ),   āᵢ = image of a in Kᵢ = A/mᵢ.        (2)
Since V = ⊕ᵢ Vᵢ with each Vᵢ a-stable, Tr_V(a) = Σᵢ Tr_{Vᵢ}(a|_{Vᵢ}). Choose a composition series of Vᵢ as Aᵢ-module; all composition factors are isomorphic to the unique simple module Kᵢ, and there are nᵢ of them. Trace is additive in short exact sequences (given 0 → W′ → W → W″ → 0 with u ∈ End(W), u(W′) ⊆ W′, a basis of W′ followed by lifts of a basis of W″ puts the matrix of u in block upper-triangular form, so Tr_W(u) = Tr_{W′}(u) + Tr_{W″}(u)); applying this along the composition series gives Tr_{Vᵢ}(a) = nᵢ·Tr_{Kᵢ}(a), and a acts on Kᵢ as multiplication by āᵢ, whose k-linear trace is Tr_{Kᵢ/k}(āᵢ). This proves (2).

*3.7 Non-degeneracy of the field trace pairing.* Let K/k be a finite separable extension of degree n. Then K = k(θ) with θ of minimal polynomial f of degree n, and f has n distinct roots θ₁,…,θ_n in k̄; the k-embeddings σᵢ : K → k̄ are σᵢ(θ) = θᵢ. Since k̄/k is flat, K ⊗_k k̄ ≅ k̄[T]/(f) ≅ ∏ᵢ k̄ (CRT, f squarefree), with x = g(θ) ↦ (g(θᵢ)) = (σᵢ(x)). Multiplication by x on K has the same matrix (in a k-basis) as multiplication by x⊗1 on K ⊗_k k̄, which is diagonal with entries σᵢ(x). Hence
  Tr_{K/k}(x) = Σ_{σ∈Hom_k(K,k̄)} σ(x).        (3)
By Dedekind's lemma on the linear independence of characters, the σ are linearly independent as functions K → k̄: if Σ λᵢσᵢ = 0 with the minimal number of nonzero λᵢ, then λ₁ ≠ 0 and after choosing u ∈ K with σ₁(u) ≠ σ₂(u), comparing Σλᵢσᵢ(uv) = 0 with σ₁(u)·Σλᵢσᵢ(v) = 0 gives a shorter nontrivial relation Σ_{i≥2} λᵢ(σᵢ(u)−σ₁(u))σᵢ = 0 (the i = 2 coefficient is nonzero), contradiction. Now if Tr_{K/k}(c·x) = 0 for all x ∈ K, then by (3) Σᵢ σᵢ(c)σᵢ = 0 as functions on K, so all σᵢ(c) = 0, and c = 0 (the σᵢ are injective and there is at least one). Thus the pairing (x,y) ↦ Tr_{K/k}(xy) on K is non-degenerate.

**Step 4. Rad(B) ⊆ N.** Let a ∈ Rad(B). By (1), Tr_V(a·b) = 0 for all b ∈ A. By (2), Σᵢ nᵢ Tr_{Kᵢ/k}(āᵢb̄ᵢ) = 0 for all b ∈ A. The map b ↦ (b̄ᵢ) ∈ ∏ᵢ Kᵢ is surjective (A → A/N is, and A/N ≅ ∏ Kᵢ). Fix j and c ∈ K_j, and choose b with b̄ⱼ = c and b̄ᵢ = 0 for i ≠ j. Then nⱼ·Tr_{Kⱼ/k}(āⱼ·c) = 0 in k. By Step 3.5, nⱼ ≥ 1, and since char k = 0 the integer nⱼ is nonzero in k, so Tr_{Kⱼ/k}(āⱼc) = 0. As c ∈ Kⱼ was arbitrary, Step 3.7 gives āⱼ = 0. This holds for every j, so ā = 0 in A/N, i.e. a ∈ N. Combined with Step 2, **Rad(B) = N**; by Step 1 the right radical equals †(N) = N as well.

**Step 5. The equivalences.** We record the linear-algebra criterion used below: for a finite-dimensional vector space W over a field k and M ∈ End_k(W), M is semisimple (every M-stable subspace has an M-stable complement) if and only if its minimal polynomial μ_M is squarefree. Proof: (⇐) If μ_M = ∏_{i=1}ᵗ fᵢ with distinct monic irreducibles fᵢ, then R := k[t]/(μ_M) ≅ ∏ᵢ k[t]/(fᵢ) is a product of fields; W is an R-module (t acts as M), Wᵢ := eᵢW satisfies W = ⊕ᵢ Wᵢ, fᵢ(M)|_{Wᵢ} = 0, and k[t]/(fᵢ) is a field acting on Wᵢ, so every M-stable subspace of Wᵢ is a k[t]/(fᵢ)-subspace and has a (hence M-stable) complement. Given an M-stable U ⊆ W, U = ⊕ᵢ(U ∩ Wᵢ) (because eᵢ(M) is a polynomial in M), and the complements in the Wᵢ sum to an M-stable complement of U. (⇒) If M is semisimple, write W = ⊕ⱼ Uⱼ with the Uⱼ irreducible M-stable. On Uⱼ, k[M] ≅ k[t]/(pⱼ) with pⱼ irreducible, and Uⱼ is a k[t]/(pⱼ)-vector space in which any nonzero vector generates (irreducibility), so Uⱼ ≅ k[t]/(pⱼ) and pⱼ(M)|_{Uⱼ} = 0 with pⱼ appearing to the first power. Hence μ_M = lcm of distinct irreducibles, i.e. squarefree. Also, for W = ⊕ᵢ Wᵢ with M-stable Wᵢ, μ_M = lcmᵢ μ_{M|Wᵢ}, so a direct sum of semisimple operators is semisimple and a summand of a semisimple operator is semisimple.

(i) ⟺ (ii): B is non-degenerate ⟺ Rad(B) = 0 ⟺ N = 0 ⟺ A is reduced, by Step 4.
(ii) ⟹ (iii): assume A reduced, so N = 0 and A ≅ ∏ᵢ Kᵢ with each Kᵢ/k finite separable. Then t = 1 works in Step 3.4, mᵢ¹ = mᵢ = ⊕_{j≠i} k·εⱼ and Aᵢ = A/mᵢ = Kᵢ, so Vᵢ is a Kᵢ-vector space of dimension nᵢ and a ∈ A acts on Vᵢ as m_{āᵢ} ⊗ Id_{k^{nᵢ}} for the identification Vᵢ ≅ Kᵢ ⊗_k k^{nᵢ} of A-modules. The operator m_{āᵢ} on Kᵢ has minimal polynomial equal to the minimal polynomial μ of āᵢ over k: for g ∈ k[t], g(m_{āᵢ}) = m_{g(āᵢ)}, which is the zero endomorphism iff g(āᵢ)·1 = 0 iff g(āᵢ) = 0. Since char k = 0, μ is irreducible hence separable (μ′ ≠ 0 and deg μ′ < deg μ, so gcd(μ,μ′) = 1), hence squarefree; thus m_{āᵢ} is semisimple by the criterion. Then m_{āᵢ} ⊗ Id has minimal polynomial dividing μ, hence squarefree, hence is semisimple on Vᵢ. Finally a is semisimple on V = ⊕ᵢ Vᵢ by the direct-sum statement.
(iii) ⟹ (ii): assume every element of A is semisimple on V, and let a ∈ N. Then a is nilpotent on V and semisimple, so its minimal polynomial on V is squarefree and divides Tᵐ, hence equals T, so a acts as 0 on V. Faithfulness of A ⊂ End_k(V) gives a = 0. So N = 0 and A is reduced.

**Step 6. Anisotropy implies (i)–(iii).** If B(a,a) ≠ 0 for every 0 ≠ a ∈ A, then no nonzero a is orthogonal to all of A (take b = a), so Rad(B) = 0.

**Step 7. Non-degenerate does not imply anisotropic: the example.** Let A = k × k, V = A as a k-vector space (dim 2), and let A act on V by left multiplication: (α,β)·(x,y) = (αx,βy), i.e. A → End_k(V) is (α,β) ↦ diag(α,β), an injective unital k-algebra homomorphism, so A is a unital subalgebra of End_k(V). Let †(x,y) = (y,x): this is k-linear, bijective, multiplicative (hence an anti-involution, A being commutative) and †² = id. For a = (x,y), b = (u,v), ab† = (x,y)(v,u) = (xv, yu), which acts on V as diag(xv, yu), of trace xv + yu. Hence
  B((x,y),(u,v)) = xv + yu.
Non-degeneracy: if B((x,y),(u,v)) = 0 for all (u,v), then (u,v) = (1,0) gives y = 0 and (u,v) = (0,1) gives x = 0, so (x,y) = 0; equivalently Rad(B) = 0 = Nil(A), as A = k × k is reduced. Take T = (1,−1) ∈ A: on V, T = diag(1,−1) is diagonal, hence semisimple (consistent with (ii)⟺(iii)); T² = (1,1) = 1, so T⁻¹ = T, and †(T) = (−1,1) = −T = −T⁻¹. But B((1,0),(1,0)) = 1·0 + 0·1 = 0 with (1,0) ≠ 0, so B is not anisotropic. (Indeed B is the hyperbolic form of rank 2.) This completes the proof of all assertions. ∎

lemma_71.statement: (The honest conditional endgame: (Pos) => (GC) => the conjecture.) Let q=p^a be a prime power and let l != p be a prime. Consider the following hypothesis (Pos), stated as a LITERAL hypothesis: for every m >= 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected variety Y over F_{q^m} of pure dimension d, and every n >= 0, writing F for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, (a) the cup product H^n(Ybar,Q_l) x H^{2d-n}(Ybar,Q_l) -> H^{2d}(Ybar,Q_l) followed by the trace isomorphism tr: H^{2d}(Ybar,Q_l) ~-> Q_l(-d) is a PERFECT pairing of Q_l-vector spaces, and tr is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where F acts on Q_l(-d) as multiplication by the scalar q^{md}; (b) with V := H^n(Ybar,Q_l) (+) H^{2d-n}(Ybar,Q_l), with F the block-diagonal automorphism of V, with <,> the perfect pairing on V whose only nonzero blocks are the pairing of (a) between the two summands (each summand being totally isotropic in itself), with dagger the adjoint anti-automorphism of End_{Q_l}(V) defined by <av,w> = <v,a^dagger w>, and with A := Q_l[F] subset End_{Q_l}(V), the form a |-> Tr_V(a a^dagger) is nonzero for every nonzero a in A. Prove that (Pos) implies (GC): for every m >= 1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected Y over F_{q^m}, arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^m} acts semisimply on H^n(Ybar,Q_l) for every n; and hence the conjecture holds, by lemma_59. Route: (1) FORMAL ADJOINTNESS, so no symmetry/duality property of the pairing is needed beyond perfectness: from the compatibility of the cup product and of tr with F one gets <Fx,Fy> = q^{md} <x,y> for all x,y in V; substituting y -> F^{-1}y gives <Fx,y> = q^{md}<x,F^{-1}y>, i.e. F^dagger = c F^{-1} with c := q^{md} in Q_l^*. (2) Conclude from lemma_69(0)-(1) that A = Q_l[F] = Q_l[F,F^{-1}] is dagger-stable and that dagger|_A is a Q_l-algebra anti-involution (sigma^2 = id_A), induced on Q_l[t^{\pm 1}] by t |-> c t^{-1}. (3) Apply lemma_65 to the commutative Q_l-subalgebra A of End_{Q_l}(V) with the anisotropic trace form of (b) to get that F is semisimple on V. (4) Since F preserves each summand of V and the sum is direct, lemma_9 (equivalently lemma_35(ii)) gives semisimplicity of F on H^n(Ybar,Q_l), which is (GC). (5) Invoke lemma_59. Finally add, as a remark proved inside the lemma, the following CORRECTED comparison (do NOT assert that clause (b) is equivalent to semisimplicity; that assertion is false). (R1) Semisimplicity of F on V is equivalent to NONDEGENERACY of the bilinear form B(a,b) := Tr_V(a b^dagger) on A: by lemma_66 one has Rad(B) = Nil(A), so B is nondegenerate iff A is reduced, and since A is a quotient of Q_l[t]/(mu_F) of the same dimension, A is reduced iff mu_F is squarefree, iff F is semisimple by lemma_60(ii) (note Q_l has characteristic 0). Hence under (a) alone, semisimplicity of F gives nondegeneracy of B but NOT the strictly stronger anisotropy demanded by (b). (R2) Under (a) together with the eigenvalue condition iota(alpha) * conj(iota(alpha)) = iota(c) for every eigenvalue alpha of F on V and a fixed embedding iota: Qbar_l -> C (automatic in the middle degree n = d once Weil I purity is known), lemma_69(4) shows that for a = P(F) with P = sum_j p_j t^j and iota(p_j) in R for all j, IF F is semisimple then the eigenvalues of a a^dagger are |P(alpha_i)|^2 and iota(Tr_V(a a^dagger)) = sum_i |iota(P(alpha_i))|^2 > 0 for a != 0; this is positivity only on the real-coefficient part of A (an embedding Q_l -> C need not have real image), and it does not give (b) on all of A. (R3) Give the explicit counterexample showing (b) is genuinely stronger: take l congruent to 1 mod 4, i in Q_l^* with i^2 = -1, c = 4, V = Q_l e_1 (+) Q_l e_2, F = diag(2i, -2i), and <x,y> = x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1. Then <Fx,Fy> = 4<x,y>, the eigenvalues +-2i satisfy the eigenvalue condition under an embedding with i -> sqrt(-1), and F is diagonal hence semisimple; but A = Q_l[F] = {diag(x,y) : x,y in Q_l} (since F^2 = -4 id and F/2i = diag(1,-1) lie in A), the adjoint is diag(x,y)^dagger = diag(y,x), and a = diag(1,0) is nonzero with a a^dagger = 0, so Tr_V(a a^dagger) = 0 and (b) fails. Explain the mechanism via lemma_72: the anti-involution sigma induced by t |-> c t^{-1} swaps the two simple factors of A_red, which forces isotropy of B. Conclude that the only genuinely missing arithmetic input is anisotropy of the *-trace form (a Standard-Conjectures-D-type positivity statement), strictly stronger than the nondegeneracy that is equivalent to (GC). Do not cite any external theorem by name; (a) is Poincare duality and (b) is a positivity statement, and neither is available here.
lemma_71.proof:
PART A. DATA AND ELEMENTARY PRELIMINARIES.

A.0 Fix arbitrary data of the kind quantified in (GC): an integer m >= 1, a smooth projective geometrically connected variety Y over k0 := F_{q^m}, and an integer n >= 0. Put Q := q^m = p^{am} (a prime power), k := overline(F_q), Ybar := Y x_{k0} k, and let F denote the Q-power (= q^m-power) arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of Ybar and of the Q_l-vector spaces H^i_et(Ybar, Q_l). Write V1 := H^n(Ybar, Q_l) and V2 := H^{2d-n}(Ybar, Q_l), where d is the pure dimension of Y.

A.1 (Why (Pos) applies to every Y occurring in (GC); pure dimensionality is automatic.) A smooth morphism to Spec(k0) is regular on fibres, so Y is a regular scheme; every local ring O_{Y,y} is then a regular local ring, hence a domain, so Y is locally integral. In a locally noetherian locally integral scheme each point lies on a unique irreducible component, whence the irreducible components are open; being irreducible components of a noetherian space they are also closed.
