Y is connected (geometrically connected implies connected after the structure map Y -> Spec k0, whose fibres over the two points of a hypothetical disconnection would give a disconnection after base change), so Y has exactly one irreducible component: Y is irreducible, hence equidimensional of dimension d := dim Y >= 0. Thus (Pos), which quantifies over Y of pure dimension d, applies with this d, and the argument below proves (GC) for all Y as in (GC).

A.2 (Finite dimensionality.) Y is proper over the finite field k0, so lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the prime power Q = p^{am}, the proper k0-variety Y, and the object K = Q_{l,Ybar} with its standard arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, gives that H^i_et(Ybar, Q_l) is finite-dimensional over Q_l for every i. Hence V1, V2 and V := V1 (+) V2 are finite-dimensional Q_l-vector spaces.

A.3 (Invertibility of F.) By lemma_6a (applied over k0 with the automorphism sigma(a) = a^Q of k), the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius F and the Q-power geometric Frobenius are mutually inverse Q_l-linear automorphisms of each H^i_et(Ybar, Q_l). In particular F in GL(V1), F in GL(V2), and the block-diagonal F = F|_{V1} (+) F|_{V2} lies in GL(V).

A.4 (Reduction to the non-zero case; automatic range 0 <= n <= 2d.) If V1 = 0 there is nothing to prove for this (m, Y, n). Assume V1 != 0. Then V != 0, which is the standing non-vanishing hypothesis of lemma_65, lemma_69, lemma_60 and lemma_66. Moreover V2 != 0: choose 0 != x in V1; by perfectness of the pairing of clause (a) there is y in V2 with e(tr(x cup y)) != 0 for some (equivalently any) trivialisation e, so V2 != 0. (In particular, since H^i_et(-, Q_l) = 0 for i < 0 by definition of sheaf cohomology, clause (a) forces n <= 2d in this case; no separate argument is needed.)

A.5 (The choice of trivialisation of Q_l(-d) is immaterial.) Q_l(-d) is a one-dimensional Q_l-vector space. Choose a Q_l-linear isomorphism e: Q_l(-d) ->~ Q_l and write M(u, v) := e(tr(u cup v)) for u in H^i(Ybar, Q_l), v in H^{2d-i}(Ybar, Q_l). Clause (a) says precisely that M: V1 x V2 -> Q_l is a perfect pairing. Replacing e by lambda*e with lambda in Q_l^* multiplies M, and hence the pairing <,> on V of Part B, by the non-zero scalar lambda. The adjoint is unchanged: if <a v, w>' = lambda<a v, w> = lambda<v, a^dagger w> = <v, a^dagger w>', uniqueness of the adjoint with respect to a non-degenerate pairing (lemma_69(0)) gives (a^dagger)' = a^dagger. Consequently the operator a |-> a^dagger, the identity F^dagger = c F^{-1} of B.4, the algebra A = Q_l[F], and all the numbers Tr_V(a a^dagger) -- and therefore clause (b) -- are independent of the choice of e. We fix e once and for all.

PART B. FORMAL ADJOINTNESS: F^dagger = c F^{-1} WITH c := q^{md}.

B.1 (The pairing on V.) For v = (x, y) and w = (x', y') in V1 (+) V2 define
    <v, w> := M(x, y') + M(y, x').
Each summand V1, V2 is totally isotropic and the only non-zero blocks are the two cross blocks, both given by the perfect pairing of clause (a) (restricted to V1 x V2 and to V2 x V1). Perfectness: if <v, w> = 0 for all w, then with w = (0, y') we get M(x, y') = 0 for all y' in V2, so x = 0; with w = (x', 0) we get M(y, x') = 0 for all x' in V1, so y = 0. Thus the left radical is zero, and since dim V1 + dim V2 = dim V < infinity the right radical is zero as well; equivalently the Gram matrix in the decomposition V1 (+) V2 is [[0, G], [G', 0]] with G, G' invertible, hence invertible. (We use only perfectness: no symmetry, no alternating property, and no relation between the two cross blocks. Replacing the second term M(y, x') by M(x', y), which differs from it by the Koszul sign (-1)^{n(2d-n)}, gives another perfect pairing satisfying B.3, and the whole argument of Parts B, C, D uses only perfectness plus B.3, so the convention is irrelevant.)

B.2 (M is F-equivariant up to the scalar c.) Two structural facts are used. (i) The cup product is compatible with F: F = (id_Y x sigma) is a morphism of the scheme Ybar, and etale cohomology is a contravariantly functorial graded ring whose product is natural for pullback, so F(u cup v) = F u cup F v. (ii) The trace map tr is F-equivariant by clause (a), where F acts on Q_l(-d) as multiplication by c := q^{md}. Hence for u in H^i(Ybar, Q_l) and v in H^{2d-i}(Ybar, Q_l):
    M(F u, F v) = e(tr(F u cup F v)) = e(tr(F(u cup v))) = e(c . tr(u cup v)) = c . e(tr(u cup v)) = c . M(u, v),
where the last equality uses that e is Q_l-linear and that c = q^{md} is a positive integer, hence an element of Q_l^* (l != p). Note that no equivariance of e is required.

B.3 (The same relation on V.) Since F is block diagonal, F v = (F x, F y). Applying B.2 to each cross term:
    <F v, F w> = M(F x, F y') + M(F y, F x') = c M(x, y') + c M(y, x') = c <v, w>   for all v, w in V.

B.4 (Identification of the adjoint.) By lemma_69(0), the perfect pairing <,> on the non-zero finite-dimensional Q_l-space V yields a well-defined unique adjoint a |-> a^dagger on End_{Q_l}(V), characterised by <a v, w> = <v, a^dagger w>, and this map is Q_l-linear and anti-multiplicative. In B.3 substitute w = F^{-1} w' (legal since F is bijective): <F v, w'> = c <v, F^{-1} w'>. By Q_l-bilinearity of <, > in the second variable, c <v, F^{-1} w'> = <v, (c F^{-1}) w'>. Hence <F v, w'> = <v, (c F^{-1}) w'> for all v, w', and uniqueness of the adjoint gives
    F^dagger = c F^{-1},   c = q^{md} in Q_l^*.

PART C. A = Q_l[F] IS dagger-STABLE AND dagger|_A IS AN ANTI-INVOLUTION.

C.1 The hypotheses of lemma_69(0)-(1) are now verified verbatim with k = Q_l, the space V (non-zero finite-dimensional: A.2, A.4), T = F (in GL(V): A.3), the scalar c (B.2), and the perfect pairing <, > (B.1), together with the relation T^dagger = c T^{-1} (B.4). We record the conclusions we use.
(i) F^{-1} in Q_l[F] by Cayley-Hamilton applied to the invertible F, so A := Q_l[F] = Q_l[F, F^{-1}] is a commutative finite-dimensional unital Q_l-subalgebra of End_{Q_l}(V).
(ii) (F^j)^dagger = c^j F^{-j} for every j in Z (j >= 0 by anti-multiplicativity on powers of F, j < 0 from (F^{-1})^dagger = c^{-1} F, which lemma_69(1) derives using only anti-multiplicativity and T^dagger = c T^{-1}).
(iii) dagger(A) subset A, and sigma := dagger|_A is a Q_l-algebra ANTI-INVOLUTION of A: it is Q_l-linear, reverses products, and sigma^2 = id_A because sigma^2 is a Q_l-algebra endomorphism of A = Q_l[F] fixing the generator F: sigma^2(F) = (c F^{-1})^dagger = c c^{-1} F = F.
(iv) Under the evaluation epimorphism Q_l[t^{+-1}] ->> A, sigma is induced by t |-> c t^{-1}: (sum_j p_j F^j)^dagger = sum_j p_j c^j F^{-j}.
We stress, following the warning in lemma_69(0), that dagger need not be an involution on all of End(V) for a non-symmetric pairing; nothing in Parts B-D requires that, since lemma_69(1) proves the involution property on A itself.

PART D. (Pos) => (GC) => THE CONJECTURE.

D.1 Clause (b) of (Pos), applied to this very m, Y, d, n, to V = H^n(+) H^{2d-n}, to F, to the pairing <, > of B.1, to dagger, and to A = Q_l[F], says exactly that the bilinear form B(a, b) := Tr_V(a b^dagger) on A satisfies B(a, a) = Tr_V(a a^dagger) != 0 for every non-zero a in A, i.e. that B is anisotropic on A. (By A.5 this assertion does not depend on the choice of e.)

D.2 Apply lemma_65 to the non-zero finite-dimensional Q_l-space V, the commutative finite-dimensional unital Q_l-subalgebra A of End_{Q_l}(V), the Q_l-linear anti-involution dagger|_A (C.1(iii)), and the anisotropy of the trace form (D.1). Its conclusion: A has no non-zero nilpotent element, and for every T in A the minimal polynomial mu_T over Q_l is squarefree and T is semisimple on V. Taking T = F, we obtain: F is semisimple on V.

D.3 The operator F on V is the direct-sum operator F|_{V1} (+) F|_{V2} for the decomposition V = V1 (+) V2, which is F-stable in each summand by definition of the cohomological Frobenius action. By lemma_9 (the direct sum is semisimple if and only if each summand operator is), F|_{V1} is semisimple on V1; the same conclusion is the 'only if' direction of lemma_35(ii) applied to the F-stable direct summand V1 of V. Since V1 = H^n_et(Ybar, Q_l) and F is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^m}, this is precisely the semisimplicity statement required of (m, Y, n).

D.4 Since (m, Y, n) were arbitrary (with pure dimensionality automatic by A.1 and the case V1 = 0 trivial by A.4), we have proved (GC): for every m >= 1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected Y over F_{q^m}, arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^m} acts semisimply on H^n_et(Ybar, Q_l) for every n >= 0. This is the first claim of the lemma.

D.5 Finally, lemma_59 states that (GC) implies the conjecture in full: for every smooth projective variety X over F_q (not assumed connected or equidimensional) and every i >= 0, geometric Frobenius acts semisimply on H^i_et(X_{overline(F_q)}, Q_l), and the induced action on H^i_et(X_{overline(F_q)}, Q_l) tensor_{Q_l} Q_l_bar is diagonalisable. Hence (Pos) implies the conjecture.

PART E. REMARK R1: SEMISIMPLICITY IS EQUIVALENT TO NONDEGENERACY OF B, NOT TO ANISOTROPY.

E.1 (Nondegeneracy <=> A reduced.) Under clause (a) alone, Parts B and C provide the Q_l-linear anti-involution dagger|_A of A. lemma_66 then gives Rad(B) = Nil(A) for B(a, b) := Tr_V(a b^dagger). Hence B is nondegenerate if and only if Nil(A) = 0, i.e. if and only if A is reduced.

E.2 (A reduced <=> mu_F squarefree.) The evaluation map Q_l[t] ->> A, P |-> P(F), has kernel (mu_F): mu_F(F) = 0 gives (mu_F) subset ker; conversely if P(F) = 0, divide P = S mu_F + R with deg R < deg mu_F; then R(F) = 0, and minimality of the degree of mu_F forces R = 0, so mu_F | P. Thus A is Q_l-isomorphic to Q_l[t]/(mu_F); in particular dim A = deg mu_F = r and 1, F, ..., F^{r-1} is a Q_l-basis of A (as in lemma_68(i)). Write mu_F = prod_i f_i^{e_i} with the f_i distinct monic irreducibles in Q_l[t]. If some e_i >= 2, put h := mu_F / f_i: then mu_F does not divide h, so h is non-zero in Q_l[t]/(mu_F), while every irreducible factor of h occurs with exponent at least the corresponding e_i (for f_i the exponent is 2(e_i - 1) >= e_i since e_i >= 2; for f_j, j != i, it is 2 e_j >= e_j), so mu_F | h^2 and h is a non-zero nilpotent: the quotient is not reduced. Conversely, if every e_i = 1, the Chinese remainder theorem for the pairwise coprime ideals (f_i) gives Q_l[t]/(mu_F) ~-> prod_i Q_l[t]/(f_i), a product of fields, hence reduced.

E.3 (mu_F squarefree <=> F semisimple.) This is lemma_60(ii), applicable since V is non-zero finite-dimensional over Q_l and F in GL(V); Q_l has characteristic 0, so squarefreeness over Q_l is the exact content of diagonalisability after scalar extension.

E.4 Chaining E.1-3: under clause (a) alone,
    F semisimple on V  <=>  mu_F squarefree  <=>  A reduced  <=>  B nondegenerate on A.
Moreover anisotropy implies nondegeneracy: if a lies in Rad(B) then B(a, a) = 0, so anisotropy forces a = 0. Thus (b) => semisimplicity (Part D) => nondegeneracy of B, and the converse fails (Part G). In particular, under (a) alone the semisimplicity supplied by (GC) yields only NONDEGENERACY of B, never the strictly stronger anisotropy demanded by clause (b). This is the same distinction recorded in the caution of lemma_74(4)(b) -- nondegeneracy of the *-trace form is equivalent to (GC), anisotropy is strictly stronger and is not equivalent to it -- and in the explicit non-degenerate-but-isotropic example contained in the statement of lemma_66.

PART F. REMARK R2: POSITIVITY ONLY ON THE REAL-COEFFICIENT PART, AND ONLY ASSUMING SEMISIMPLICITY.

F.1 Fix an embedding iota: Q_l_bar -> C and assume the eigenvalue condition iota(alpha) * conj(iota(alpha)) = iota(c) for every eigenvalue alpha of F on V. Let alpha_1, ..., alpha_N in Q_l_bar^* be the eigenvalues of F counted with algebraic multiplicity; they are non-zero since prod_i alpha_i = +-det(F) != 0. By lemma_69(2), for P = sum_j p_j t^j in Q_l[t^{+-1}] the eigenvalues of P(F) on V_{Q_l_bar}, with multiplicity, are P(alpha_1), ..., P(alpha_N); by lemma_69(3) applied to T^dagger = c T^{-1}, the multisets {alpha_i} and {c/alpha_i} coincide; this is the content of lemma_69(4)'s hypotheses.

F.2 Now assume in addition that F is semisimple on V, and take a = P(F) with P = sum_j p_j t^j and iota(p_j) in R for every j. By C.1(iv), a^dagger = Q(F) with Q(t) := sum_j p_j c^j t^{-j}. Both a and a^dagger are Laurent polynomials in F, so they preserve each eigenspace of F on V_{Q_l_bar} and act on it by scalars. Extending iota to kappa on the field generated over Q_l by the alpha_i and the p_j, and using the eigenvalue condition in the form kappa(c) kappa(alpha_i)^{-1} = conj(kappa(alpha_i)) together with iota(p_j) = conj(iota(p_j)):
    kappa(Q(alpha_i)) = sum_j iota(p_j) kappa(c)^j kappa(alpha_i)^{-j} = sum_j iota(p_j) conj(kappa(alpha_i))^j = conj(sum_j iota(p_j) kappa(alpha_i)^j) = conj(kappa(P(alpha_i))).
Hence a a^dagger acts on the alpha_i-eigenspace by kappa(P(alpha_i)) conj(kappa(P(alpha_i))) = |kappa(P(alpha_i))|^2 >= 0, and summing over i with multiplicity,
    iota(Tr_V(a a^dagger)) = sum_{i=1}^{N} |kappa(P(alpha_i))|^2.
If a != 0 then some P(alpha_i) != 0: otherwise all eigenvalues of a = P(F) vanish, and since F is semisimple a is semisimple with only the eigenvalue 0, hence a = 0, contradiction. So the sum is strictly positive. This is exactly the positivity claimed in R2, including the fact that the eigenvalues of a a^dagger are |P(alpha_i)|^2.

F.3 Why F.2 does not give clause (b). (i) An embedding Q_l -> C need not have real image. For instance, if l = 1 (mod 4) then Q_l contains i with i^2 = -1: F_l^* is cyclic of order l - 1 divisible by 4, so x^2 + 1 has a root in F_l^*, its derivative 2x is non-zero there because l is odd, and Hensel lifting in Z_l gives i. For such i, iota(i) = +-sqrt(-1) is not real. The subset {P(F) : iota(p_j) in R for all j} of A is therefore in general a proper subset, not even a Q_l-subspace, so F.2 does not cover all a in A. (ii) F.2 takes semisimplicity of F as a hypothesis, so it cannot be used to establish it. Conclusion: (a) plus the eigenvalue condition yields positivity of Tr_V(a a^dagger) only on the real-coefficient part of A, and clause (b) remains an extra arithmetic input. (The eigenvalue condition itself is the content of Weil I purity in the middle degree n = d, where it is automatic once purity is known; we do not use it in Part D.)

PART G. REMARK R3: EXPLICIT COUNTEREXAMPLE SHOWING (b) IS GENUINELY STRONGER.

G.1 Setup. Take a prime l = 1 (mod 4) and i in Q_l^* with i^2 = -1 (existence justified in F.3(i)). Let c := 4 in Q_l^*, let V := Q_l e_1 (+) Q_l e_2, let F := diag(2i, -2i) (F e_1 = 2i e_1, F e_2 = -2i e_2), and let <x, y> := x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1 for x = x_1 e_1 + x_2 e_2, y = y_1 e_1 + y_2 e_2.

G.2 <, > is perfect: its Gram matrix in the basis (e_1, e_2) is G = [[0, 1], [1, 0]], with det G = -1 != 0.

G.3 The formal content of clause (a) holds with this c. F x = (2i x_1, -2i x_2) and F y = (2i y_1, -2i y_2), so
    <F x, F y> = (2i x_1)(-2i y_2) + (-2i x_2)(2i y_1) = -4 i^2 (x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1) = 4 <x, y> = c <x, y>,
using i^2 = -1. (Here the pairing is symmetric, so dagger is an honest involution on all of End(V); the example does not exploit any asymmetry of the pairing.)

G.4 The eigenvalue condition of R2 holds. The eigenvalues are alpha_1 = 2i, alpha_2 = -2i. For an embedding iota: Q_l_bar -> C with iota(i)^2 = -1, iota(alpha_1) conj(iota(alpha_1)) = |2 iota(i)|^2 = 4 = iota(c), and the same computation gives iota(alpha_2) conj(iota(alpha_2)) = 4 = iota(c).

G.5 F is semisimple: it is diagonal in the basis (e_1, e_2). Its minimal polynomial is t^2 + 4 = (t - 2i)(t + 2i), which is squarefree, in agreement with R1/E.3.

G.6 Computation of A. F^2 = diag((2i)^2, (-2i)^2) = diag(-4, -4) = -4 id, so every polynomial in F is diagonal: Q_l[F] subset {diag(x, y) : x, y in Q_l}. Conversely (2i)^{-1} F = diag(1, -1) lies in A because 2i in Q_l^*, and for arbitrary x, y in Q_l,
    diag(x, y) = ((x + y)/2) id + ((x - y)/2) diag(1, -1) in A,
since l is odd so 2 in Q_l^*. Hence A = Q_l[F] = {diag(x, y)} ~ Q_l x Q_l (consistent with E.2: deg mu_F = 2 = dim A).

G.7 Computation of the adjoint on A. For a = diag(x, y) and b = diag(x', y') and u, v in V,
    <a u, v> = (x u_1) v_2 + (y u_2) v_1,     <u, b v> = u_1 (y' v_2) + u_2 (x' v_1).
Equality for all u, v forces x' = y and y' = x, i.e. diag(x, y)^dagger = diag(y, x). Consistency check with B.4: F^dagger = diag(-2i, 2i), while c F^{-1} = 4 diag(1/(2i), -1/(2i)) = 4 diag(-i/2, i/2) = diag(-2i, 2i); equal, as required.

G.8 Failure of clause (b). Take a := diag(1, 0) in A, which is non-zero. Then a^dagger = diag(0, 1) and a a^dagger = diag(1*0, 0*1) = 0, so Tr_V(a a^dagger) = 0. Thus a |-> Tr_V(a a^dagger) is NOT anisotropic on A: clause (b) fails, even though the formal content of (a) holds (G.3), the eigenvalue condition holds (G.4), and F is semisimple (G.5). This shows that the equivalence 'clause (b) <=> semisimplicity' is false; what holds is the nondegeneracy equivalence of R1, and indeed B is nondegenerate here, as E.1 predicts from A_red = A ~ Q_l x Q_l being reduced: explicitly B(diag(x, y), diag(u, v)) = Tr_V(diag(x, y) diag(v, u)) = x v + y u, whose matrix in the basis diag(1,0), diag(0,1) is [[0, 1], [1, 0]], invertible (this is exactly the example quoted inside lemma_66).

G.9 Mechanism, via lemma_72. A = A_red ~ Q_l x Q_l is a product of two simple factors with primitive idempotents e_1 = diag(1, 0) and e_2 = diag(0, 1). The anti-involution sigma = dagger|_A (an automorphism, A being commutative), which by C.1(iv) is induced on Q_l[t^{+-1}] by t |-> c t^{-1}, sends e_1 to e_1^dagger = diag(0, 1) = e_2 != e_1: it interchanges the two simple factors. lemma_72 then forces B to be isotropic; concretely e_1 e_1^dagger = e_1 e_2 = 0 maps to e_1 sigma(e_1) = 0 in A_red, is nilpotent, and therefore has trace zero, exactly as in G.8. In general, the eigenvalue condition pairs each eigenvalue alpha with c/alpha, and sigma acts on A_red = prod_i Q_l[t]/(f_i) as the permutation of the factors induced by t |-> c t^{-1}; whenever no irreducible factor f_i of mu_F is fixed by that involution, anisotropy of B is impossible. In the present example the two factors correspond to the roots 2i and -2i, and 4/(2i) = 2/i = -2i, so the involution swaps them.

G.10 Conclusion of the comparison. (R1) Under (a) alone, semisimplicity of F on V is equivalent to NONDEGENERACY of B(a, b) = Tr_V(a b^dagger) on A = Q_l[F], via Rad(B) = Nil(A) (lemma_66), A ~ Q_l[t]/(mu_F), reducedness equivalent to squarefreeness of mu_F, and lemma_60(ii); hence clause (b), which demands the strictly stronger anisotropy, is not equivalent to semisimplicity. (R2) Under (a) plus the eigenvalue condition iota(alpha) conj(iota(alpha)) = iota(c), lemma_69(4) gives positivity iota(Tr_V(a a^dagger)) = sum_i |iota(P(alpha_i))|^2 > 0 only for those a = P(F) whose coefficients are real under iota, and only after assuming semisimplicity; since an embedding Q_l -> C need not have real image, this is not clause (b). (R3) The example of G.1-G.9 satisfies the formal content of (a), the eigenvalue condition, and semisimplicity, yet violates (b), with the mechanism explained by lemma_72. Therefore the only genuinely missing arithmetic input in Part D is the anisotropy statement (b) -- a positivity statement of Standard-Conjectures-D type -- which is strictly stronger than the nondegeneracy condition that is equivalent to (GC) (cf. lemma_74). No external theorem is cited by name anywhere above: (a) is Poincare duality for smooth projective varieties and (b) is a positivity statement, and neither is available here; Parts A-D prove (Pos) => (GC) => the conjecture from the cited lemmas alone.

lemma_76.proof:
We write k := Q_ell, K := kbar = Qbar_ell, R := k[t^{+-1}] = k[t^{\pm 1}]. V is a nonzero finite-dimensional k-vector space, T in GL(V), and V is an R-module via t.v := T(v) (this is well defined because T is invertible). Facts from lemma_60 that we use but do NOT reprove: (a) R is a principal ideal domain; (b) for an operator on a finite-dimensional k-space, semisimplicity is equivalent to squarefreeness of the minimal polynomial (lemma_60(ii)); (c) T is semisimple on V if and only if it is semisimple on each primary piece V[f^{\infty}] (lemma_60(v)); (d) V[f^{\infty}] := \cup_{N>=1} ker f(T)^N. Lemmas 68 and 74 are not used anywhere. Linear-algebra facts not in lemma_60 (Cayley--Hamilton, Bezout, primary decomposition, Jordan form for a nilpotent operator, flatness of field extensions) are proved inline below.

=== 0. PRELIMINARIES ===

0.1 (The primes of R and the quotients R/(f^2).) The units of R are the c.t^n with c in k^*, n in Z. Let f in k[t] be monic irreducible, f != t. Then f is irreducible in R: if f = ab in R, write a = t^{-m}a_0, b = t^{-n}b_0 with a_0,b_0 in k[t]; then a_0 b_0 = t^{m+n} f in k[t]; since f != t is prime in the UFD k[t] and f | a_0b_0, say a_0 = f a_1; then a_1 b_0 = t^{m+n}, so a_1 = c t^{m'} is a monomial, hence a = c t^{m'-m} is a unit of R. Thus (f) is a maximal (prime) ideal of R, and R/(f) is a field of k-dimension deg f. Since f != t and f is irreducible, f(0) != 0, so gcd(t, f^2) = 1 in k[t]; by Bezout t is invertible in k[t]/(f^2), hence localisation at t gives an isomorphism of k[t]-modules k[t]/(f^2) ->~ R/(f^2). Consequently R/(f^2) != 0, dim_k R/(f^2) = 2 deg f, and its ideals are exactly (f^i)/(f^2), i = 0,1,2 (ideals of R/(f^2) correspond to ideals (h) of R with (f^2) subset (h), i.e. to h | f^2 in k[t] up to units, i.e. h in {1, f, f^2}). EDGE CASE, recorded explicitly: for f = t one has R/(t^2) = 0 because t is a unit of R. Hence in part (ii) the assertion is read (as it must be) over monic irreducibles f != t, equivalently over the f that can divide chi_T; for such f the module R/(f^2) is nonzero, so "no R-submodule isomorphic to R/(f^2)" is the same as "no nonzero cyclic R-submodule with annihilator exactly (f^2)". Also, since T in GL(V), 0 is not an eigenvalue, so t never divides chi_T.

0.2 (Cayley--Hamilton and the relation of mu_T and chi_T.) Cayley--Hamilton holds: chi_T(T) = 0. (Proof: for A the matrix of T, (tI - A) adj(tI - A) = det(tI - A) I = chi_T(t) I in Mat_n(k[t]); substituting t = A on the left kills the first factor, giving 0 = chi_T(A), i.e. chi_T(T) = 0.) Hence mu_T | chi_T. Conversely, if p in k[t] is monic irreducible with p | chi_T, choose a root alpha in K of p; alpha is a root of chi_{T_K} = chi_T (characteristic polynomial is unchanged by base change), so alpha is an eigenvalue of T_K with eigenvector 0 != v in V tensor K; from mu_T(T_K) = 0 we get 0 = mu_T(alpha) v, so mu_T(alpha) = 0, and since p is the minimal polynomial of alpha over k, p | mu_T. Thus: p | chi_T  <=>  p | mu_T, for monic irreducible p. In particular the irreducible factors of chi_T are exactly those of mu_T.

0.3 (Primary decomposition; the pieces are the ker f(T)^{e_f}.) Write chi_T = prod_{i=1}^{u} f_i^{e_i} with the f_i distinct monic irreducibles (necessarily != t by 0.1) and e_i = v_{f_i}(chi_T) >= 1. For each i put F_i := chi_T / f_i^{e_i}; then gcd(F_1,...,F_u) = 1, so by Bezout there are c_i in k[t] with sum_i c_i F_i = 1. Set eps_i := c_i(T) F_i(T) in End_k(V). Then: (i) sum_i eps_i = id_V; (ii) eps_i eps_j = 0 for i != j, because F_i F_j = chi_T . (chi_T/(f_i^{e_i} f_j^{e_j})) is divisible by chi_T and chi_T(T) = 0; (iii) eps_i^2 = eps_i, by (i) and (ii). Hence V = (+)_i im eps_i. We identify im eps_i = ker f_i(T)^{e_i}: if v = eps_i v then f_i(T)^{e_i} v = c_i(T) chi_T(T) v = 0; conversely if f_i(T)^{e_i} v = 0 then for j != i, F_j = f_i^{e_i} . prod_{m != i,j} f_m^{e_m}, so eps_j v = 0, hence v = eps_i v in im eps_i. Finally V[f_i^{\infty}] = ker f_i(T)^{e_i}: the inclusion "supset" is the definition of the union; for "subset", if h(T)^N v = 0 with h := f_i, write v = sum_j eps_j v; for j != i, eps_j v lies in ker f_j(T)^{e_j} cap ker f_i(T)^N, and since f_i^N and f_j^{e_j} are coprime, Bezout gives id = A(T) f_i(T)^N + B(T) f_j(T)^{e_j} on that intersection, so eps_j v = 0 and v = eps_i v in ker f_i(T)^{e_i}. Each piece W_i := V[f_i^{\infty}] is T-stable (f_i(T)^N commutes with T) and T-invertible on it, hence an R-submodule; and W_i != 0 since e_i >= 1 will force dim W_i = e_i deg f_i >= 1 (0.4). All other irreducibles g have V[g^{\infty}] = 0: g not dividing chi_T means g not dividing mu_T, so g(T) is invertible (Bezout with mu_T) and ker g(T)^N = 0.

0.4 (dim_k V[f^{\infty}] = e_f deg f = m_f, and the root-multiplicity formula.) Restricting to W_i, mu_{T|W_i} | f_i^{e_i}, so by 0.2 applied to T|_{W_i} the only possible irreducible factor of chi_{T|W_i} is f_i; write chi_{T|W_i} = f_i^{n_i} with n_i >= 0 and dim_k W_i = deg chi_{T|W_i} = n_i deg f_i. Since V = (+)_i W_i as T-stable sum, chi_T = prod_i chi_{T|W_i} = prod_i f_i^{n_i}; uniqueness of factorisation in k[t] gives n_i = e_i. Therefore dim_k V[f_i^{\infty}] = e_i deg f_i =: m_{f_i}, which is the "total multiplicity" of the statement. Moreover, over K of characteristic 0 the polynomial f_i is separable, so f_i = prod_{j=1}^{deg f_i} (t - alpha_{ij}) with the alpha_{ij} distinct, and chi_{T_K} = chi_T = prod_i prod_j (t - alpha_{ij})^{e_i}; the remaining factors are nonzero at alpha_{ij}. Hence mult_{alpha_{ij}}(chi_{T_K}) = e_i for every j, and m_{f_i} = e_i deg f_i = sum_{alpha: f_i(alpha)=0} mult_alpha(chi_{T_K}), exactly as claimed in the statement.

0.5 (Semisimplicity on one primary piece.) For f | chi_T with piece W := V[f^{\infty}]: T|_W is semisimple  <=>  f(T)|_W = 0. Indeed mu_{T|W} | f^{e_f}. If f(T)|_W = 0 then mu_{T|W} | f, which is squarefree (irreducible, char 0), so T|_W is semisimple by lemma_60(ii). Conversely, if T|_W is semisimple, lemma_60(ii) says mu_{T|W} is squarefree; the squarefree divisors of f^{e_f} are 1 and f; mu_{T|W} = 1 would force W = 0, impossible by 0.4; hence mu_{T|W} = f and f(T)|_W = 0. (The same argument applies over any field of characteristic 0, in particular over K, by lemma_64(iii), which also gives that semisimplicity of an operator is unchanged by extending the ground field.)

0.6 (Base change of the kernels.) For every m >= 1, tensoring the exact sequence 0 -> V[f^m] -> V -> V (last map f(T)^m) with the flat k-module K gives V[f^m] tensor K = ker(f(T_K)^m on V_K); hence dim_k V[f^m] = dim_K V_K[f^m]. Likewise, on the piece W = V[f^{\infty}], the operator f(T)|_W is zero iff f(T_K)|_{W_K} is zero, since a k-linear map is zero iff its scalar extension is.

=== 1. PROOF OF (i) ===

Fix a monic irreducible f | chi_T; write e := e_f, W := V[f^{\infty}] = ker f(T)^e, m_f := e deg f = dim_k W (0.3, 0.4). Let alpha_1,...,alpha_r (r = deg f) be the distinct roots of f in K, and put U_j := ker(T_K - alpha_j)^e on W_K; by the argument of 0.3 applied over K to the split polynomial f (or by CRT, K[t]/(f^e) = prod_j K[t]/((t-alpha_j)^e)), W_K = (+)_j U_j, and these are the f-primary pieces of T_K.

Step 1 (reduction to the piece). V[f] = ker f(T) subset ker f(T)^e = W, so V[f] = ker(f(T)|_W).
Step 2 (compute the dimension). By 0.6, dim_k V[f] = dim_K ker(f(T_K)|_{W_K}) = sum_j dim_K ker(f(T_K)|_{U_j}). On U_j we have f(t) = (t - alpha_j) u_j(t) with u_j := prod_{i != j}(t - alpha_i); u_j and (t - alpha_j)^e are coprime, so u_j(T_K) is invertible on U_j (Bezout). Hence ker(f(T_K)|_{U_j}) = ker(N_j) where N_j := (T_K - alpha_j)|_{U_j} (a nilpotent operator). Therefore
   dim_k V[f] = sum_{j=1}^{r} dim_K ker N_j.
Step 3 (the inequality). Since ker N_j subset U_j, dim_k V[f] <= sum_j dim_K U_j = dim_K W_K = dim_k W = m_f. This proves the inequality. It is an equality iff dim ker N_j = dim U_j for every j, i.e. iff N_j = 0 for every j.
Step 4 (the equality criterion). N_j = 0 for all j  <=>  f(T_K)|_{W_K} = 0  <=>  f(T)|_W = 0 (0.6)  <=>  T|_W semisimple (0.5). Thus dim_k V[f] = m_f if and only if T is semisimple on the f-primary piece V[f^{\infty}].
Step 5 (global statement). By lemma_60(v), T is semisimple on V iff T is semisimple on V[f^{\infty}] for every f | chi_T; combined with Step 4 this gives: T semisimple on V  <=>  dim_k V[f] = m_f for every f | chi_T.
Step 6 (the parenthetical normalisation check). For deg f = 1, f = t - alpha, we have m_f = e_f = mult_alpha(chi_T) and dim_k V[f] = dim ker(T - alpha) = number of Jordan blocks of T_K at alpha; so (i) reads "number of blocks at alpha <= multiplicity of alpha, with equality iff T is semisimple at alpha", the classical statement, and over K all irreducibles are linear so both readings of m_f agree. With the exponent reading the inequality is false in general: take V = k[t]/(f) with f monic irreducible of degree 2 and T = multiplication by t. Then chi_T = f (companion matrix), so e_f = 1 but m_f = 1.2 = 2 = dim_k V; f(T) = 0, so V[f] = V has dimension 2, and indeed 2 = m_f with equality, correctly reflecting that T is semisimple (mu_T = f is squarefree), whereas the exponent reading would assert 2 <= 1. This confirms that the total-multiplicity normalisation m_f = e_f deg f = dim V[f^{\infty}] used above and in (v) is the correct one.

=== 2. PROOF OF (ii) ===

(=>) Assume T semisimple and let f be monic irreducible, f != t. Suppose W' subset V is an R-submodule with W' isomorphic to R/(f^2). Then f(T)^2 kills W' (as f^2 = 0 in R/(f^2)), but f(T) does not kill W': in R/(f^2) the element f bar = f.1 bar is nonzero, so the image x of 1 bar satisfies f(T)x != 0. Now decompose with respect to 0.3: for w in W', w = sum_i w_i with w_i in W_i := V[f_i^{\infty}]. Since W' is R-stable, f(T)^2 w_i = 0 for each i. For i with f_i != f, f(T) is invertible on W_i: f_i and f^{e} are coprime, so Bezout gives A f + B f_i^{e} = 1 and A(T) f(T) = id on W_i = ker f_i(T)^{e}; hence w_i = 0. Thus W' subset W_f, on which f(T) = 0 by 0.5 (T semisimple implies f(T)|_{W_f} = 0), contradicting f(T)x != 0. Hence no such W' exists.
(<=) Conversely, suppose T is not semisimple. By lemma_60(v) some piece W := V[f^{\infty}] (f | chi_T, so f != t) carries a non-semisimple T|_W, hence f(T)|_W != 0 by 0.5. The set { m >= 1 : f(T)^m|_W != 0 } is nonempty (contains 1) and bounded above by e - 1 (f(T)^e = 0 on W), so it has a maximum m. Choose v in W with f(T)^m v != 0 and set x := f(T)^{m-1} v (nonzero, since f(T)x != 0). Then f(T)^2 x = f(T)^{m+1} v = 0 by maximality of m, and f(T)x != 0. Consider the R-linear map phi: R -> V, h |-> h(T)x. Its kernel contains (f^2), and by 0.1 the only ideals of R containing (f^2) are (f^2), (f), R; the kernel is not R (x != 0) and not (f) (f(T)x != 0). So ker phi = (f^2) and R.x = im phi is an R-submodule of V isomorphic to R/(f^2) (nonzero). This is the contrapositive of (ii).

=== 3. PROOF OF (iii) ===

(<=) Suppose there exist a monic irreducible f and x, y in V with y != 0, f(T)y = 0, f(T)x = y. First, f != t: f = t would give y = T x ... more precisely f(T) = T would give y = T x and 0 = f(T) y = T y, impossible since T is invertible and y != 0. Second, the exhibited f divides chi_T: the annihilator of y is a nonzero ideal (h) of R with (f) subset (h) != R (y != 0), so h | f and h nonunit, hence h = f up to a unit, i.e. f | mu_T (as mu_T generates the annihilator of V and is divisible by the annihilator of each element); then f | chi_T by 0.2. Third, the map R -> V, h |-> h(T)x, has kernel containing (f^2) (f(T)^2 x = f(T) y = 0) and, as in 0.1/2, not equal to (f) (f(T)x = y != 0) nor to R (x != 0, else y = 0); hence kernel = (f^2), and R.x is an R-submodule isomorphic to R/(f^2). By (ii), T is not semisimple. Note also x in ker f(T)^2 subset V[f^{\infty}] and y in ker f(T) subset V[f^{\infty}], so the chain lies inside one f-primary piece, and R.x is a T-stable (indeed Frobenius-stable) subspace containing the two-step chain k.y subset k.x + k.y + ...
(=>) If T is not semisimple, the construction in (<=) of section 2 produces x with f(T)^2 x = 0 and f(T)x != 0 for some f | chi_T; setting y := f(T)x gives y != 0, f(T)y = f(T)^2 x = 0, f(T)x = y, with x, y in V[f^{\infty}].

=== 4. PROOF OF (iv): BLOCK COUNT ===

4.1 A nilpotent counting lemma (proved from scratch; this also fixes the directness argument that a naive Jordan-decomposition proof needs). Let N be nilpotent on a finite-dimensional vector space U over a field. Then:
(a) dim ker N^2 - dim ker N = dim(ker N cap im N). Proof: N maps ker N^2 into ker N; it is surjective onto ker N cap im N (if w in ker N cap im N, w = Nv, then N^2 v = Nw = 0, so v in ker N^2); its kernel is ker N. Hence 0 -> ker N -> ker N^2 -> ker N cap im N -> 0 is exact.
(b) U decomposes as a direct sum of N-cyclic subspaces: U = (oplus_{j=1}^{s} V_j) (+) Z with V_j = span(v_j, N v_j, ..., N^{b_j} v_j), N^{b_j+1} v_j = 0, N^{b_j} v_j != 0 (so V_j has basis N^i v_j, 0 <= i <= b_j, and dim V_j = b_j + 1), and Z a subspace of ker N; the total number of summands equals dim ker N. Proof by induction on dim U. If N = 0 take Z = U. Otherwise dim im N < dim U, so by induction im N = (+)_j C_j with C_j cyclic for N|_{im N} generated by w_j, N^{b_j} w_j = 0, N^{b_j - 1} w_j != 0, and the number s of summands equals dim ker(N|_{im N}) = dim(ker N cap im N). Lift w_j to v_j in U with N v_j = w_j; then N^{b_j+1} v_j = N^{b_j} w_j = 0 and N^{b_j} v_j = N^{b_j-1} w_j != 0, so V_j := sum_{i=0}^{b_j} k N^i v_j has dimension b_j+1 (independence: sum_{i=0}^{b_j} c_i N^i v_j = 0, apply N to get sum_{i=0}^{b_j-1} c_i N^{i+1} v_j = 0 in C_j where N^{i+1}v_j = N^i w_j form a basis, giving c_0 = ... = c_{b_j-1} = 0, then c_{b_j} = 0), N V_j = C_j, and V_j cap ker N = k.N^{b_j} v_j = k.N^{b_j-1} w_j (dimension 1). DIRECTNESS of sum V_j: if sum c_j = 0 with c_j in V_j, applying N gives sum N c_j = 0 with N c_j in C_j, and the sum of the C_j is direct, so N c_j = 0 for all j, i.e. c_j in V_j cap ker N = k N^{b_j} v_j subset C_j; then sum c_j = 0 again by directness of the C_j gives c_j = 0 for all j. SPANNING: for u in U, Nu in im N = (+)_j C_j = (+)_j N V_j, so Nu = N(w) with w in sum V_j, hence u - w in ker N; thus U = sum V_j + ker N. Since (sum V_j) cap ker N = (+)_j (V_j cap ker N) (if sum c_j in ker N, apply N and use directness of the C_j as before), this intersection has dimension s = dim(ker N cap im N). Choose Z subset ker N with ker N = ((sum V_j) cap ker N) (+) Z; then dim Z = dim ker N - s and dim sum V_j = dim im N + s, so dim(sum V_j + ker N) = dim im N + dim ker N = dim U, confirming U = (oplus_j V_j) (+) Z, and the number of summands is s + dim Z = dim ker N.
(c) In any such decomposition the number of summands of dimension >= 2 equals dim(ker N cap im N) (each V_j contributes exactly the line V_j cap ker N cap im N, and Z contributes none), hence by (a) equals dim ker N^2 - dim ker N; in particular this number is an invariant of N. Over an algebraically closed field the decomposition in (b) is the Jordan decomposition: V_j is a Jordan block of size b_j + 1 at eigenvalue 0 and Z is a sum of 1x1 blocks, so (c) says: dim ker N^2 - dim ker N = number of Jordan blocks of size >= 2. More generally dim ker N^m = sum_j min(dim V_j, m), so the multiset of block sizes is determined by the numbers dim ker N^m, and the number of blocks of exact size r is 2 d_r - d_{r-1} - d_{r+1}, where d_m := dim ker N^m (d_0 = 0), because d_r - d_{r-1} = #{blocks of size >= r} (the sequence d_m is concave, so this number is nonnegative).

4.2 Application. Fix f | chi_T, e = e_f, W = V[f^{\infty}], roots alpha_1,...,alpha_r of f in K, U_j = ker(T_K - alpha_j)^e subset W_K as in section 1, N_j := (T_K - alpha_j)|_{U_j}. As in Step 2 of section 1, f(T_K)^m = N_j^m . u_j(T_K)^m on U_j with u_j(T_K) invertible, and f(T_K)^m is invertible on the other primary pieces of T_K, so V_K[f^m] = (+)_j ker N_j^m for every m >= 1. By 0.6, D_m := dim_k V[f^m] = dim_K V_K[f^m] = sum_j dim_K ker N_j^m. Hence, using 4.1(a) and 4.1(c):
   dim_k V[f^2] - dim_k V[f] = D_2 - D_1 = sum_j (dim_K ker N_j^2 - dim_K ker N_j) = sum_j dim_K(ker N_j cap im N_j) = (total number of Jordan blocks of T_K of size >= 2 belonging to the roots of f),
and similarly D_1 = sum_j dim ker N_j = total number of Jordan blocks of T_K belonging to the roots of f. This proves the displayed formula of (iv). (Over K, f splits into DISTINCT roots because char K = 0 and f is irreducible hence separable; that is exactly where characteristic 0 is used.)
Finally, V[f^2] = V[f]  <=>  D_2 = D_1  <=>  no N_j has a block of size >= 2  <=>  every N_j = 0  <=>  f(T_K)|_{W_K} = 0  <=>  f(T)|_W = 0 (0.6)  <=>  T|_W semisimple (0.5, and the same criterion over K, which is legitimate by lemma_64(iii)). This is the "in particular" of (iv), and it agrees with Step 4 of section 1.

=== 5. SUMMARY OF THE LINEAR-ALGEBRA EQUIVALENCES ===

For V != 0, T in GL(V), f | chi_T, and m_f := e_f deg f = dim V[f^{\infty}], the following are equivalent: (a) dim_k V[f] = m_f for every f | chi_T; (b) V has no R-submodule isomorphic to R/(f^2) for any monic irreducible f != t; (c) there are no f, x, y with y != 0, f(T)y = 0, f(T)x = y; (d) V[f^2] = V[f] for every f | chi_T; (e) T is semisimple on V. Indeed (a) <=> (e) is section 1 (Steps 4--5), (b) <=> (e) is section 2, (c) <=> (e) is section 3, (d) <=> (e) is 4.2 together with lemma_60(v). If V = 0, then chi_T = 1, there is no f | chi_T, (a) and (d) hold vacuously, (b) and (c) hold since V has no nonzero submodule and no nonzero y, and (e) holds trivially; so the equivalence remains true for V = 0 as well.

=== 6. PROOF OF (v): GEOMETRIC PACKAGING ===

Well-definedness of the geometric data. Let m >= 1, let Y be smooth projective geometrically connected over F_{q^m} (a proper variety over the prime power q^m), and put V := H^n_et(Y_{Fbar_q}, Q_ell). By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to K = Q_{ell,Y_{Fbar_q}} with its standard arithmetic Frobenius structure, V is finite-dimensional over Q_ell. By lemma_6a (applied with F_{q^m} in place of F_q) the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F_ar on V is a Q_ell-linear automorphism with inverse the geometric Frobenius; so T := F_ar lies in GL(V) and V is an R = Q_ell[t^{+-1}]-module via t.v := T(v), exactly as in the linear algebra above. (V may be 0 for some n, e.g. n > 2 dim Y; this case is handled by the last sentence of section 5.)

Statement (GC_2) is then: for every m >= 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected Y/F_{q^m}, and every n >= 0, with V and T as above, the equivalent conditions (a)--(d) of section 5 hold, where in (a) m_f is the TOTAL multiplicity v_f(chi_T) . deg f = dim V[f^{\infty}] (as proved in 0.4). The parenthetical requirement of the target is thus satisfied: with the exponent reading, a semisimple T whose chi_T has a nonlinear irreducible factor would fail (a) (section 1, Step 6 gives the model example), whereas with the total multiplicity (a) is equivalent to semisimplicity.

(GC_2) => (GC). By definition of (GC) in lemma_59, we must show that for every m >= 1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected Y over F_{q^m}, arithmetic Frobenius over F_{q^m} acts semisimply on H^n(Y_{Fbar_q}, Q_ell) for every n >= 0. This is exactly condition (e) of section 5, which is implied by (GC_2) via any of the readings (a)--(d).

(GC) => (GC_2). If T = F_ar is semisimple on V, then by section 5 the equivalent conditions (a), (b), (c), (d) all hold for that triple (m, Y, n). Since this is true for every triple, (GC_2) holds.

Hence (GC_2) <=> (GC). Finally, (GC_2) implies the conjecture: by the implication just proved, (GC_2) gives (GC), and lemma_59 states that (GC) implies the full conjecture, i.e. that for every smooth projective X/F_q (not assumed connected or equidimensional) and every i >= 0, geometric Frobenius acts semisimply on H^i_et(X_{Fbar_q}, Q_ell), equivalently acts diagonalizably after tensoring with Qbar_ell (the equivalence being also lemma_5/lemma_64(iii)).

Explicit geometric target. Unwinding (c) and (iv) for V = H^n(Y_{Fbar_q}, Q_ell) and T = F_ar: (GC_2) says precisely that THERE IS NO FROBENIUS-STABLE JORDAN BLOCK OF SIZE > 1 IN ANY PRIMARY PIECE OF ANY H^n. Concretely: for no m, Y, n, monic irreducible f | chi_{F_ar} do there exist x with F_ar-stable cyclic span Q_ell[F_ar].x on which f(F_ar) realises a non-split two-step chain 0 != y in ker f(F_ar) with y = f(F_ar)x (condition (c)); equivalently, for every f, the f-primary piece H^n[f^{\infty}] satisfies H^n[f^2] = H^n[f] (condition (d)), i.e. dim H^n[f^2] - dim H^n[f] = 0; and by (iv) this difference is exactly the total number of Jordan blocks of size >= 2 of F_ar (over Qbar_ell) belonging to the roots of f, so (GC_2) asserts that after extending scalars to Qbar_ell, every Jordan block of arithmetic Frobenius on every H^n has size 1, block by block, inside every primary piece. Equivalently by (i), the number of Jordan blocks of F_ar belonging to the roots of f, namely dim H^n[f], attains its maximal possible value m_f = v_f(chi_T) deg f = dim H^n[f^{\infty}] for every f.
